teile.einleitung: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is an important document of the United Nations. It was adopted on 10 December 1948 in Paris and describes in 30 articles the rights to which all people are entitled. Its first idea is that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
wichtigste: The UN General Assembly adopted the Declaration on 10 December 1948.
This happened in the Palais de Chaillot in Paris.
The Declaration has 30 articles.
The vote was 48 in favour, 0 against and 8 abstentions.
Eleanor Roosevelt led the commission that drew up the Declaration.
The Declaration is a resolution with no direct legal force.
Article 1 says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights.
Every year on 10 December Human Rights Day is celebrated.

abschnitte.text: After the **Second World War** and the Holocaust the states wanted to prevent such crimes from happening again. In 1945 they founded the **United Nations**, UN for short. They wanted to set down which rights every person has, no matter where he or she lives. So the Universal Declaration of Human Rights came into being.

The **UN Commission on Human Rights**, led by **Eleanor Roosevelt**, drew up the Declaration. She was the widow of the American president Franklin D. Roosevelt. The first draft was written by the Canadian jurist John Peters Humphrey. The Frenchman **René Cassin** played a major part, and the Chinese Peng Chun Chang brought in ideas from Confucianism.

On 10 December 1948 the **General Assembly** voted in the Palais de Chaillot in Paris. 48 states voted in favour, none against, and 8 abstained. Among the states that abstained were the Soviet Union, Saudi Arabia and South Africa. South Africa abstained partly because of its policy of racial segregation.

The Declaration has 30 **articles**. Article 1 says that all human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights. Article 3 guarantees the right to life, liberty and security of person. Further articles ban slavery and torture and name rights such as freedom of opinion, freedom of religion and the right to education.

The Declaration is a **resolution** with no direct legal force. All the same it has great influence, because many constitutions and treaties build on it. Binding, for example, are the European Convention on Human Rights of 1950 and later UN covenants. Anyone who sees their rights violated can turn in Europe to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg.

Switzerland only joined the UN in 2002, after a **popular vote**. In Geneva the **UN Human Rights Council** has its seat, where states discuss human rights. The Swiss Federal Constitution contains a catalogue of fundamental rights of its own. Many Swiss organisations campaign for human rights worldwide.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rights that every person has simply because he or she is a human being.
A decision that expresses an opinion but is not legally binding.
The assembly of all the member states of the UN.
Saying neither yes nor no in a vote.
The worth that every person has and that must be respected.

gewusst: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights is regarded as one of the most translated documents in the world, and it exists in over 500 languages.
René Cassin received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1968.
Eleanor Roosevelt called the Declaration a “Magna Carta for all mankind”.

teile.einleitung: The Arab Spring is the name for a wave of protests and uprisings in Arab countries from the end of 2010. Many people demanded more freedom, justice and an end to corruption and dictatorship. In some countries rulers fell, in others long wars followed.
wichtigste: The trigger was the self-immolation of the vegetable seller Mohamed Bouazizi on 17 December 2010 in Tunisia.
The Tunisian president Ben Ali fled abroad on 14 January 2011.
In Egypt President Hosni Mubarak resigned on 11 February 2011.
In Libya a UN resolution allowed a no-fly zone, and Gaddafi was killed in October 2011.
In Syria a long civil war developed.
In 2015 the Tunisian National Dialogue Quartet received the Nobel Peace Prize.
The results of the Arab Spring were very different.

abschnitte.text: On 17 December 2010 in the town of **Sidi Bouzid** the young vegetable seller **Mohamed Bouazizi** set himself on fire. He wanted to protest against the arbitrariness of the authorities, who had taken his goods from him. He died a few weeks later of his injuries. His act set off protests throughout Tunisia.

Thousands of people took to the streets against poverty, unemployment and **corruption**. After more than 23 years in power, President **Zine el-Abidine Ben Ali** fled to Saudi Arabia on 14 January 2011. Tunisia got a new constitution and free elections. In 2015 the Tunisian **National Dialogue Quartet** received the Nobel Peace Prize.

In Egypt too, hundreds of thousands gathered from January 2011 on **Tahrir Square** in Cairo. On 11 February 2011 President **Hosni Mubarak**, who had ruled for about 30 years, resigned. In 2012 Mohamed Morsi became the first freely elected president of Egypt. In 2013 the military removed him again.

In Libya the ruler **Muammar Gaddafi** took violent action against rebels. Resolution 1973 of the UN Security Council made a **no-fly zone** over Libya possible on 17 March 2011. Gaddafi was killed near Sirte on 20 October 2011. In **Syria** the government of Bashar al-Assad took harsh action against protests, which turned into a civil war, and Assad's rule only ended on 8 December 2024.

Many demonstrators were young people. They used **social media** such as Facebook and Twitter to arrange meetings and spread videos. In this way the whole world quickly learned what was happening. Some governments therefore tried to switch off the internet.

Hopes for democracy were only partly fulfilled. Tunisia long counted as a success story, but from 2021 democracy there was restricted again. In Libya, Syria and Yemen wars followed, and millions of people had to flee. In 2011 **Switzerland** froze assets of the overthrown rulers in Swiss bank accounts.

begriffe.erklaerung: Rule in which one person or group governs alone and without free elections.
When someone abuses power to enrich himself, for example through bribery.
An area over which certain aircraft are not allowed to fly.
A war between different groups inside a country.
A rapid, fundamental overthrow of the balance of power.

gewusst: The name “Arab Spring” was given to the events by Western media, echoing earlier freedom movements.
In Tunisia the events are also called the Jasmine Revolution, after the country's national flower.
Within a few weeks the protests spread from Tunisia as far as Bahrain and Yemen.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages the sickle was the most important tool for the grain harvest. With it farmers cut the ripe stalks in summer.
wichtigste: The sickle has a curved blade.
For mowing grass people used the large scythe with a long handle.
Cut grain was tied together into sheaves.
Grain was harvested in summer.
With the flail the grains were beaten out of the ears.
What was left was the straw.
Poor people were allowed to gather ears left lying after the harvest.

abschnitte.text: The **sickle** has a **curved blade** with a short handle. As early as the Stone Age people cut grain with sickle-like tools made of flint. In the Middle Ages the blades were made of **iron**. With one hand the farmer held a bunch of stalks firmly, and with the other he cut them off with the sickle.

Besides the sickle there was the **scythe**. It has a long blade and a **long handle**. With it people could work standing up. The scythe was used mainly for **mowing grass** for hay. For grain people used the sickle for a long time, because fewer grains fell out of the ears.

Grain ripened in **summer**. Then **the whole family** helped with the harvest, including children and old people. The cut stalks were tied into bundles, the **sheaves**. The sheaves were stood up in the field to dry and then brought into the barn. The work was hard and lasted from early until late.

Later the grains were beaten out of the ears. This is called **threshing**. For this people used the **flail**, a wooden staff with a movable striking piece. The grains were ground into flour. What was left was the **straw**. It was needed, for example, as bedding for the animals or for roofs.

After the harvest some ears always remained lying in the field. **Poor people** were allowed to gather them. This is called **gleaning**. In this way people without a field of their own also got some grain. This custom is already mentioned in the Bible.

gewusst: The moon in its thin form is often called a “crescent moon” (in German “Mondsichel”, moon sickle) because it looks like a sickle.
In many regions grain was still cut with the sickle until the 19th century.

t140ae7w.t: The Battle of Tours and Poitiers

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Tours and Poitiers took place in the year 732 in the Frankish Empire. The Frankish mayor of the palace Charles Martel defeated a Muslim army from al-Andalus there.
wichtigste: The battle took place in 732 between the cities of Tours and Poitiers.
Charles Martel led the army of the Franks.
The Muslim army came from al-Andalus, Muslim Spain.
Its leader Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi fell in the battle.
Duke Odo of Aquitaine had lost earlier and asked Charles for help.
The Chronicle of 754 calls the victors “Europenses”.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of the 8th century Muslim armies conquered large parts of Spain. This territory was called **al-Andalus**. From there armies also marched north into the Frankish Empire. In 732 the governor **Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi** led an army into Aquitaine in the south-west of France. Duke **Odo of Aquitaine** lost against him and asked the Frank **Charles Martel** for help.

The Muslim army marched further north in the direction of **Tours**. There stood the rich **church of Saint Martin**, one of the most important shrines of the Franks. It tempted with its treasures. Between **Tours and Poitiers** Charles Martel confronted them with his army. Where exactly the fighting took place is still not known.

The Franks withstood the attacks, and **Abd al-Rahman fell**. During the night the Muslim army withdrew. The **Chronicle of 754** for the first time calls the victors **“Europenses”**, that is, Europeans. In the past the battle was seen as the rescue of Europe. Today many historians see it more cautiously, as an important but not the only decisive victory. Charles Martel, however, gained a great deal of prestige from it.

gewusst: Charles Martel was the grandfather of Charlemagne.
The nickname “Martel” means “hammer”.

teile.einleitung: The Concordat of Worms is a treaty of 1122 between Emperor Henry V and Pope Callixtus II. It ended the long Investiture Controversy over who may install bishops in their office.
wichtigste: The concordat consists of two documents, the Heinricianum and the Calixtinum.
It distinguished between the spiritual office and the worldly property of a bishop.
Ring and staff as spiritual symbols remained reserved to the Church.
The king now only invested with the regalia, symbolised by the sceptre.
In the German part of the empire the investiture came before the consecration.
In Italy and Burgundy the investiture followed within six months after the consecration.
The First Lateran Council confirmed the agreement in 1123.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages bishops were not only clergy but also powerful lords of the land. Kings therefore liked to install them themselves. This installation is called **investiture**. The Church reformers under Pope Gregory VII no longer wanted to tolerate this. A quarrel between pope and emperor lasting decades followed, the **Investiture Controversy**. Famous is the journey of Henry IV to Canossa in 1077.

In 1122 Emperor **Henry V** and Pope **Callixtus II** came to an agreement in Worms. The treaty consists of two documents. The imperial one is called the **Heinricianum**, the papal one the **Calixtinum** after the pope. The emperor gave up installing bishops with **ring and staff**, the symbols of spiritual office. The election was to be **canonical and free**, that is, according to the rules of the Church.

The core of the concordat is a distinction. The **spiritualities**, that is, the spiritual office, were granted by the Church. The **temporalities** or **regalia**, that is, worldly rights and property, were granted by the king. As a sign of this the **sceptre** was used. This separation goes back to the reflections of scholars such as **Ivo of Chartres**.

In the **German part of the empire** the person elected first received the regalia and was consecrated afterwards. The king was allowed to be **present** at the election and, in a dispute, to step in for the more reasonable party. In this way he kept a lot of influence. In **Italy and Burgundy** the investiture came only after the consecration, within **six months**. There the king's influence was smaller. At that time the Kingdom of Burgundy also included a large part of present-day western Switzerland.

In 1123 the **First Lateran Council** in Rome confirmed the agreement. It was the first ecumenical council in the West. With that the settlement between pope and emperor was official. But the rivalry of the two powers had not entirely vanished. It shaped the Middle Ages for a long time to come.

gewusst: The word “concordat” means agreement and is still used today for treaties between states and the Catholic Church.
In Switzerland, too, there are concordats: that is what treaties between cantons are called.

teile.einleitung: Amerigo Vespucci was a merchant and seafarer from Florence. He recognised that the land in the west was not Asia but a new continent. That is why America bears his name today.
wichtigste: Amerigo Vespucci was born in Florence in Italy.
He first worked as a merchant.
He wrote that the new land was a “New World”.
The name America comes from his first name Amerigo.
In 1507 the name “America” appeared for the first time on a map of the world.
The mapmaker Martin Waldseemüller wrote it on the southern part.

abschnitte.text: Amerigo Vespucci was born in 1454 in **Florence** in **Italy**. He first worked as a **merchant** for the rich Medici family. Later he moved to **Seville** in Spain. There he helped to fit out ships for voyages of discovery. Soon he sailed across the Atlantic himself.

Around the year 1500 Vespucci took part in several voyages. They led to the coasts of **South America**, among others on behalf of Portugal. He sailed far south along the coast of present-day Brazil. On the way he observed the stars and tried to determine the position of places. How many voyages he made exactly is disputed among experts.

Columbus believed until his death that he had arrived in **Asia**. Many others believed that too. Vespucci, by contrast, wrote that the land in the west was a **“New World”**, that is, a **new continent**. His letters were printed and read all over Europe. So he became very well known.

The mapmaker **Martin Waldseemüller** worked in Alsace and Lorraine. He read Vespucci's accounts. In **1507** he wrote the name **“America”** on his **map of the world**. The name stood first on the southern part, that is, on **South America**, where Vespucci had sailed. **Amerigo** is his **first name**, Vespucci his family name. In this way Amerigo became the name of a whole double continent.

gewusst: Of Waldseemüller's great map of the world only a single printed copy survives, and it lies in Washington today.
Vespucci later became chief pilot of Spain and trained sailors.

teile.einleitung: The **University of Paris** came into being around the year 1200 and quickly became one of the most important universities in Europe. In the Middle Ages it was famous above all for theology. Part of it is known today as the Sorbonne.
wichtigste: The University of Paris came into being around 1200.
Theology held the highest rank there in the Middle Ages.
In 1231 Pope Gregory IX confirmed its rights with the bull “Parens scientiarum”.
The Sorbonne is named after Robert de Sorbon.
The basic course included the trivium: grammar, rhetoric and dialectic.

abschnitte.text: In Paris there were famous schools at the town's churches from early on. Around **1200** the university grew out of them. Masters, that is, teachers, taught here and joined together as a community. **Theology** held the highest rank among the subjects. Paris became the leading centre of theology in the West. Well-known scholars such as **Thomas Aquinas** taught there.

abschnitte.titel: The Magna Carta of the university
abschnitte.text: There were repeated quarrels between the university and the town. Once teachers and students went on strike for a long time and left Paris. In **1231** Pope **Gregory IX** confirmed the rights of the university with the bull **“Parens scientiarum”**. A bull is an important document of the pope. It guaranteed the university **self-government** and is regarded as its “Magna Carta”.

**Robert de Sorbon** was chaplain to King **Louis IX**. In **1257** he founded a **college** for poor students of theology. A college was a house where students lived and studied. It was called the **Sorbonne** after him. Later this name came to be used for the whole university. The university district is still called the **Latin Quarter** today, because Latin was spoken there.

First all students attended the **faculty of arts**. There they learned the **seven liberal arts**. The **trivium** covered the language subjects **grammar**, **rhetoric** and **dialectic**, that is, the art of argument. The **quadrivium** covered arithmetic, geometry, music and astronomy. Only after that came a higher subject such as theology, law or medicine.

gewusst: Teaching in the Middle Ages was in Latin, which is why students from all over Europe could study in Paris.
Today the old University of Paris is divided into several separate universities.

teile.einleitung: A quipu is a knotted cord of the Incas in South America. The Incas had no alphabetic script, so they recorded numbers and other information with knots on coloured strings.
wichtigste: “Quipu” means “knot” in the Quechua language.
The Incas had no writing with letters.
With quipus they counted and remembered numbers.
They counted in the decimal system, as we do today.
The strings were made of cotton or the wool of llamas and alpacas.
The colours of the strings also had a meaning.

abschnitte.text: The **Incas** had a large empire in the Andes but **no alphabetic script**. They recorded important things with **quipus**. The word comes from the **Quechua** language and simply means **“knot”**. A quipu consists of a main cord from which many other strings hang. Knots were tied in these strings.

With the knots the Incas mainly recorded **numbers**, for example how many llamas or sacks of maize there were. They counted in the **decimal system**, that is, with ones, tens, hundreds and so on. Each place had its own position on the string. The type of knot showed which digit was meant. In this way even large numbers could be written down exactly.

The strings were spun from **cotton** or from the wool of **llamas and alpacas**. They came in **different colours**. The colour probably showed what the record was about, for example maize or animals. Special experts could tie and read the quipus. Exactly how much information they hold has still not been fully researched.

gewusst: Today a few hundred quipus still exist in museums around the world.
A quipu could consist of hundreds of individual strings.

teile.einleitung: The **Bayeux Tapestry** is a strip of pictures almost 70 metres long from the Middle Ages. It tells how the Norman duke William conquered England in 1066. It is one of the most important picture sources of the Middle Ages.
wichtigste: The tapestry shows William's conquest of England in 1066.
It is almost 70 metres long but only about 50 centimetres high.
It is really an embroidery of wool on linen.
The short texts above the pictures are in Latin.
Halley's Comet can be seen on the tapestry.
Today it is displayed in Bayeux in Normandy.

abschnitte.text: The name is not quite accurate. The Bayeux Tapestry is an **embroidery**. The pictures were stitched with coloured **woollen threads** onto a cloth of **linen**. The strip is almost **70 metres** long but only about **50 centimetres** high. That is roughly as long as a row of 15 cars.

The tapestry tells the story of the **conquest of England**. Duke **William** of Normandy claimed the English throne. In **1066** he crossed the English Channel with an army. In the **Battle of Hastings** he defeated the English king **Harold**. Afterwards he was called **William the Conqueror**.

The pictures follow one another like a **comic strip** and are read from left to right. Above the pictures are short texts in **Latin**, the written language of the Middle Ages. You can see ships, castles, meals and battles. **Horses** appear especially often, because the knights fought on horseback. A **comet** with a tail is also embroidered: in 1066 **Halley's Comet** was in the sky, and people took it for a sign.

Probably **Bishop Odo of Bayeux** commissioned the tapestry. He was a half-brother of William and appears on the tapestry himself several times. The tapestry was probably made soon after the conquest. Today it is displayed in a museum in the town of **Bayeux**. Bayeux lies in **Normandy** in the north of France.

gewusst: The Bayeux Tapestry is part of the UNESCO Memory of the World register.
Halley's Comet comes back near the Sun about every 76 years.

teile.einleitung: The **Swahili Coast** lies on the east coast of Africa, roughly in present-day Kenya and Tanzania. In the Middle Ages rich trading towns flourished here. They were connected by sea with Arabia, Persia and India.
wichtigste: The name Swahili comes from the Arabic word for “coasts”.
Swahili is a Bantu language with many Arabic loanwords.
The monsoon winds made trade across the Indian Ocean possible.
Kilwa Kisiwani was one of the richest towns in the 14th century.
Houses and mosques were built mainly of coral stone.
From 1505 the Portuguese attacked the towns.

abschnitte.text: The Arabic word **Sawahil** means “coasts”. It referred to the people who lived on the coast of East Africa. Their language, **Swahili**, belongs to the **Bantu languages**. Through trade many **Arabic loanwords** were added. Today Swahili is an important common language in East Africa, spoken by millions of people.

The **monsoon winds** change direction with the seasons. That is why sailing ships could travel to Africa in one half of the year and back again in the other. Merchants brought cloth, porcelain and glass beads. From Africa came **gold**, **ivory** and other goods. In this way the coastal towns became rich.

**Kilwa Kisiwani** in present-day Tanzania was one of the richest towns on the coast in the 14th century. It controlled the gold trade from the interior through the port of **Sofala** and minted its own coins. The traveller **Ibn Battuta** visited Kilwa in **1331** and praised the town as one of the most beautiful in the world. Other important places were **Mombasa**, **Malindi** and **Lamu**. Ruins of the Great Mosque and of the palace of **Husuni Kubwa** in Kilwa still survive today.

The Swahili towns built their mosques and stone houses mainly of **coral stone**. The coral limestone was quarried on the coast and laid with lime mortar. This is how, for example, the Great Mosque of Kilwa and the old town of **Lamu** came into being. These buildings show how prosperous and well organised the towns were.

In **1498** **Vasco da Gama** reached the town of **Malindi**. Its ruler was at odds with Mombasa and gave him a pilot for the voyage to India. A few years later the Portuguese wanted to dominate trade in the Indian Ocean. In **1505** **Francisco de Almeida** conquered and plundered the town of Kilwa. After that many Swahili towns lost their power.

gewusst: The ruins of Kilwa Kisiwani and the old town of Lamu are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
A pilot is a seaman who knows the local waters and shows a ship the way.

teile.einleitung: A knightly tournament was a great festival with competitions in the Middle Ages. Knights showed in front of many spectators how well they could fight on horseback.
wichtigste: A tournament was a contest of knights in front of an audience.
In jousting, the tjost, two knights rode at each other with lances.
In the buhurt two groups of riders fought against each other.
Tournament lances often had a blunt tip so that nobody was seriously injured.
Later a wooden barrier separated the two riders.
The loser often had to give his horse and armour to the winner.
Tournaments also served as practice for war.

abschnitte.text: Tournaments were held in Europe from the 11th and 12th centuries. They often lasted several days and attracted many spectators. There was music, food and coloured tents. **Heralds** called out the names of the knights and recognised them by their **coats of arms**. For young knights a tournament was the chance to become famous.

The best-known contest was the **tjost**, jousting. Two knights rode at each other and tried to hit the opponent with the lance or lift him out of the saddle. Later a **wooden barrier** stood between them so that the horses would not collide. In the **buhurt** two whole groups rode against each other, mostly with blunt weapons.

Nobody was supposed to be killed in a tournament. That is why the lances were often blunt. One special tip was the **coronel**: it had several short prongs, spread the force of the blow and did not slip off. Even so there were injuries again and again, for the knights crashed together with great force. For this reason the Church viewed tournaments critically for a long time and at times banned them.

The loser often had to hand over his **horse and armour** to the winner. The defeated man could buy them back with money. In this way a skilful knight could become rich at tournaments. At the same time the knights practised fighting on horseback and so were prepared for **war**.

Tournaments had a lot to do with the ideal of **chivalry**. A lady sometimes gave a knight a **scarf** or a sleeve. He wore it at the tournament as a sign of her favour. Songs and stories also told of such tournaments and made the winners famous.

gewusst: The French king Henry II died in 1559 of an injury he suffered in a joust.
The word “tournament” comes from the Old French word for “to turn”, because the riders turned again and again.

teile.einleitung: The Benz Patent Motor Car Number 1 is regarded as the first real car with a petrol engine. Carl Benz built it in Mannheim and applied for a patent in 1886. The vehicle had three wheels.
wichtigste: Carl Benz built the Patent Motor Car in Mannheim.
On 29 January 1886 he applied for a patent for it.
The car had three wheels: two at the back and one at the front.
It went at most about 16 kilometres per hour.
It was steered with a tiller instead of a steering wheel.
Gottlieb Daimler built a motor carriage with four wheels almost at the same time.

abschnitte.text: In the past carriages and wagons were mostly drawn by **horses**. Many inventors dreamed of a vehicle that drives itself. **Carl Benz** had a workshop in **Mannheim**. There he built a vehicle with a small **petrol engine**. That is why the car was also called a “carriage without horses” at first.

On **29 January 1886** Carl Benz applied to the patent office for his motor car. A **patent** protects an invention so that nobody may simply copy it. This patent is regarded as the **birth certificate of the car**. That is why 1886 counts as the birth year of the car. In the summer of 1886 Benz drove publicly through Mannheim for the first time.

The Patent Motor Car had **three wheels**: two large ones at the back and a smaller one at the front. It looked almost like a big tricycle. There was no round steering wheel yet. The front wheel was steered with a **tiller**. The engine had only one cylinder and less than one horsepower. The car went at most about **16 km/h**, as fast as a bicycle often goes today.

Almost at the same time **Gottlieb Daimler** was also working on a motor vehicle. In the same year he built a carriage with an engine and four wheels. The two inventors did not know each other personally. Later, in 1926, their companies were merged into the company **Daimler-Benz**. The original of the Patent Motor Car stands today in the **Deutsches Museum** in Munich.

gewusst: The patent specification of Carl Benz is part of the UNESCO Memory of the World.
The Patent Motor Car had no reverse gear.

teile.einleitung: In the 19th century many people moved to the towns to work in factories. Workers' families often lived in cramped and poor conditions. Some factory owners therefore built homes of their own for their workers, so-called workers' housing estates.
wichtigste: With industrialisation the towns grew very quickly.
Workers' families often lived in one or two rooms.
Toilets were mostly simple privies in the yard for everyone.
Water was often fetched from the well.
Dirty water spread cholera.
Factory owners built workers' housing estates close to the factory.

abschnitte.text: With **industrialisation** more and more factories arose. Many people from the countryside moved to the towns because they found work there. The towns grew faster than homes could be built. Wages were small, but rents were high. So many families had to live very close together.

Often a whole family lived in one or two rooms. To earn money, some rented out a bed to a **lodger**. He was only allowed to sleep there and had to leave during the day. There was hardly any bathroom of one's own. Many families shared a simple **privy in the yard** or on the stairs. Water was fetched from the **well** and carried home in buckets.

There was hardly any **sewerage** yet, that is, pipes for waste water. Waste water therefore often got into the drinking water. So diseases such as **cholera** spread quickly. Only when towns built clean water pipes and sewers did things improve.

In **Berlin** huge blocks of flats with many storeys and narrow back courtyards were built. They were called **rental barracks**. In them very many people lived in little space. The flats at the back often hardly got any sunlight.

Some factory owners built homes of their own for their workers, close to the factory. In this way the workers quickly got to work. Such houses are called a **workers' housing estate**. A well-known example is the estates of the **Krupp** company in Essen. In Switzerland textile factories, for example in the Zurich Oberland, built so-called **board-and-lodging houses** for their workers' families.

gewusst: A lodger sometimes rented a bed for only a few hours, while somebody else was at work.
Many workers' housing estates of that time are still lived in today and are protected as monuments.

teile.einleitung: Philip IV was King of France from 1285 to 1314. Because of his looks he was called “the Fair”. He strengthened the power of the king and became involved in a serious dispute with the Pope.
wichtigste: Philip IV quarrelled with Pope Boniface VIII over taxes on church property and over the power of the Pope.
In 1302 he summoned the Estates General to seek support.
In the same year his army of knights lost the Battle of the Golden Spurs at Kortrijk.
In 1303 his followers attacked the Pope at Anagni.
Later he had the Order of the Templars persecuted.

abschnitte.text: Philip IV also wanted to tax the **clergy** in France. Over this he fell out with Pope **Boniface VIII**. In 1302, in the bull **“Unam sanctam”**, the Pope claimed that spiritual power took precedence over worldly power. Philip firmly rejected this. To win support he summoned the **Estates General** in 1302, an assembly of nobility, clergy and towns.

In 1303 followers of Philip, among them **Guillaume de Nogaret** and Sciarra Colonna, attacked the Pope in his residence at **Anagni** and held him prisoner. This is called the **Outrage of Anagni**. Boniface VIII was set free again but died a few weeks later in Rome. Soon afterwards the popes lived for a long time in **Avignon**, under strong French influence.

abschnitte.titel: The Battle of the Golden Spurs
abschnitte.text: In 1302 the **Battle of the Golden Spurs at Kortrijk** took place in Flanders. There **foot soldiers** from Flemish towns defeated a French **army of knights**. After the battle the victors collected many golden spurs from the knights. This booty gave the battle its name. The victory showed that well-ordered foot soldiers could beat knights.

gewusst: In 1307 Philip IV had the members of the Order of the Templars arrested throughout France.
The Estates General were later summoned again and again, the last time in 1789, shortly before the French Revolution.

teile.einleitung: In the 13th century the Mongol Empire was the largest continuous land empire in history. It stretched from Korea to Eastern Europe.
wichtigste: The Mongol Empire was the largest continuous land empire.
The capital was Karakorum in present-day Mongolia.
In 1241 the Mongols won at Legnica in Silesia.
After the death of Ögedei they withdrew from Central Europe.
In 1258 Hülegü conquered Baghdad.
Later the empire broke up into four parts.

abschnitte.text: In the **13th century** the Mongols created the **largest continuous land empire** in history. It stretched from **Korea** to **Eastern Europe**. The capital was **Karakorum** in present-day Mongolia. Under **Ögedei**, a son of Genghis Khan, it was expanded.

In **1241** the Mongols defeated a Polish-German army of knights at **Legnica** in Silesia. But then they withdrew again. Great Khan **Ögedei** had died in December 1241. Leading princes returned to elect a successor. Europe was afterwards spared further large campaigns.

**Hülegü**, a grandson of Genghis Khan, conquered Baghdad in **1258**. He had the city plundered and ended the **Abbasid Caliphate**. Afterwards he founded the **Ilkhanate** in Persia. In **1260** the **Mamluks** of Egypt stopped the Mongols at **Ain Jalut** in Palestine. Egypt thus remained unconquered.

The Mongols built a network of post stations, the **Yam**. There messengers received fresh horses and food. In this way news travelled up to several hundred kilometres a day. The trade routes across Asia became safer. This period is called the **Pax Mongolica**, the “Mongol peace”. Merchants and envoys travelled from Eastern Europe to China.

After the death of Great Khan **Möngke** in **1259** there were struggles over the succession. The empire broke up into four parts: the **Golden Horde**, the **Ilkhanate**, the **Chagatai Khanate** and the **Yuan dynasty** in China. The Golden Horde ruled over large parts of Eastern Europe until the 15th century. Russian princes had to pay it tribute.

gewusst: The Venetian Marco Polo also travelled to China along the routes of the Pax Mongolica.
The emperor of the Yuan dynasty was Great Khan of all the Mongols in name only.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages many towns were surrounded by a wall. You could only get into the town through a **town gate**. Some of these gates still stand today, including in Switzerland.
wichtigste: You entered the walled town through the town gate.
Gatekeepers checked who wanted to come in.
Merchants often had to pay a toll at the gate.
The Spalentor in Basel is a well-known old town gate.
The Zytglogge in Bern was at first a town gate.

abschnitte.text: A town wall had only a few openings. These openings were the **town gates**. They were usually strongly built, often as a tower with a passage. Many gates could be closed with heavy wooden doors and a **portcullis**. A portcullis is a grille that is lowered from above. At night and in times of danger the gates stayed shut.

At the gate stood **gatekeepers**. They watched who came into the town and stopped strangers or suspicious people. Merchants who brought goods into the town often had to pay a **toll**. A toll is a charge on goods. With this money the town paid, for example, for the upkeep of its walls. In this way the gate was also an important source of income.

In **Basel** stands the **Spalentor**. It was part of the old Basel town fortifications and has a colourful tiled roof. In **Bern** the **Zytglogge** is famous. It was at first a gate in the town wall. When the town grew and new walls were built farther out, it lost this function. Later the tower was given a famous clock, which still attracts many visitors today.

gewusst: Many town gates were torn down in the 19th century because they were in the way of traffic.
The clock on the Zytglogge shows not only the time but also has moving figures.

teile.einleitung: For Muslims, Muhammad is the prophet who proclaimed the message of Islam. He lived in the 6th and 7th centuries on the Arabian Peninsula.
wichtigste: Muhammad was born in Mecca around 570.
In 622 he moved to Yathrib, which was later called Medina.
This move is called the Hijra.
The Islamic calendar begins with the Hijra.
The holy book of Islam is the Quran, handed down in Arabic.
Muhammad died in Medina in 632.

abschnitte.text: Muhammad was born around **570** in **Mecca** on the **Arabian Peninsula**. At that time Mecca was a trading city. The **Kaaba**, a cube-shaped shrine, stands there. Today it stands in the courtyard of the Great Mosque. Muslims all over the world pray in its direction, and Mecca is the most important place of pilgrimage in Islam.

For Muslims the **Quran** contains the **revelations** that Muhammad received. The Quran was handed down in **Arabic**. That is why the Arabic language spread widely along with Islam. Many Muslims learn parts of the Quran by heart.

In Mecca, Muhammad and his followers had many opponents. In the year **622** they moved to **Yathrib**. This move is called the **Hijra**. Afterwards Yathrib was called “City of the Prophet”, or **Medina** for short. There the first Muslim community with its own order was formed. The year 622 marks the beginning of the **Islamic calendar**.

There was fighting between Medina and Mecca. In **624** the Muslims won the battle of **Badr** against a larger army from Mecca. This strengthened the standing of the young community. At **Uhud** they were defeated in 625. Later Muhammad returned to Mecca.

Islam has **five pillars**: the **declaration of faith**, **prayer**, **alms** for the needy, **fasting** in the month of Ramadan and the **pilgrimage** to Mecca. Muhammad died in **632** in Medina. After that, **caliphs** took over the leadership of the community.

gewusst: In the Islamic calendar the year follows the moon and is therefore about eleven days shorter than our year.
Many Muslims who celebrate Ramadan also live in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The **Delhi Sultanate** was a Muslim empire in northern India. It lasted from 1206 to 1526 and was ruled by several ruling families. Famous buildings such as the Qutb Minar date from this time.
wichtigste: Qutb ud-Din Aibak founded the Delhi Sultanate in 1206.
The Qutb Minar in Delhi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site today.
Razia Sultana ruled from 1236 to 1240 as the only woman ruler.
Alauddin Khalji repelled invasions by the Mongols.
Timur plundered Delhi in 1398.
With the First Battle of Panipat the sultanate ended in 1526.

abschnitte.text: **Qutb ud-Din Aibak** was a former military slave in the service of the Ghurid Muhammad. In **1206** he made himself ruler in Delhi. The first ruling family is therefore also called the **Slave dynasty**. Later further dynasties followed, for example the **Khalji**, the **Tughluq** and finally the **Lodi**. The sultans were Muslims and ruled over a country in which most people were Hindus.

Under Qutb ud-Din Aibak the building of the **Qutb Minar** began. This is a victory tower of red sandstone, about **73 metres** tall. His successors Iltutmish and Firuz Shah continued building it. The tower is decorated with bands of inscriptions. Today it is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** and one of the landmarks of Delhi.

**Razia Sultana** was the daughter of Iltutmish and ruled from **1236 to 1240**. She was the only woman on the throne but was overthrown by the nobility. **Alauddin Khalji** ruled from 1296 to 1316. He repelled several attacks by the Mongols and fixed prices in the markets. **Muhammad bin Tughluq** moved the capital for a time to **Daulatabad** and had copper coins minted instead of silver money. Because these coins were forged in huge numbers, the reform failed.

The Moroccan traveller **Ibn Battuta** came to Delhi around 1334. The sultan Muhammad bin Tughluq received him generously. Ibn Battuta worked for several years as a **qadi**, that is, a judge. Later the ruler sent him as an envoy to China. His travel accounts are an important source on this period.

In **1398** the Central Asian conqueror **Timur** marched into India and plundered Delhi. Many people died in the process, and the sultanate recovered only slowly. In **1526** **Babur** defeated the last Lodi sultan, Ibrahim, in the **First Battle of Panipat**. This ended the Delhi Sultanate. The **Mughal Empire** began.

gewusst: The Delhi Sultanate lasted about 320 years.
Under Alauddin Khalji there were fixed prices in the markets so that he could pay a large army.

teile.einleitung: **Theodoric the Great** was king of the Ostrogoths. He conquered Italy and ruled it from Ravenna for more than 30 years. In German heroic legends he lives on as Dietrich von Bern.
wichtigste: Theodoric was king of the Germanic Ostrogoths.
As a child he lived for about ten years as a hostage in Constantinople.
In 493 he defeated Odoacer and ruled over Italy.
His capital was Ravenna, where his mausoleum also stands.
In the legends he is called Dietrich von Bern, meaning Verona.
Under Emperor Justinian I the Ostrogothic kingdom was destroyed.

abschnitte.text: Theodoric came from a royal family of the **Ostrogoths**. As a child he was sent as a **hostage** to the court of the Eastern Roman emperor in **Constantinople**. A hostage was then a pledge that a treaty would be kept. He lived there for about ten years. He came to know Roman culture and administration. In the 470s he became king of the Ostrogoths.

In **488** Emperor **Zeno** commissioned Theodoric to march to Italy. The emperor wanted to draw the Ostrogoths away from the Balkans and get rid of **Odoacer**, who ruled Italy. After several years of war Odoacer surrendered in **493** in Ravenna. Soon afterwards Theodoric killed him at a banquet. Now Theodoric was ruler of Italy.

Theodoric ruled from **Ravenna**, where the last Western Roman emperors had already lived. He let the Roman administration carry on and employed Roman officials. Through marriages he made alliances with other Germanic kingdoms. He himself married **Audofleda**, a sister of the Frankish king **Clovis I**. At the end of his reign mistrust grew. The philosopher **Boethius**, author of “The Consolation of Philosophy”, was accused of treason and executed around 524.

Theodoric died in the year **526**. His **mausoleum** still stands in Ravenna today. The special thing is the roof: the dome consists of a **single block of limestone** from Istria. It weighs an estimated **230 tonnes**. How people got this huge stone up there in those days is still impressive today.

abschnitte.titel: End of the kingdom and the legend
abschnitte.text: After Theodoric's death the Ostrogothic kingdom grew weaker. The Eastern Roman emperor **Justinian I** wanted to restore the old Roman Empire. After almost 20 years of war his armies decisively defeated the Ostrogoths in **552**. In German heroic legends Theodoric lives on as **Dietrich von Bern**. By “Bern” is meant the Italian city of **Verona**, not the Swiss federal city.

gewusst: Theodoric's mausoleum is part of the UNESCO World Heritage in Ravenna.
In the Nibelungenlied Dietrich von Bern appears as a hero.

teile.einleitung: Saladin was a famous Muslim ruler in the 12th century. He defeated the crusaders, conquered Jerusalem and was already seen in his own time as wise and generous.
wichtigste: Saladin was a Kurd and founded the Ayyubid dynasty.
As sultan he ruled first over Egypt, later also over Syria.
In 1187 he defeated the crusaders at the Battle of Hattin.
In doing so he captured King Guy of Lusignan.
Afterwards he conquered Jerusalem and released the Christians in return for ransom.
Barbarossa, Richard the Lionheart and Philip II marched against him in the Third Crusade.
Saladin died in Damascus in 1193.

abschnitte.text: Saladin was actually called Salah ad-Din, which means “Righteousness of the Faith”. He was born around 1137 in Tikrit in present-day Iraq and belonged to the **Kurdish** people. He rose in the service of a Syrian ruler. Later he became **Sultan of Egypt** and also conquered **Syria**. He founded the ruling family of the **Ayyubids**.

In the summer of **1187** Saladin met the army of the crusaders at **Hattin** near the Sea of Galilee. The crusaders suffered from heat and lack of water. Saladin won clearly and captured **Guy of Lusignan**, the King of Jerusalem. Guy was later released again.

In the same year Saladin conquered **Jerusalem**. The Christian inhabitants were allowed to **buy their freedom with ransom** and leave the city. Many poor people who could not pay, however, were taken prisoner. Even so, Saladin’s conduct was seen as far milder than the conquest of Jerusalem by the crusaders in 1099.

After the loss of Jerusalem three rulers set off on the **Third Crusade**: Emperor Frederick **Barbarossa**, King **Richard I** of England, called the Lionheart, and King **Philip II** of France. Barbarossa drowned in a river on the way. Richard and Saladin fought against each other for a long time. In 1192 they concluded the **Treaty of Jaffa**: Jerusalem remained Muslim, but Christian pilgrims were allowed to visit the city.

Saladin died in **1193** in **Damascus**, where his tomb can still be seen today. Many Christians also admired him as a chivalrous opponent. The German writer Gotthold Ephraim **Lessing** had him appear in the play **“Nathan the Wise”**. It is about tolerance between Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

gewusst: Saladin is said to have given away so much that when he died there was hardly any money left for his funeral.
Richard the Lionheart and Saladin never met in person, despite their long struggle.

teile.einleitung: Abel Tasman was a Dutch seafarer of the 17th century. In 1642 he was the first European to see New Zealand. An island, a sea and a national park bear his name today.
wichtigste: Abel Tasman came from the Netherlands.
He sailed for the Dutch East India Company, a trading firm.
In 1642 he reached the island that is now called Tasmania.
In December 1642 he was the first European to see the coast of New Zealand.
The sea between Australia and New Zealand is called the Tasman Sea.
In the north of New Zealand's South Island lies Abel Tasman National Park.

abschnitte.text: Abel Tasman was born in 1603 in the **Netherlands**. So he lived in the **17th century**. He worked for the **Dutch East India Company**, VOC for short. This large **trading firm** traded mainly in **spices** from Asia. Its headquarters in Asia was Batavia, present-day Jakarta.

The VOC wanted to know what lay in the south of the world. In **1642** it sent Tasman off with two ships. He sailed far to the south and reached a large island. He named it Van Diemen's Land after a governor. Later the island was given the name **Tasmania** after him. It lies south of Australia.

In **December 1642** Tasman was the first European to see the coast of **New Zealand**. In a bay there was a clash with the **Māori** who lived there. Sailors lost their lives. Tasman never set foot in New Zealand himself and sailed on. On the way back he came to Tonga and Fiji.

Many places recall Abel Tasman. The sea between Australia and New Zealand is called the **Tasman Sea**. In the north of New Zealand's South Island lies **Abel Tasman National Park** with golden beaches and forests. The island of **Tasmania** also bears his name. Tasman died in 1659 in Batavia.

gewusst: The name New Zealand comes from the Dutch province of Zeeland.
Tasman once sailed right around Australia without seeing the mainland.

teile.einleitung: A drawbridge is a bridge that can be pulled up. At castles it led over the moat to the gate. When it was up, nobody could get in.
wichtigste: The drawbridge led over the moat to the castle gate.
It hung on chains or ropes and was pulled up with a winch.
Counterweights made the pulling up easier.
Drawbridges were mostly made of wood, often reinforced with iron.
Pulled up, the bridge closed the entrance.

abschnitte.titel: Over the moat to the gate
abschnitte.text: Many castles were surrounded by a **moat**. Sometimes it was filled with water, sometimes dry. Over the moat the **drawbridge** led directly to the **castle gate**. When it was pulled up, a deep ditch lay between the enemy and the castle. The raised bridge also closed the gate like an extra door.

The bridge hung on **chains** or **ropes**. With a **winch** in the gatehouse it was pulled up. This was heavy work. On some drawbridges, therefore, large **counterweights** hung. They pulled the bridge up almost by themselves, rather as on a seesaw.

A drawbridge mostly consisted of **wood**. Wood was light enough for the bridge to be pulled up. It was often reinforced with **iron** so that it lasted longer. Behind the drawbridge a **portcullis** of wood and iron sometimes protected the entrance as well. So a castle had several obstacles at the gate.

Today you can still see drawbridges at many old castles and palaces. Modern bridges that can be opened exist too. They let ships through on rivers and canals. They are called **bascule bridges** or **lift bridges**. So the idea is still useful today.

gewusst: The famous Tower Bridge in London is a bascule bridge whose roadways lift for ships.
In the Netherlands there are many small drawbridges over canals that are still used every day.

teile.einleitung: Historians use “imperial church system” to describe the close link between monarchy and Church in the empire of the Ottonians and Salians. The kings relied on bishops and imperial abbeys and in return gave them land and rights.
wichtigste: Bishops and abbots received land, county rights and regalia from the king.
In return they performed the servitium regis, service to the king.
Immunity protected church property from royal counts.
The court chapel trained later imperial bishops.
Bruno, a brother of Otto I, was at the same time Archbishop of Cologne and Duke of Lotharingia.
Today many researchers regard the term as too schematic.

abschnitte.text: As early as the Early Middle Ages there was the system of **proprietary churches**. A **landlord** who built a church on his land appointed the priest and used its income. The term was coined by the Swiss legal historian **Ulrich Stutz**. Later the kings treated the great churches of the empire in a similar way. They appointed bishops and abbots and expected loyalty.

The kings often gave bishops **county rights** and **regalia**, that is, royal rights such as **tolls, market rights and the right to mint coins**. With **immunity**, royal counts were not allowed to enter church property. The bishops exercised the rights there themselves or through an **advocate**. In this way they became powerful **territorial lords** in the king’s service. An example is **Bruno**, brother of Otto I, from 953 Archbishop of Cologne and at the same time Duke of Lotharingia.

In return, bishoprics and imperial abbeys owed the king the **servitium regis**, service to the king. This included **hospitality**, that is, housing the travelling court, as well as payments and providing **troops**. Many bishops came from the **court chapel**. There clergy served the king in worship and in the chancery before he made them bishops.

The phrase **“Ottonian-Salian imperial church system”** is a **modern scholarly label**. Historians such as **Timothy Reuter** stressed in 1982 that the kings had already used the Church in this way in Carolingian times. Besides, it was **not a planned system** that anyone had deliberately created. That is why the term is often regarded today as **too schematic**. With the **Investiture Controversy** in the 11th and 12th centuries the relationship between king and Church changed greatly.

gewusst: Bishoprics in the area of present-day Switzerland, such as Chur, Basel and Constance, also belonged to the imperial church.
Some bishops were so powerful that they ruled over whole territories like princes.

teile.einleitung: A town hall is the building in which the council of a town meets. In the Middle Ages magnificent town halls were built in many towns, and they still stand today.
wichtigste: The name comes from the town council, which meets there.
The council was made up of councillors, often rich merchants or craftsmen.
The council was often led by the mayor, in Bern by the Schultheiss.
Court hearings were also held in the town hall.
The Basel town hall is bright red.
The Zurich town hall stands on the Limmat.

abschnitte.text: The German word for town hall, **Rathaus**, comes from **“Rat”** (council) and “beraten” (to advise or deliberate). In the town hall the **town council** met to decide the affairs of the town. It made rules for all citizens, for example for markets, walls and taxes. Its members were called **councillors**. They were mostly rich merchants or craftsmen who were elected for a fixed period.

In many towns a **mayor** led the council. He was the head of the town. In **Bern** this office was called **Schultheiss**. In the medieval town hall **court hearings** were also held. The council decided on disputes and crimes and was often at the same time the court.

abschnitte.titel: The red town hall in Basel
abschnitte.text: The **Basel town hall** stands on the market square and shines bright **red**. It was built at the beginning of the 16th century and extended later. The façade is painted with **colourful pictures**. To this day the government and parliament of the canton of Basel-Stadt meet there. It is one of the best-known buildings in the city.

abschnitte.titel: Zurich and the pride of towns
abschnitte.text: The **Zurich town hall** stands right on the **Limmat** and is even partly built out into the river. Today the parliament of the canton of Zurich meets there. Towns often built their town hall especially beautifully to show their **wealth** and their pride. That is why many town halls have **towers, paintings and decoration**. A magnificent town hall showed every visitor how important the town was.

gewusst: In many Swiss municipalities the administration building is still called the town hall or municipal house today.
The Basel town hall was built between 1504 and 1514, shortly after Basel joined the Swiss Confederation in 1501.

teile.einleitung: Alexander Fleming was a Scottish doctor and researcher. In 1928 he discovered penicillin by chance in London. This first antibiotic has saved the lives of millions of people since.
wichtigste: Alexander Fleming was born in Scotland in 1881.
He did research at St Mary's Hospital in London.
In 1928 he discovered penicillin by chance.
Penicillin is produced by a mould called Penicillium.
It helps against bacteria, but not against viruses.
Medicines such as penicillin are called antibiotics.
In 1945 he received the Nobel Prize in Medicine with Howard Florey and Ernst Chain.

abschnitte.text: Alexander Fleming was born in **1881** in **Scotland**. He grew up on a farm. Later he moved to **London** and studied medicine. He worked as a researcher at **St Mary's Hospital** in London. There he studied how to fight **bacteria**.

In **1928** Fleming went on **holiday**. In his laboratory he left dishes with bacteria standing. When he came back, **mould** was growing on one dish. Around the mould the bacteria had disappeared. Fleming realised that the fungus produces a substance that **kills** bacteria. So he discovered penicillin **by chance**.

Penicillin is produced by a **mould**. The fungus is called **Penicillium**, and the substance is named after it. Penicillin kills **bacteria** or slows their growth. Against **viruses**, for example in flu or a cold, it does not help. Medicines such as penicillin are called **antibiotics**. The word comes from Greek and means roughly “against life”.

abschnitte.titel: Florey, Chain and the Nobel Prize
abschnitte.text: Fleming could not yet make penicillin in large quantities. Around 1940 **Howard Florey** and **Ernst Chain** found out how to **purify** it and use it as a **medicine**. In the Second World War it was then made in factories and saved many wounded soldiers. In **1945** all three received the **Nobel Prize in Medicine**. Fleming died in 1955 in London.

Fleming himself warned that bacteria can become **resistant** to penicillin. This is called **resistance**. Today this is a big problem in medicine. That is why antibiotics should only be taken when a doctor prescribes them. In **Switzerland** most antibiotics are only available with a **prescription**.

gewusst: Fleming's laboratory at St Mary's Hospital in London is a small museum today.
Even before penicillin, Fleming discovered a substance against bacteria in tears and saliva, lysozyme.

teile.einleitung: The 95 Theses are a text that the monk and professor Martin Luther published in 1517. In it he criticised above all the Church's trade in indulgences. The theses set off the Reformation, which changed Europe, and Switzerland too, greatly.
wichtigste: Martin Luther published the 95 Theses in 1517.
They were aimed above all against the sale of indulgences.
With an indulgence people were promised the remission of punishments for sins in return for money.
Luther wrote the theses in Latin.
He sent them with a letter to Archbishop Albrecht of Brandenburg.
Thanks to printing they spread far within a few weeks.
Reformation Day on 31 October recalls this.

abschnitte.text: **Martin Luther** lived from 1483 to 1546 and was an Augustinian monk. He taught as professor of biblical studies at the university in **Wittenberg** in Saxony. Luther was troubled by the question of how a person can stand before God. He came to the conclusion that faith alone and the grace of God count.

The Church taught that for sins one is punished even after death in **purgatory**. With an **indulgence letter** one could buy, for money, a remission of these punishments. The Dominican monk **Johann Tetzel** preached for the indulgence near Wittenberg. The saying is attributed to him: “As soon as the coin in the coffer rings, the soul from purgatory springs”.

On 31 October 1517 Luther sent his 95 Theses in Latin to Archbishop **Albrecht of Brandenburg**. He wanted to discuss them with scholars. Luther criticised that forgiveness cannot be bought. Part of the indulgence money was, besides, intended for the new building of **St Peter's Basilica** in Rome.

abschnitte.titel: The famous nailing of the theses
abschnitte.text: According to tradition Luther nailed the theses to the door of the **Castle Church** in Wittenberg. Historians today say it is uncertain whether it really happened that way, with a hammer. Church doors did indeed serve at the time as a kind of notice board. The present door of the Castle Church is made of bronze and shows the text of the theses.

Friends translated the theses into German and had them printed. Thanks to **printing** with movable type they were known throughout Germany within a few weeks. In 1521 the pope excommunicated Luther, and the emperor declared him an outlaw. Luther hid in the Wartburg and translated the New Testament into German there.

The theses were the beginning of the **Reformation**, from which the Protestant churches arose. In Switzerland **Huldrych Zwingli** worked as a reformer in Zurich from 1519. In Geneva John Calvin later carried the Reformation further. To this day there are Reformed and Catholic cantons in Switzerland with different traditions.

begriffe.erklaerung: A claim that can be discussed.
According to the teaching of the time, the remission of punishments for sins, often in return for money.
A movement in the 16th century that wanted to renew the Church and led to the rise of Protestant churches.
According to Catholic teaching, a place of purification after death.
Exclusion from the Church by the pope.

gewusst: Luther originally did not want to found a new church with the theses, but only to discuss abuses.
In several German federal states 31 October is a public holiday.
Luther's translation of the Bible helped a common German written language to develop.

teile.einleitung: Abolitionism is the name for the movement that wanted to abolish slavery and the slave trade. It arose in the 18th century and in the 19th century achieved the banning of slavery in many countries.
wichtigste: Britain banned the slave trade in 1807 and slavery in 1833.
William Wilberforce fought against it in the British Parliament for decades.
Haiti came into being in 1804 out of an uprising of enslaved people.
Harriet Tubman led many to freedom along the Underground Railroad.
The novel “Uncle Tom's Cabin” of 1852 strengthened the movement in the USA.
France finally abolished slavery in 1848.
Brazil was the last country in the Americas to abolish slavery, in 1888.

abschnitte.text: For centuries millions of people were carried off from **Africa** and forced to work in America as **slaves**. They had no rights and counted as property. In the 18th century more and more people began to resist this. The movement is called **abolitionism**, from the Latin word for abolition. Among the first were religious groups such as the **Quakers**.

abschnitte.titel: The fight in the British Parliament
abschnitte.text: In Britain **William Wilberforce** brought motions against the slave trade into Parliament again and again from 1789. Many people supported him with signatures and boycotts. In 1807 the **Slave Trade Act** banned the trade in enslaved people in the British Empire. Slavery itself was only abolished with the law of **1833**. Wilberforce died in 1833, shortly after this decision.

In the French colony of **Saint-Domingue** the enslaved rose up from 1791. In 1804 **Haiti** was proclaimed there as an independent republic. France had already abolished slavery in 1794, but **Napoleon** reintroduced it in 1802. Only in **1848** did **Victor Schoelcher** push through the final abolition in the French colonies.

In the USA many enslaved people fled from the South to the North. A secret network of helpers was called the **Underground Railroad**. **Harriet Tubman** escaped from Maryland in 1849 and returned several times to free others. The novel **“Uncle Tom's Cabin”** by **Harriet Beecher Stowe** appeared in 1852 and became a bestseller. It sharpened the quarrel between the Northern and Southern states, which ended in the Civil War. In 1865 slavery was banned in the whole of the USA.

As the last country in the Americas, **Brazil** abolished slavery in 1888 with the **“Golden Law”**. No other country had brought in so many enslaved people from Africa. Switzerland had no colonies. All the same, **Swiss merchants and firms** also earned money from the trade in enslaved people, for example through shares in ships. This is being researched today by historians.

gewusst: The Universal Declaration of Human Rights of 1948 bans slavery in all its forms.
Harriet Tubman is said to have gone back to the South to free about 70 people, and she was never caught.

teile.einleitung: The Berlin Blockade was the first great crisis of the Cold War. From 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949 the Soviet Union closed all land and water routes to West Berlin. The Western powers supplied the city for almost a year by an airlift, one of the greatest relief operations in history.
wichtigste: The blockade lasted from 24 June 1948 to 12 May 1949.
The reason given was the introduction of the Deutsche Mark in the Western zones.
About two million people in West Berlin were cut off from roads, railways and canals.
The US military governor Lucius D. Clay ordered the airlift.
Most aircraft landed at Tempelhof airport.
The pilot Gail Halvorsen dropped sweets on small parachutes for children.
The blockade sped up the founding of two German states in 1949.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War Germany was divided into four **occupation zones**. Berlin too was divided into four sectors, although the city lay in the middle of the Soviet zone. The three Western sectors of the USA, Britain and France formed West Berlin. Between the Western powers and the Soviet Union mistrust grew ever greater, for they had quite different ideas of what Germany should look like in future.

On 20 June 1948 the Western powers introduced the **Deutsche Mark** in their zones, and soon afterwards in West Berlin too. The Soviet Union rejected this and used it as a reason for the **blockade**. From 24 June 1948 all roads, railway lines and waterways to West Berlin were closed, and electricity from the east was cut off too. The Soviet Union hoped to push the Western powers out of Berlin in this way.

The American military governor **Lucius D. Clay** ordered in June 1948 that the city should be supplied from the air. American and British aircraft flew food, medicines and above all coal to Berlin almost around the clock. They landed mainly at **Tempelhof**, but also at Gatow and at the newly built Tegel airport. At peak times an aircraft landed every few minutes. In all, the aircraft brought more than two million tonnes of goods into the city in over 270,000 flights.

The American pilot **Gail Halvorsen** began to drop chocolate and chewing gum for the Berlin children on small handkerchief parachutes. Soon many other pilots joined in. The children therefore affectionately called the aircraft **raisin bombers**. The action showed that former enemies in war could become friends. For this Halvorsen was greatly revered in Germany until his death in 2022.

Because the airlift worked, the Soviet Union gave up and lifted the blockade on 12 May 1949. In accidents during the airlift several dozen people lost their lives. They are recalled by the **Airlift Memorial** in front of Tempelhof airport. The blockade deepened the division of Germany: in May 1949 the Federal Republic of Germany came into being, in October 1949 the GDR. For many West Germans the Americans and British changed from occupiers into protectors through the airlift.

begriffe.erklaerung: The closing of all access routes so that nothing can get in or out.
Supplying a place only by aircraft when the land route is closed.
The decades-long conflict between the USA and the Soviet Union without direct war between the two.
A part of a city that is administered by a particular power.

gewusst: Almost two thirds of the freight of the airlift was coal for heating and for power stations.
Tegel airport was built during the blockade in only about three months, with the help of many Berlin women too.
The Airlift Memorial has three prongs that stand for the three air corridors to West Germany.

teile.einleitung: The **Forbidden City** is a huge palace in the middle of Beijing, the capital of China. For almost 500 years the Chinese emperors lived here. Today it is a museum that millions of people visit every year.
wichtigste: The Forbidden City lies in the middle of Beijing.
It was the palace of the Chinese emperors.
Ordinary people were not allowed in without permission.
It was finished around 1420 after about 14 years of building.
It has almost 1,000 buildings, most with yellow roofs.
Today the Forbidden City is a large museum.

abschnitte.text: The Forbidden City was the **palace of the Chinese emperors**. Here they lived with their families, their officials and many servants. It was built under an emperor of the **Ming dynasty**. The building took about **14 years** and was finished around **1420**. Afterwards emperors lived here for almost **500 years**, first of the Ming, then of the **Qing**.

Without the emperor's permission **nobody** was allowed in. For ordinary people the palace was therefore forbidden, hence the name. A high **wall** and a broad **moat** surround the whole site. In this way the palace was well shut off and protected. You could only get in through a few large gates.

In the Forbidden City stand **almost 1,000 buildings**. It is one of the largest palaces in the world. Almost all the roofs are covered with **yellow tiles**. **Yellow** was the colour of the emperor. The buildings are made of wood and richly painted. Many halls lie exactly one behind the other on a line from south to north.

In **1912** the last emperor abdicated, and China became a republic. A few years later the Forbidden City became the **Palace Museum**. Today you can see precious paintings, porcelain and other treasures there. Every year millions of people visit the palace. The Forbidden City is part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**.

gewusst: The last emperor of China was called Puyi, and he was still a child when the empire ended.
On the roof edges sit small animal figures, and the more important a building was, the more of them there are.

teile.einleitung: The American Revolution was the struggle of 13 British colonies in North America for their independence. It began with protests against British taxes and led to the War of Independence from 1775 to 1783. From it came the United States of America, with one of the oldest constitutions in the world still in force.
wichtigste: 13 British colonies in North America fought for their independence.
The protest was: “No taxation without representation”.
At the Boston Tea Party on 16 December 1773 colonists threw tea into the harbour.
The war began on 19 April 1775 with the battles of Lexington and Concord.
On 4 July 1776 the colonies declared their independence.
The surrender at Yorktown in 1781 decided the war.
In the Peace of Paris in 1783 Britain recognised the USA.
In 1787 the Constitution of the USA was adopted in Philadelphia.

abschnitte.text: After an expensive war against France, Britain wanted to make the colonies pay more. The **Stamp Act** of 1765 demanded a tax on newspapers, documents and other printed matter. The colonists protested because they had no representatives in the British Parliament. Their principle was **“No taxation without representation”**, that is, no taxes without a say.

On 5 March 1770 British soldiers shot several citizens in Boston, which was called the **Boston Massacre**. On 16 December 1773 colonists disguised as Native Americans threw tea into the harbour, the **Boston Tea Party**. The British Parliament responded in 1774 with the Intolerable Acts and, among other things, closed the port of Boston. The mood grew ever tenser.

On 19 April 1775 the armed struggle began with the battles of **Lexington and Concord**. **George Washington** became commander-in-chief of the American army. In January 1776 Thomas Paine argued forcefully for independence in his pamphlet “Common Sense”. On 4 July 1776 the colonies adopted the **Declaration of Independence**, which Thomas Jefferson had mainly written.

The victory at **Saratoga** in 1777 is regarded as the turning point of the war. It convinced France to make an alliance with the Americans. The young French nobleman **Marquis de La Fayette** fought as a general at Washington's side. In October 1781 British troops surrendered at Yorktown, and in 1783 Britain recognised independence in the Peace of Paris.

In 1787 the constitutional convention in Philadelphia adopted the **Constitution of the United States**. It divides power between president, Congress and courts, which is called the **separation of powers**. In 1789 George Washington became the first president of the USA. The Constitution is still in force today, supplemented by amendments such as the Bill of Rights.

The American Revolution showed that a people can govern itself. It was a model for the **French Revolution** of 1789. The Swiss Federal Constitution of 1848, too, took over ideas from the USA, for example a parliament with two chambers. So the National Council and the Council of States correspond roughly to the American House of Representatives and Senate.

begriffe.erklaerung: A territory that is ruled by a foreign country.
When a country governs itself and is subject to nobody else.
The most important law of a state, which sets out the rules for the state and its citizens.
Dividing the power of the state among different bodies so that nobody becomes too powerful.
A short printed booklet meant to spread an opinion.

gewusst: 4 July is still the national holiday of the USA.
The pamphlet “Common Sense” sold tens of thousands of copies within a few months.
La Fayette was later so revered in the USA that many places are named after him.

teile.einleitung: Battlements are the toothlike pieces of wall at the top of castle walls and towers. Behind them the defenders could shelter and shoot through the gaps.
wichtigste: Battlements protected the defenders on the wall.
The gaps between the battlements are called embrasures.
An arrow slit is a narrow slit in the wall.
From the battlements people often shot with bow and arrow, later with crossbows.
Some gaps had wooden shutters.

abschnitte.text: On top of castle walls you often see a row of **teeth**. The high pieces of wall are the **battlements**. The gaps in between are called **embrasures**. Behind the battlements ran a narrow passage, the **wall walk**. There the defenders stood when the castle was attacked.

Behind a battlement a defender could **hide**. Through the gap next to it he could **shoot**. Mostly the defenders used **bow and arrow**, later also **crossbows**. Some gaps had **wooden shutters**. They protected the men when no shooting was going on.

An **arrow slit** is a narrow slit in the wall. It is **wide on the inside and narrow on the outside**. This gave the archer room on the inside to aim. From outside, though, the opening was hard to hit. Arrow slits were found in walls, towers and even in the battlements themselves.

Battlements can be seen on many castles in Switzerland. Especially beautiful are the **swallowtail battlements** on the castles of **Bellinzona** in Ticino. They are notched at the top like the tail of a swallow. Later battlements were also placed as **decoration** on town halls and town gates, without serving for defence any more.

gewusst: The three castles of Bellinzona are part of the UNESCO World Heritage.
On chess pieces the teeth on the rook recall battlements.

teile.einleitung: A circumnavigation is a journey by ship once all the way around the Earth. The first was achieved from 1519 to 1522 by a Spanish fleet led by Ferdinand Magellan. Only the ship Victoria came back and proved that one can sail around the Earth by sea.
wichtigste: The first circumnavigation took place from 1519 to 1522.
It began under Ferdinand Magellan, who died on the way.
Only the ship Victoria completed the voyage, under Juan Sebastián Elcano.
The returning sailors noticed that a day was missing from their calendar.
Francis Drake led the second circumnavigation, which ended in 1580.
Jeanne Baret is regarded as the first woman to have gone around the world.
The Swiss Bertrand Piccard flew around the Earth nonstop in a balloon in 1999 and in 2015 to 2016 in the solar aeroplane Solar Impulse 2.

abschnitte.text: In 1519 the Portuguese **Ferdinand Magellan** set out with five ships on behalf of Spain. He wanted to reach the Spice Islands, today's Moluccas, by sailing west. He found the strait at the southern tip of South America that is now called the **Strait of Magellan**. Magellan died in 1521 in a fight in the Philippines.

Juan Sebastián **Elcano** carried on with the last ship, the **Victoria**. He sailed across the Indian Ocean and around the Cape of Good Hope back to Spain. In September 1522 only 18 men of the original crew arrived. Elcano received a coat of arms with the motto “Primus circumdedisti me”, which means “You were the first to sail around me”.

The returning sailors had noted down every day carefully in the logbook. All the same, on arrival a day was missing for them. Because they had always sailed west, that is, with the sun, they had experienced one sunrise fewer. Today the **date line** in the Pacific deals with this problem.

The Englishman **Francis Drake** sailed around the world from 1577 to 1580 in his ship Golden Hind. In 1616 Dutchmen sailed for the first time around the stormy **Cape Horn** at the southern tip of South America. In the 18th century the Briton **James Cook** explored the Pacific on several voyages around the world. On a French expedition in the 1760s Jeanne Baret travelled disguised as a man and so became the first woman to go around the world.

In March 1999 the Swiss **Bertrand Piccard** and the Briton Brian Jones were the first to fly around the Earth nonstop in a balloon. Their balloon was called Breitling Orbiter 3. From 2015 to 2016 Piccard and André Borschberg flew around the world in the solar aeroplane **Solar Impulse 2**. It needed not a drop of fuel, only the power of the sun.

begriffe.erklaerung: A journey by ship once all the way around the Earth.
A narrow stretch of water between two seas.
An imaginary line in the Pacific where the date changes.
A ship's diary in which all important events are written.
A piece of land that sticks far out into the sea.

gewusst: Of the roughly 240 men who set out with Magellan, only 18 came back with the Victoria.
The cargo of spices that the Victoria brought home was so valuable that it covered the costs of the voyage.
Solar Impulse 2 had wings wider than those of a large passenger aeroplane, but weighed only about as much as a car.

teile.einleitung: The Ostrogothic Kingdom was a kingdom of the Germanic Ostrogoths in Italy. It lasted from about 493 until the 550s and ended after a long war against the Byzantine Empire.
wichtigste: Its founder was King **Theoderic the Great**, and its capital was Ravenna.
The Goths provided the army, and the Romans carried on the administration.
After Theoderic’s death his daughter Amalasuntha ruled for her son Athalaric.
Her murder in 535 gave Emperor Justinian a reason for war.
The Byzantine general Belisarius took Ravenna in 540.
King Totila won back large parts of Italy and fell in 552.

abschnitte.text: At the end of the 5th century **Theoderic** marched into Italy with the Ostrogoths. In 493 he took power and made **Ravenna** his capital. He ruled for more than three decades and was later called **Theoderic the Great**. His stone tomb in Ravenna still survives today. His rule is seen as a time of relative calm in Italy.

In the Ostrogothic Kingdom the tasks were divided: the **Goths** made up the **army**, while the **Romans** carried on the civil **administration**. There was also a divide in faith. The Goths were **Arians**, a Christian movement with its own teaching. The Romans were Catholic Christians. Both groups lived side by side, but by their own rules.

After Theoderic’s death his educated daughter **Amalasuntha** ruled for her young son **Athalaric**. She was murdered in 535. Emperor **Justinian** used this as a reason for war. His general **Belisarius** took Ravenna in 540 and captured King Witigis. Afterwards King **Totila** won back large parts of Italy and even took Rome several times.
