In 552 he fell in the battle of **Busta Gallorum** against the general Narses, and soon afterwards the kingdom ended.

gewusst: Theoderic’s tomb in Ravenna has a roof made from a single huge block of stone.
Several buildings from the time of the Ostrogoths in Ravenna are UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

teile.einleitung: The East-West Schism is the split of Christendom into a Western and an Eastern church. The year 1054 is regarded as its symbolic beginning, but the separation developed over a long time.
wichtigste: Schism means split.
In 1054 papal envoys and the Patriarch of Constantinople excommunicated each other.
The disputes were about, among other things, the Filioque and the bread at communion.
The sack of Constantinople in 1204 deepened the split.
A union in 1439 did not last long.
In 1965 the excommunications were lifted, but the split remains.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages there were two great centres of Christendom: **Rome** in the West and **Constantinople** in the East. Over time they drifted apart. In the West people spoke Latin, in the East Greek. This separation gave rise to the **Roman Catholic** and the **Orthodox Church**.

In **1054** an embassy of the Pope travelled to Constantinople. It was led by Cardinal **Humbert of Silva Candida**. His opponent was the Patriarch **Michael Cerularius**. On **16 July 1054** Humbert laid a **bull of excommunication** against him on the altar of the **Hagia Sophia**. The Patriarch in turn replied with an excommunication of his own.

One point of dispute was the **Filioque**. In the creed the West added that the Holy Spirit proceeds “and from the Son”. The Eastern Church rejected this addition. They also argued about the bread at the **Eucharist**: the West used **unleavened** bread, the East **leavened** bread. This is called the **azymes dispute**. In addition there was the question of how much power the Pope should have.

The year **1204** was especially bad. In the **Fourth Crusade** Western crusaders conquered and plundered **Constantinople**. Afterwards they set up a **Latin Empire**. Many people in the East did not forget this for a long time. In **1439** the **Council of Ferrara-Florence** decided on a union. The Byzantine emperor hoped for help against the Ottomans. But in the East the clergy and the people largely rejected the union.

Only in **1965** did Pope **Paul VI** and Patriarch **Athenagoras** lift the mutual excommunications of 1054. This happened at the end of the **Second Vatican Council**. The church split itself, however, remains. Today there are many talks between the churches.

gewusst: There are also Orthodox parishes in Switzerland, for example Serbian, Greek and Russian ones.
The word “orthodox” means “of the right belief”.

teile.einleitung: Gunpowder is the oldest known explosive. It was invented in China and later changed the way war was fought in Europe.
wichtigste: Gunpowder consists of saltpetre, sulphur and charcoal.
Chinese alchemists probably discovered it while looking for a potion for eternal life.
The oldest known recipe was written down in China in the year 1044.
The Chinese “fire lance” was a tube of powder attached to a spear.
In Europe, according to legend, the monk Berthold Schwarz was regarded as the inventor.

abschnitte.text: Gunpowder is a mixture of three substances: **saltpetre**, **sulphur** and **charcoal**. Saltpetre makes up the largest part. It supplies the oxygen so that the powder burns very quickly. This produces a lot of hot gas and a loud bang. In a closed tube this gas can push a ball out.

Gunpowder was discovered in **China**. **Alchemists** were probably looking for a **potion for eternal life** and mixed various substances in doing so. The oldest known recipe was written down in the year **1044** in a book on the art of war. At first the powder was used for incendiary weapons and **fireworks**.

An early weapon was the **fire lance**. This was a tube of powder attached to a **spear**. When the powder was lit, a jet of flame shot forward. From such tubes the first **firearms** gradually developed. Along the trade routes the knowledge later reached the west.

In **Europe** gunpowder became known in the 13th century. According to legend it was invented by the monk **Berthold Schwarz** in Freiburg im Breisgau. Whether he really lived, however, is not certain. In the 14th century the first **cannons** appeared. They could destroy the walls of castles and towns. In this way castles gradually lost their value as protection.

gewusst: Many fireworks, for example on 1 August in Switzerland, still work today with gunpowder or similar mixtures.
Until the 19th century gunpowder was the most important propellant for guns and cannons.

teile.einleitung: The plague is a terrible disease caused by a bacterium. In the Middle Ages, as the “Black Death”, it killed about a third of the people in Europe. At that time nobody knew where the disease came from.
wichtigste: The plague is an infectious disease caused by a bacterium.
The great plague of the Middle Ages is also called the Black Death.
It was often spread by fleas that lived on rats.
The plague came to Europe on ships from 1347.
About a third of the people in Europe died of it.
It spread especially fast in crowded towns.
The word quarantine comes from the time of the plague.
Today the plague can be treated with antibiotics.

abschnitte.text: The plague is caused by the bacterium **Yersinia pestis**. It was discovered in 1894 by the doctor **Alexandre Yersin**, who was born in the canton of Vaud. The most common form is **bubonic plague**, in which large, painful swellings appear on the neck, under the arms or in the groin. In pneumonic plague the disease is passed directly from person to person by coughing.

The bacterium lives mainly in rodents such as rats. **Fleas** suck the blood of the sick animals and then bite people. This is how the bacterium gets into the blood. Because there were many rats in towns and little cleanliness, fleas found new victims everywhere.

The great plague came from Asia and reached the island of Sicily in 1347 on **ships**. From the port cities it spread across the whole of Europe within a few years. By about 1353 around a third of the population had died, in some towns even more. Switzerland, too, was hit hard in 1348 and 1349.

People did not know where the disease came from. Many thought it was a punishment from God or believed in poisonous vapours in the air. Jews were wrongly blamed, and there were cruel **persecutions**, including in Basel and Zurich. Whoever could fled to the countryside or kept away from the sick.

Port cities such as Venice and Ragusa, today’s Dubrovnik, made arriving ships wait for a while. People were only allowed ashore if nobody fell ill. Later this waiting period lasted 40 days, in Italian “quaranta giorni”. From this came the word **quarantine**, which we still use today.

Since **antibiotics** exist, the plague can be treated well if you see a doctor early. But it has not disappeared completely. In some parts of the world, for example in Madagascar, there are still individual cases. In Switzerland the plague no longer occurs today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny living thing made of a single cell that can cause diseases.
A form of plague with large, swollen lumps on the body.
A period during which people must stay apart so that no disease spreads.
A medicine that kills bacteria.
A disease that spreads to very many people in a short time.

gewusst: The well-known beaked masks of plague doctors do not come from the Middle Ages but from the 17th century.
The discoverer of the plague bacterium, Alexandre Yersin, grew up in French-speaking Switzerland.
After the Black Death so many workers were missing that farmers and craftsmen could sometimes demand higher wages.

teile.einleitung: Richard the Lionheart was King of England from 1189 to 1199. He became famous as a brave fighter, above all in the Third Crusade. To this day he appears in many stories, for example about Robin Hood.
wichtigste: Richard was King of England from 1189 and ruled for ten years.
He received the nickname Lionheart because he was regarded as very brave.
In the Third Crusade he fought against Sultan Saladin.
In 1191 he conquered the city of Acre together with the French king.
On the journey home he was captured in Austria in 1192.
Only in return for a huge ransom was he freed in 1194.
After his death in 1199 his brother John Lackland became king.

abschnitte.titel: A king with a lion’s heart
abschnitte.text: **Richard** was King of **England** from **1189**. He was regarded as a very **brave fighter**, so it was said that he had the heart of a lion. Richard, however, spent most of his life in **France**, where his family owned large territories. He spoke mainly **French** and probably hardly any English. He was only rarely in England itself.

Richard took part in the **Third Crusade** to the Holy Land. Together with the French king he conquered the port city of **Acre** in **1191** after a long siege. His great opponent was **Saladin**, sultan and ruler of Egypt and Syria. Richard and Saladin had great respect for each other. Richard could not conquer **Jerusalem**, however, and in the end he made a treaty with Saladin.

On the journey home Richard was taken prisoner in **Austria** in **1192**. **Duke Leopold** of Austria had him arrested and locked up in **Dürnstein Castle** on the Danube. Later he handed him over to the emperor. England had to pay a **huge ransom**. Only then was Richard freed in **1194**.

Richard died in **1199** in France of a wound from a fight. His brother **John**, called **John Lackland**, became king. In many stories about **Robin Hood** the good King Richard returns at the end. He rewards Robin Hood and puts an end to the unjust rulers. These stories, however, are legends and not established history.

gewusst: In front of the Parliament in London stands a large equestrian statue of Richard the Lionheart.
Only ruins are left today of Dürnstein Castle in the Wachau.

teile.einleitung: Ada Lovelace was an English mathematician of the 19th century. She was one of the first people to write a program for a calculating machine. That is why she is regarded as a pioneer of computers.
wichtigste: Ada Lovelace was born in London in 1815 and lived until 1852.
Her father was the famous poet Lord Byron.
She was especially gifted at mathematics.
She worked together with the inventor Charles Babbage.
In 1843 she wrote instructions that many see as the first computer program.
Through her marriage she became Countess of Lovelace.
The programming language “Ada” is named after her.

abschnitte.text: Ada was born in **1815** in **London**. Her father was the English poet **Lord Byron**. He left the family when Ada was still a baby. Her mother encouraged above all **mathematics**. Even as a child Ada received a lot of teaching and showed great talent for numbers and technology.

As a young woman Ada got to know the inventor **Charles Babbage**. He was an English mathematician. Babbage planned a large mechanical calculating machine, the **Analytical Engine**. It was to calculate with cogwheels and read instructions from punched cards. The machine was never completely built. Ada was enthusiastic and described everything it could do.

In **1843** Ada translated an article about Babbage's machine. She added long **notes** of her own. In them are exact **step-by-step instructions** with which the machine was to calculate certain numbers. Many see in this the **first computer program**. Ada also recognised that such machines could not only calculate but could, for example, also work with music.

In 1835 Ada married **William King**. In 1838 he became **Earl of Lovelace**. That is why she was called **Countess of Lovelace**. She died as early as **1852**, at only 36 years old. For a long time her work was almost forgotten. Only in the 20th century, when real computers existed, was its importance recognised.

Today Ada Lovelace is honoured as a **pioneer of computers**. A **programming language** bears her name: **“Ada”**. Every year in October there is **Ada Lovelace Day**. On this day people remember women in science and technology. So she is a role model for many young people.

gewusst: Ada Lovelace lived about a hundred years before the first electronic computers.
Babbage's machines were so complicated that one of his calculating machines was only completed to his plans in 1991.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages a guild was an association of craftsmen of the same trade, such as bakers, smiths or tailors. The guilds decided who was allowed to work and how good the goods had to be. In Zurich they even helped to govern the town, and the Sechseläuten still recalls them today.
wichtigste: A guild was an association of craftsmen of one trade.
A craftsman passed through the stages of apprentice, journeyman and master.
To become a master, a journeyman had to make a masterpiece.
The members gathered in the guildhall.
The guild monopoly meant that only guild members were allowed to practise the craft.
In 1336 Rudolf Brun gave the guilds in Zurich a say in the council.
The Zurich spring festival Sechseläuten still recalls the guilds today.

abschnitte.text: In medieval towns craftsmen joined together in **guilds**. There were guilds for bakers, butchers, smiths, shoemakers, weavers and many other trades. The guild fixed prices, working hours and the quality of the goods. It also helped sick members as well as widows and orphans.

As an **apprentice** a boy learned for several years with a master and often lived in his house. Afterwards he became a **journeyman** and often went travelling to learn more in other towns. To become a master he had to make a **masterpiece**. Only as a master was he allowed to run a workshop of his own and train apprentices.

The **guild monopoly** meant that in a town only guild members were allowed to practise a craft. In this way the craftsmen protected themselves from too much competition. The number of masters was often limited. For newcomers it was therefore hard to open a workshop of their own.

In 1336 **Rudolf Brun** introduced a new constitution in Zurich. After that, representatives of the guilds sat on the town council alongside the rich merchants. Until the end of the Old Swiss Confederacy in 1798 the guilds had a say in Zurich. In Basel, Schaffhausen and other towns, too, guilds had a great deal of political power.

Every guild had a **guildhall** where the members met, held discussions and celebrated. In Zurich many guildhalls stand on the Limmat, for example the Guildhall zur Meisen. Often a sign above the door shows which craft was at home there. Today many guildhalls house restaurants.

At the **Sechseläuten** in April the Zurich guilds parade through the town in old costumes. In the evening the **Böögg** is burned on the Sechseläutenplatz, a snowman made of cotton wool and firecrackers. The faster its head explodes, the better the summer is supposed to be. The name comes from the ringing of the bell at six o'clock, which formerly marked the end of the winter working hours.

begriffe.erklaerung: An association of the craftsmen of one trade in a town.
A craftsman who has finished his apprenticeship but is not yet a master.
A particularly good piece of work, made as a test to become a master.
The rule that only guild members were allowed to practise a craft.
A snowman figure that is burned at the Sechseläuten in Zurich.

gewusst: To this day some journeymen in Europe go on a traditional journey of travel called the “Walz”.
The Zurich guilds still exist today, but they mainly look after traditions and no longer have political power.
Because the crafts were so important, many family names such as Miller, Smith or Weaver come from old trades.

teile.einleitung: The Vikings were seafarers, traders and warriors from Scandinavia. From about 800 to 1050 they sailed across seas and rivers in their fast longships. They plundered monasteries, but also traded and founded settlements as far away as Iceland, Greenland and America.
wichtigste: The Vikings came from Scandinavia, that is, from present-day Norway, Sweden and Denmark.
They travelled over the sea in longships made of wood.
The Viking Age began around 793 with the raid on a monastery in England.
Besides fighting, the Vikings did a lot of trading.
They wrote with characters called runes.
Odin was their chief god, and Thor had a mighty hammer.
Leif Eriksson came to America as early as the year 1000.
Horns on helmets are a later invention.

abschnitte.text: The Vikings built their **longships** of wood, mostly oak. The ships were narrow, light and had a shallow draught, so they could also sail up rivers. They sailed with a large sail or were rowed. Well-preserved ships such as the **Oseberg ship** can be seen in a museum in Norway.

In 793 Vikings raided the monastery of **Lindisfarne** in England, which is regarded as the beginning of the Viking Age. Monasteries were rich and hardly protected. But the Vikings were also skilful **traders** who sold furs, amber and slaves and bought silver. Swedish Vikings travelled along Russian rivers as far as Constantinople, present-day Istanbul.

From about 870 Vikings settled the large island of **Iceland**. Erik the Red founded settlements in Greenland around 985. His son **Leif Eriksson** reached North America around the year 1000 and called the land Vinland. The remains of a Viking settlement were found at L'Anse aux Meadows on the island of Newfoundland in Canada.

The Vikings wrote with **runes**, characters made of straight strokes that were easy to carve in wood or stone. Their alphabet is called the **Futhark** after its first characters. In Scandinavia many rune stones that commemorate the dead still stand today. Their stories were later written down in Iceland as sagas.

The chief god was **Odin**, the god of wisdom and war. His son **Thor** swung the mighty hammer Mjölnir and was in charge of thunder and lightning. According to Viking belief, fallen warriors went to Valhalla. Around the year 1000 the Scandinavians gradually became Christians.

The Vikings did not wear **horned helmets** in battle, which is an invention of the 19th century, for example for theatre and opera. Their helmets were simple round iron helmets. Many Vikings were really farmers, fishermen and craftsmen. According to most experts the Viking Age ends around 1066.

begriffe.erklaerung: A region in the north of Europe with Norway, Sweden and Denmark.
A narrow, fast wooden ship of the Vikings with a sail and oars.
Old characters of the Germanic peoples and the Vikings.
An old story from Iceland about heroes, families and adventures.
In Viking belief, the hall of Odin for fallen warriors.

gewusst: The English weekday Thursday is named after the god Thor.
The Vikings came to America almost 500 years before Christopher Columbus.
The parliament of Iceland, the Althing, was founded as early as the year 930.

teile.einleitung: The Scientific Revolution was a period in the 16th and 17th centuries in which researchers began to explain the world in a completely new way. Instead of only believing old books, they observed, measured and experimented for themselves. In doing so they found out that the Earth goes around the Sun.
wichtigste: The Scientific Revolution took place mainly in the 16th and 17th centuries.
In 1543 Nicolaus Copernicus placed the Sun at the centre of the planetary system.
Johannes Kepler showed in 1609 that planets move around the Sun in elliptical orbits.
Galileo Galilei discovered the moons of Jupiter with the telescope around 1610.
Andreas Vesalius had his great anatomy book printed in Basel in 1543.
William Harvey described the circulation of the blood in 1628.
Isaac Newton set out the law of gravitation in 1687.

abschnitte.text: For a long time the **geocentric view of the world** of Ptolemy held, in which the Earth stands in the middle. In his book of 1543 **Nicolaus Copernicus** put the Sun in the middle. The theologian Andreas Osiander added an unsigned preface that presented the theory as a mere calculating model. Copernicus died in the same year in which his book appeared.

The Dane **Tycho Brahe** observed the sky without a telescope, but very precisely. With his data **Johannes Kepler** calculated that planets move in elliptical orbits, and published this in 1609. Around 1610 **Galileo Galilei** pointed a telescope at the sky and saw four moons that circle Jupiter. This showed that not everything revolves around the Earth.

The Church rejected the new teaching at the time, because it contradicted the customary interpretation of the Bible. In 1633 the **Inquisition** condemned Galileo. He had to renounce his teaching and lived under house arrest until his death. Only in 1992 did Pope John Paul II officially rehabilitate Galileo.

The physician **Andreas Vesalius** cut open corpses himself and in this way corrected the old teaching of the Greek physician Galen. His work “De humani corporis fabrica” was printed in **Basel** in 1543. The Englishman **William Harvey** described in 1628 that the heart pumps the blood around the body in a circuit. In Basel the physician Paracelsus, who came from Einsiedeln, had already taught around 1527.

The Englishman **Isaac Newton** published his work “Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica” in 1687. In it are the **laws of motion** and the law of gravitation. Newton showed that the same force makes an apple fall and keeps the Moon in orbit around the Earth. With that the Scientific Revolution is regarded as complete.

The researchers developed the **scientific method**. You make a guess, test it with observations and experiments and check it by calculating with mathematics. New inventions such as the telescope, microscope and pendulum clock helped. This way of researching is still the basis of all the natural sciences today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A view of the world in which the Sun stands in the middle.
A view of the world in which the Earth stands in the middle.
An elongated, oval shape of a circle.
The force of attraction between bodies, for example between the Earth and the Moon.
The study of how the body is built.

gewusst: The four large moons of Jupiter that Galileo discovered are now called the Galilean moons.
Tycho Brahe had an artificial nose made of metal because he had lost his real one in a duel.
Vesalius was only 28 years old when his famous anatomy book appeared in Basel.

teile.einleitung: Notre-Dame de Paris is one of the most famous churches in the world. The Gothic cathedral stands on an island in the Seine and was rebuilt after a great fire in 2019.
wichtigste: Notre-Dame stands in Paris on the Île de la Cité in the Seine.
“Notre-Dame” means “Our Lady” and refers to Mary.
Building began in 1163 and took almost 200 years.
In 1804 Napoleon crowned himself emperor here.
In April 2019 the roof burned and the pointed spire collapsed.
In December 2024 the cathedral reopened.

abschnitte.text: Notre-Dame stands in **Paris**, on the **Île de la Cité**. This island lies in the middle of the **Seine**. The oldest part of the city was already there. The name **Notre-Dame** means “Our Lady”. This refers to **Mary**, the mother of Jesus.

The foundation stone was laid in the year **1163**. Building work lasted almost **200 years**, until about 1345. Notre-Dame is a masterpiece of **Gothic** architecture. Typical features are the pointed arches, the tall windows and the coloured **rose windows**. On the outside, flying buttresses support the high walls.

In December **1804** a special coronation took place in Notre-Dame. **Napoleon Bonaparte** became Emperor of the French. The Pope was present, but Napoleon placed the crown on his own head **himself**. The painter **Jacques-Louis David** recorded the event in a huge painting.

The writer **Victor Hugo** wrote a novel about the cathedral in **1831**. In it **Quasimodo** rings the bells of Notre-Dame. The book became very famous. It also helped people value the old church again, and it was restored in the 19th century.

In **April 2019** a fire broke out in the roof. The slender, pointed **spire** collapsed. The two great main towers remained standing. People all over the world followed the fire. After more than five years of work, Notre-Dame reopened in **December 2024**.

gewusst: The roof frame made of old oak beams was called “the forest” because of its many beams.
In front of Notre-Dame lies the zero point from which road distances in France are measured.

teile.einleitung: The **Migration Period** is the name for a time when many peoples in Europe left their homelands and moved into new regions. It began around 375 and lasted into the 6th century. During this time the Western Roman Empire fell.
wichtigste: The Migration Period traditionally began in the year 375.
It was set off by the Huns, a people of horsemen from Asia.
The most famous king of the Huns was Attila.
In 476 Odoacer deposed the last Western Roman emperor.
The Vandals plundered Rome in 455.
In western Switzerland the Burgundians settled, in German-speaking Switzerland the Alamanni.

abschnitte.text: Around **375** the **Huns**, a people of horsemen from Asia, pushed into Europe. They defeated the **Ostrogoths** by the Black Sea. Many peoples fled west before them. That is why the year 375 is regarded as the beginning of the Migration Period. The most famous king of the Huns was **Attila**. He led great campaigns as far as Gaul and Italy.

In the Migration Period it was not only warriors who moved but **whole peoples** with their families and animals. Many were **Germanic peoples**, such as the Goths, Vandals, Franks or Lombards. They often moved into the **Roman Empire**, where there was fertile land and rich cities. Some fought against the Romans, others served them as soldiers. In time they founded kingdoms of their own.

The Western Roman Empire grew ever weaker. In **455** the **Vandals** plundered the city of Rome. That is where the word **vandalism** for wilful destruction comes from. In **476** the Germanic commander **Odoacer** deposed the last Western Roman emperor. He sent the imperial insignia to Constantinople and ruled Italy as king. With that the **Western Roman Empire** ended, while the Eastern Roman Empire carried on.

The area of present-day Switzerland changed too. The **Burgundians** settled in the west, around **Lake Geneva**. They took over the Latin language of the local people, and from it **French** later developed. The **Alamanni** moved into the north and east of present-day Switzerland. **Swiss German** descends from their language. So the language border in Switzerland is still connected today with the Migration Period.

gewusst: Many names of regions recall the peoples of the Migration Period, for example Burgundy after the Burgundians or Lombardy after the Lombards.
France takes its name from the Germanic people of the Franks.

teile.einleitung: The Song dynasty ruled over China from 960 to 1279. During this time trade, science and art flourished, and important inventions such as paper money appeared.
wichtigste: The Song dynasty ruled in China from 960 to 1279.
The first capital was Kaifeng.
In 1127 the Jurchen of the Jin dynasty conquered the north.
The Southern Song moved their court to Hangzhou.
Under the Song the state issued paper money, one of the first in the world.
Around 1040 Bi Sheng invented printing with movable type made of fired clay.
In 1279 the Mongols ended Song rule.

abschnitte.text: In the year **960** a general founded the **Song dynasty**. The first capital was **Kaifeng** in the north of China. In **1127** the **Jurchen** of the **Jin dynasty** conquered the north. The court fled south to **Hangzhou**. That is why people distinguish between the Northern Song and the Southern Song.

Under the Song the state issued **paper money**, one of the first in the world. In the province of **Sichuan** the **jiaozi** was introduced, the first state-issued paper money. Before that people had needed heavy strings of metal coins. Paper money was much easier to carry and made trade easier.

Around **1040** **Bi Sheng** invented printing with **movable type** made of fired clay. Each character was a small piece of its own that could be put together again and again. The **compass** was also used at sea in this period. **Gunpowder** was used for weapons and fireworks. The fine **porcelain** of the Song was famous too.

The **officials** of the state were chosen mainly through **difficult examinations**. Anyone who wanted to pass had to know many old writings and be able to write well. In this way men from ordinary families could also rise if they studied hard. Around the year **1100** about **100 million people** lived in the Song empire.

In the 13th century the **Mongols** attacked China. They conquered the north first and then, step by step, the south as well. In **1279** Song rule ended. The Mongol **Kublai Khan** founded the **Yuan dynasty** and now ruled the whole of China.

gewusst: A famous painting from the Song period shows life in a town by a river. The scroll is more than five metres long.
Hangzhou was regarded at that time as one of the largest and richest cities in the world.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages many new towns appeared in Europe, including in Switzerland. A town wall protected the people, and the market was full of bustle. People who lived in a town often had more freedoms than farmers in the countryside.
wichtigste: Medieval towns were surrounded by a town wall.
At night the town gates were closed.
At the market people bought and sold their goods.
The Dukes of Zähringen founded the town of Bern.
The free inhabitants of a town were called citizens.
The streets were mostly narrow and winding.
Fires were dangerous because many houses were made of wood.
“Town air makes you free” meant that serfs who had fled could become free in a town.

abschnitte.text: A **town wall** with towers and ditches protected the town from enemies. You could only get in through the **town gates**, which were closed at night. At the gate merchants often had to pay a toll. In Murten you can still walk along the old town wall today.

Many Swiss towns were founded in the High Middle Ages. The **Dukes of Zähringen** founded, among others, Fribourg and, in 1191, the town of **Bern**. Bern lies in a loop of the Aare, which protects the town on three sides. Other towns such as Zurich, Basel or Geneva were older and grew strongly in the Middle Ages.

In the centre lay the **market**, where farmers, craftsmen and merchants offered their goods. The largest building was often the **church**, whose tower could be seen from far away. In the **town hall** the councillors who governed the town met. Craftsmen joined together in guilds and later had a say as well.

The free inhabitants of a town were called **citizens**. They had rights, but also duties, for example to defend the town. A saying went “Town air makes you free”. A serf who fled from the countryside and lived undiscovered in the town for a certain time could become free.

The streets were mostly narrow and winding, and many people simply threw their rubbish into the street. Pigs ran around freely, and it often smelled bad. Because many houses were made of wood, a fire could destroy whole districts. After a great **town fire** in 1405 Bern was rebuilt mainly in sandstone.

At night the **night watchman** walked through the streets with a lantern and a spear. He called out the hours and watched for thieves. It was especially important that he spotted fires early and raised the alarm. In some Swiss towns there are still night watchmen today for tourists.

begriffe.erklaerung: A free inhabitant of a town with certain rights and duties.
A thick wall around the town as protection from enemies.
The building where the government of a town meets.
A peasant who depended on a lord and was not allowed to move away freely.
A fee that had to be paid when bringing goods into the town.

gewusst: The Zytglogge in Bern was formerly a town gate and for a time afterwards a prison.
In medieval towns there were often streets named after the craftsmen who worked there.
Most medieval towns had only a few thousand inhabitants, far fewer than today.

teile.einleitung: In the **Treaty of Tordesillas** in 1494, Spain and Portugal divided the newly discovered parts of the world between themselves. An imaginary line in the Atlantic was to be the boundary. The consequences can still be seen today, for example in the language of Brazil.
wichtigste: The treaty was signed in 1494 at Tordesillas in the Kingdom of Castile.
The dividing line lay 370 leagues west of the Cape Verde Islands.
A league was an old measure of distance of a few kilometres.
Because of the treaty, Portuguese is spoken in Brazil today.
The native peoples were not asked.
The Treaty of Zaragoza in 1529 fixed a boundary on the other side of the world.

abschnitte.text: After the first voyage of Columbus in 1492, **Spain** and **Portugal** quarrelled over who should own the new territories. Both countries were then the most important sea powers of Europe. In **1494** they made a treaty at **Tordesillas**. The place lies on the River Duero near Valladolid and belonged to the Kingdom of **Castile**.

The treaty fixed a line from pole to pole. It ran **370 leagues** west of the **Cape Verde Islands**, that is, about **2,000 kilometres**. A **league** was an old Spanish and Portuguese measure of distance of a few kilometres, whose exact length was not uniform. Territories west of the line were to belong to Spain, east of it to Portugal. An earlier boundary line of 1493 had lain much closer to Africa.

Portuguese ships sailed around Africa to India. On the way they had to sail far out into the **South Atlantic** to use favourable winds. A line too close to Africa would have hindered these routes. That is why Portugal wanted the boundary moved farther west. It succeeded in the Treaty of Tordesillas.

The eastern part of South America lay east of the line. Portugal took it into possession from **1500**. That is why **Portuguese** is spoken in **Brazil** today, while Spanish is spoken in most other countries of South America. After the first voyage around the world, the two countries also quarrelled over the Spice Islands, the **Moluccas**. In the **Treaty of Zaragoza** of **1529** Spain sold its claims there to Portugal.

The two sea powers distributed lands in which **millions of people** lived. The **native peoples** were not asked, and their rights played no role. Other European countries such as England, France or the Netherlands also later refused to recognise the division. Today the treaty is seen as an example of how Europe wanted to divide the world among itself.

gewusst: Brazil later became much larger than the line of Tordesillas actually allowed.
The exact course of the line could not be measured at the time, because there was no precise method yet for determining longitude.

teile.einleitung: The **Vandals** were a Germanic people. During the Migration Period they travelled right across Europe to North Africa. There they founded a kingdom of their own with its capital at Carthage.
wichtigste: Around 406 the Vandals crossed the Rhine with the Alans and Suebi.
Under King Gaiseric they crossed over to North Africa in 429.
In 439 they conquered Carthage and made it their capital.
In 455 they plundered the city of Rome.
Their last king, Gelimer, surrendered to an Eastern Roman army in 534.
The word vandalism goes back to their name.

abschnitte.text: At the turn of the year **406 to 407** the Vandals crossed the **Rhine** together with the **Alans** and **Suebi**, probably near Mainz. Afterwards they moved through **Gaul**, present-day France, plundering as they went. Finally they came to **Spain**. There they stayed for about 20 years.

In **429** King **Gaiseric** led his people across the **Strait of Gibraltar** to North Africa. At its narrowest point this stretch of sea separates Spain and Morocco by only about **14 kilometres**. About **80,000 people** are said to have crossed. In **430** the Vandals besieged the city of **Hippo Regius** in present-day Algeria. During the siege the famous Church Father **Augustine**, who was bishop of the city, died there.

In **439** the Vandals conquered **Carthage** in present-day Tunisia. It was one of the richest cities of the Western Roman Empire. Gaiseric made Carthage his capital. With a **fleet** of their own the Vandals controlled the western Mediterranean. Gaiseric ruled for about 50 years and made his people a sea power.

abschnitte.titel: The sack of Rome and the end
abschnitte.text: In **455** the Vandals sailed to Italy and **plundered Rome**. They took many treasures with them to Africa. About 80 years later the Eastern Roman emperor sent an army to Africa. The last king, **Gelimer**, had to surrender in **534**. He was taken to **Constantinople** and afterwards received an estate in Asia Minor. With that the kingdom of the Vandals came to an end.

Today senseless destruction is called **vandalism**. The word was coined in **1794** in France. It referred to the sack of Rome, in which the Vandals were imagined as especially destructive. Many historians today think that the Vandals were no worse than other conquerors of their time. The name has stuck all the same.

gewusst: Gaiseric ruled for about 50 years, as long as hardly any other king of his time.
The Vandals probably came originally from the area of present-day Poland.

teile.einleitung: In the year 1066 Duke William of Normandy conquered England. This Norman Conquest changed the country greatly, from its language to the owners of the land.
wichtigste: Edward the Confessor died childless in January 1066.
Several men claimed the English throne.
Harald Hardrada of Norway fell at Stamford Bridge.
William landed in the south of England a few days later.
In 1086 he had the Domesday Book compiled.
Normans replaced the Anglo-Saxon nobility.

abschnitte.text: On **5 January 1066** the English king **Edward the Confessor** died without a son. Three men at once claimed the throne: **Harold Godwinson**, **William of Normandy** and the King of Norway, **Harald Hardrada**. Harold Godwinson was crowned king first.

In September 1066 Harald Hardrada landed in **northern England**. At **Stamford Bridge** he was defeated and killed by the English army. A few days later William landed in the **south**. In October the decisive battle took place at **Hastings**. Harold Godwinson fell, and William became king at Christmas 1066. He is called **William the Conqueror**.

William had many castles built. In London a stone keep was built, the **White Tower**. From it the **Tower of London** developed. There were uprisings in northern England. In **1069 to 1070** William put them down by having villages and supplies destroyed. This **devastation of the North** led to famines.

In **1086** William had a great survey drawn up, the **Domesday Book**. It recorded the **landholdings**, livestock and taxable wealth of almost all of England. It gave the Crown a basis for taxes and feudal rights. Many places in the north are still recorded in it as waste.

William seized the land of the defeated **Anglo-Saxons**. He gave it out as **fiefs** to his followers. By about 1086 the Anglo-Saxon high nobility had almost completely been pushed out. At court people now spoke **Anglo-Norman**, a form of Old French. This remained so for about three centuries. That is why many English words come from French.

gewusst: The Bayeux Tapestry, an embroidery about 70 metres long, tells the story of the conquest in pictures.
English words such as “beef” and “pork” come from the French of the Normans.

teile.einleitung: Adam Smith was a Scottish philosopher and economist of the 18th century. His book “The Wealth of Nations” of 1776 is regarded as the founding work of classical economics. He is best known for the image of the “invisible hand”.
wichtigste: Adam Smith was born in 1723 in Kirkcaldy in Scotland.
He taught moral philosophy in Glasgow.
In 1759 his work “The Theory of Moral Sentiments” appeared.
In 1776 he published “The Wealth of Nations”.
With the “invisible hand” he described how self-interest can serve the common good through the market.
He explained the advantages of division of labour using a pin factory.
He sharply criticised mercantilism.

abschnitte.text: Adam Smith was born in **1723** in **Kirkcaldy** in **Scotland**. He studied at Glasgow and Oxford. Later he taught **moral philosophy** at the University of **Glasgow**. He is one of the main figures of the **Scottish Enlightenment**. Among his friends was the philosopher David Hume.

As early as **1759** Smith published the **“Theory of Moral Sentiments”**. In this work he stresses **sympathy** as the basis of living together. People put themselves in the place of others and want to be respected by them. This shows that Smith did not rely only on **self-interest**. For him morality and the economy belonged together.

From 1764 to 1766 Smith accompanied the young **Duke of Buccleuch** as **tutor** on a journey. It led through France and to **Geneva**. There he met the philosopher **Voltaire** several times, whom he greatly admired. In France he also got to know economists who were thinking about agriculture and trade. These encounters shaped his later main work.

In **1776** **“The Wealth of Nations”** appeared, in the same year as the American Declaration of Independence. Smith asked what the wealth of a country depends on. His answer: on **work** and on free **exchange**. Using the example of a **pin factory** he explained the **division of labour**. Ten specialised workers together made over 48,000 pins a day, while one person without division of labour could hardly make twenty.

Smith wrote that whoever seeks his own advantage often promotes the good of society without intending to. He spoke of an **“invisible hand”**. The term, however, appears only once in the work. Smith sharply criticised **mercantilism**. This doctrine saw the wealth of a country in hoarded gold and silver and relied on **customs duties**. To this day people with very different opinions appeal to Smith.

gewusst: In his last years Adam Smith worked, of all things, as a customs officer in Edinburgh.
From 2007 his picture could be seen on the British 20-pound note.

teile.einleitung: Bartolomeu Dias was a seafarer from Portugal. In 1488 he was the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa, showing that there is a sea route to the east.
wichtigste: Bartolomeu Dias sailed on behalf of the Portuguese king.
In 1488 he was the first European to sail around the southern tip of Africa.
Because of the violent storms he called the cape “Cape of Storms”.
The king gave it the name “Cape of Good Hope”.
The cape lies in present-day South Africa.
Because his crew wanted to go home, Dias had to turn back.

abschnitte.text: In the 15th century spices from Asia were very valuable in Europe. The kings of **Portugal** were looking for a **sea route to India** so as to trade directly. So they sent ships ever farther south along the coast of Africa. In 1487 **Bartolomeu Dias** was given the task of going farther than anyone before him.

Dias sailed south with small ships called **caravels**. Violent storms drove the ships far out to sea. When Dias turned east and north again, he noticed that he had already sailed around the southern tip of Africa. That was in 1488. Now it was known: beyond Africa the sea goes on to the east.

On the way back Dias saw the famous cape. Because he had experienced such bad weather there, he called it the **Cape of Storms**. The Portuguese king later gave it a new name: **Cape of Good Hope**. He now hoped for the sea route to India. The cape lies near **Cape Town** in present-day **South Africa**.

Dias really wanted to sail on to India. But the **crew** was tired and afraid. So he had to turn back. A few years later **Vasco da Gama** reached India by this route. Dias himself lost his life in 1500 in a storm near the cape.

gewusst: The southernmost point of Africa is not the Cape of Good Hope but the nearby Cape Agulhas.
On the way Dias set up stone pillars to show that Portugal had been there.

teile.einleitung: Easter Island is a small island in the middle of the Pacific, very far from any mainland. It is famous for its huge stone figures, the moai.
wichtigste: The locals call their island **Rapa Nui**.
The Dutchman Jacob Roggeveen reached it on Easter Sunday 1722.
This is where the name Easter Island comes from.
Since 1888 the island has belonged to Chile.
Hundreds of large stone figures, the moai, stand on the island.

abschnitte.text: The best-known monuments on the island are the **moai**, large stone figures with long faces. The inhabitants carved them many centuries ago, mostly from the rock of an old volcano. Many moai stood on stone platforms and looked inland. They probably recalled important ancestors. Experts are still researching how the heavy figures were transported.

The island was settled by **Polynesians**, who crossed the Pacific in boats. Their descendants call the island, their people and their language **Rapa Nui**. The Dutchman **Jacob Roggeveen** was searching the Pacific for an unknown southern land. He reached the island as the first known European on **Easter Sunday 1722** and therefore named it Easter Island.

Since **1888** Easter Island has belonged to **Chile**, although it lies thousands of kilometres from the South American mainland. At around 160 square kilometres the island is quite small. Today people live mainly from tourism. A large part of the island is a national park and a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: Easter Island is one of the most remote inhabited islands in the world.
The island had its own script of signs called Rongorongo, which has still not been reliably deciphered.

t1r6gw36.t: The atomic bombings of Hiroshima and Nagasaki

teile.einleitung: In August 1945, shortly before the end of the Second World War, the USA dropped two atomic bombs on the Japanese cities of Hiroshima and Nagasaki. It was the first and so far only time that nuclear weapons have been used in a war. Over 200,000 people died of the consequences by the end of 1945.
wichtigste: On 6 August 1945 the atomic bomb “Little Boy” was dropped on Hiroshima.
The bomber that dropped it was called Enola Gay.
On 9 August 1945 the bomb “Fat Man” fell on Nagasaki, because the main target Kokura was covered by cloud.
The bombs were developed in the American Manhattan Project.
By the end of 1945 an estimated 200,000 people or more had died.
The survivors are called hibakusha in Japan.
On 2 September 1945 Japan signed the surrender on the USS Missouri.

abschnitte.text: During the Second World War the USA feared that Germany might build an atomic bomb. So the American government started the secret **Manhattan Project**. Thousands of experts worked on it, and the scientific director at the Los Alamos laboratory was the physicist **Robert Oppenheimer**. On 16 July 1945 the first atomic bomb exploded in the desert of New Mexico in a test called **Trinity**.

Germany had surrendered in May 1945, but Japan fought on. On the morning of 6 August 1945 the bomber **Enola Gay** dropped the bomb **Little Boy** over Hiroshima. It contained **uranium** and exploded at 8.15 local time above the city. A huge fireball, a blast wave and fires destroyed most of the city centre. By the end of 1945 an estimated 140,000 people had died in Hiroshima.

Three days later a second bomber took off with the bomb **Fat Man**, which contained **plutonium**. The real target was the city of **Kokura**, but there cloud and smoke blocked the view. The crew therefore flew on to Nagasaki and dropped the bomb there. In Nagasaki an estimated 70,000 people had died by the end of 1945.

Many people died at once from the heat and blast wave, others weeks later from their burns. The bombs also released dangerous **radiation**. Years later survivors fell ill with **radiation sickness** and with cancer, for example leukaemia. The survivors are called **hibakusha** in Japan, and many of them still tell of their experiences today so that something like this never happens again.

On 8 August 1945 the Soviet Union also declared war on Japan. On 15 August the Japanese emperor **Hirohito** announced on the radio that Japan was giving up. On 2 September 1945 Japan signed the surrender on the battleship **USS Missouri** in Tokyo Bay. With that the Second World War was over. Whether the atomic bombs were necessary to end the war is still debated today.

In Hiroshima today stands the **Peace Park** with a museum. The ruin of the **Atomic Bomb Dome** was left standing as a memorial and has been part of the UNESCO World Heritage since 1996. Every year on 6 August a memorial ceremony takes place there. In 2024 the organisation of survivors, **Nihon Hidankyo**, received the Nobel Peace Prize for its work against nuclear weapons.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bomb that produces a huge explosion by splitting atomic nuclei.
A heavy atomic nucleus, for example of uranium, is split, and a great deal of energy is released.
Invisible energy that arises in an atomic explosion and can make the body ill.
The Japanese word for the survivors of the atomic bombings.
The declaration that one gives up a war and yields.

gewusst: The girl Sadako Sasaki from Hiroshima folded hundreds of paper cranes while she was ill, which is why paper cranes are a symbol of peace today.
The ruin of the Atomic Bomb Dome was formerly an exhibition hall for industrial products.
Little Boy and Fat Man are the only atomic bombs ever used in a war.

teile.einleitung: William the Conqueror was Duke of Normandy and became King of England in 1066. His conquest changed England for ever: language, nobility and buildings were given a new stamp.
wichtigste: William was Duke of Normandy in the north of France.
In 1066 he crossed the English Channel with his army.
In the Battle of Hastings he defeated King Harold.
On Christmas Day 1066 he was crowned in Westminster Abbey.
He had the Tower built in London, and its oldest part is called the White Tower.
In 1086 he had all possessions written down in the Domesday Book.

abschnitte.text: William was born around 1028 in **Normandy**. Normandy lies in the north of **France**. As a child he already became **duke** after his father died. For a long time he had to hold his own against opponents in his own country. The Normans were partly descended from Vikings who had settled there.

In 1066 the English king Edward died without children. **Harold** became the new king. William thought the crown was due to him. He built a fleet and brought his army and many **horses** across the **English Channel**. The English Channel is the sea between France and England.

In October 1066 the armies met at **Hastings**. The battle lasted a whole day. King Harold fell in the fighting. Afterwards William could conquer England. On **25 December 1066**, Christmas Day, he was crowned king in **Westminster Abbey** in London.

To secure the land William had many **castles** built. In London a strong stone castle arose, the **Tower of London**. Its oldest part is called the **White Tower**. Norman nobles received land and replaced the English nobility. At court people now spoke French, which is why the English language still has many French words today.

In 1086 William had a count made throughout England of who owned what. **Land, people and animals** were written down. Everything is in the **Domesday Book**. In this way the king knew exactly how much tax he could demand. The book is today an important source for the history of England. William died in 1087.

gewusst: The conquest is shown on the Bayeux Tapestry, an embroidery about 70 metres long.
The Domesday Book is kept today in the National Archives in London.

teile.einleitung: The Behaim Globe is the oldest surviving terrestrial globe in the world. It was made around 1492 in Nuremberg according to the details of Martin Behaim. Because it is so round, it was also called the “Earth apple”.
wichtigste: The Behaim Globe is the oldest surviving terrestrial globe.
It was made around 1492 in Nuremberg.
Martin Behaim, a merchant from Nuremberg, supplied the details for it.
The globe was also called the “Erdapfel”, the Earth apple.
America is missing from it, because it was not yet known in Europe.
Today the globe stands in the Germanic National Museum in Nuremberg.

abschnitte.text: **Martin Behaim** came from a merchant family in **Nuremberg**. He lived for a long time in **Portugal**, where many seafarers set out on voyages of discovery at that time. When he came back to his home town, he had a globe built there. The work lasted from about 1492 to 1494. A painter painted the sphere with countries, seas, pictures and many inscriptions.

The globe is a **sphere** with a diameter of about half a metre. Because of its round shape it was called the “**Erdapfel**”, the Earth apple. Educated people had known for a long time that the Earth is round. The Behaim Globe therefore shows it as a sphere. It is the oldest terrestrial globe that still exists today.

The globe was finished before people in Europe knew about **America**. Christopher Columbus had indeed set sail in 1492, but the news was not yet known. That is why where America lies there is mostly **sea** to be seen. Asia is much too large on the globe, and the Atlantic looks very narrow. This is how people imagined at that time that one could sail quickly across the Atlantic to Asia.

Nuremberg lies in **Bavaria** in **Germany**. There the Behaim Globe stands today in the **Germanic National Museum**. It is an important witness of how people saw the world at the end of the Middle Ages. Researchers still examine it closely today to understand all the pictures and texts on it.

gewusst: On the Behaim Globe there are over a thousand place names and many small explanations.
The word “globe” comes from Latin and means “sphere”.

teile.einleitung: Sandro Botticelli was an important painter of the Renaissance in Florence. His paintings “Primavera” and “The Birth of Venus” are among the most famous paintings in the world.
wichtigste: Botticelli lived from about 1445 to 1510.
He lived and worked most of the time in Florence.
His nickname means roughly “little barrel”.
In the “Adoration of the Magi” he painted members of the Medici family.
The “Primavera” shows a garden with goddesses and flowers.
Around 1481 he painted frescoes in the Sistine Chapel in Rome.
His most famous paintings hang today in the Uffizi.

abschnitte.text: Botticelli was actually called **Alessandro Filipepi**. He was born around 1445 in **Florence** and spent almost his whole life there. He probably inherited his nickname from his older brother, who was called “Botticello”. This means roughly **“little barrel”**. Botticelli trained with the painter Filippo Lippi and later opened a workshop of his own.

abschnitte.titel: In the service of the Medici
abschnitte.text: The rich **Medici** family ruled Florence at the time and supported artists. Botticelli created many pictures for their circle. In the **“Adoration of the Magi”** he painted members of the Medici as companions of the Three Kings. At the right edge of the picture he probably painted himself, looking at the viewer.

The **“Primavera”** is Italian and means **“spring”**. The painting shows a garden full of flowers with goddesses and other figures from old myths. Researchers have identified hundreds of different plants in it. Just as famous is **“The Birth of Venus”**: the goddess is blown ashore on a large shell. Both paintings hang today in the **Uffizi**, a museum in Florence.

Around **1481** the Pope called Botticelli to Rome. Together with other well-known painters he decorated the walls of the **Sistine Chapel** with **frescoes**. A fresco is painted on fresh, still damp plaster. The famous ceiling of the chapel was only painted later by Michelangelo.

In Florence the monk **Girolamo Savonarola** later preached. He called on people to repent and criticised luxury and worldly art. Under his influence Botticelli is said to have painted mainly serious, **religious pictures**. Botticelli died in 1510. After that he was almost forgotten for a long time; only in the 19th century was he admired greatly again.

gewusst: “The Birth of Venus” is shown on the Italian 10-cent coin.
Botticelli painted many pictures not in oil paint but in tempera, a paint that was often bound with egg yolk.

teile.einleitung: Moai are huge stone figures on Easter Island in the Pacific. The people of the island, the Rapa Nui, made them many hundreds of years ago in honour of their ancestors.
wichtigste: Moai are large stone figures with big heads.
Most were carved from volcanic rock in the Rano Raraku crater.
They were meant to represent dead ancestors.
There are almost 1,000 moai.
Many stand on stone platforms called ahu.
Most look inland.

abschnitte.text: **Moai** are huge stone figures with big heads. They stand on **Easter Island** in the Pacific. About **a thousand** moai are known on the island. Most are around **4 metres** tall and weigh about **12 tonnes**. The largest moai that was put up measures almost 10 metres.

Most moai were carved from soft **volcanic rock**. The most important quarry was **Rano Raraku**, an old volcanic crater made of **tuff**. Almost half of all moai still lie or stand there today. Some were never finished and are still stuck in the rock.

The moai were meant to represent important **ancestors**. People believed that they protected the village. Many stand on large stone platforms called **ahu**. Most stand on the coast but look **inland** towards the villages. It seems as if they were watching over the people.

Some moai wear red hats called **pukao**. They were carved from reddish **volcanic slag** in the **Puna Pau** quarry and probably represent hair knots. Eyes were set into some moai. The white part was made of **coral**, the pupil of dark **obsidian** or red slag. With eyes, a moai was thought to be alive.

gewusst: Many moai fell over in the course of time and were only set up again in the 20th century.
Easter Island belongs to Chile today.

teile.einleitung: Rudolf of Habsburg was a count from the area of present-day Switzerland who became King of the Romans in 1273. With him began the rise of the Habsburgs to one of the most powerful families in Europe.
wichtigste: Rudolf was first Count of Habsburg, whose ancestral castle stands in the present-day canton of Aargau.
In 1264 he inherited the lands of the Counts of Kyburg and gained a lot of territory in eastern and central Switzerland.
In 1273, aged about 55, he was elected king.
This ended the kingless period, the Interregnum.
In 1278 he defeated King Ottokar II of Bohemia on the Marchfeld.
He gave the Duchy of Austria to his sons.
He was never crowned by the Pope and therefore remained king, not emperor.

abschnitte.text: Rudolf was born in 1218. His family had its ancestral castle, the **Habsburg**, in the present-day canton of **Aargau**. As a **count** he already owned a lot of land on the Upper Rhine and in the Swiss Plateau. In 1264 the **Kyburgs**, a powerful family of counts, died out. Rudolf inherited their territories and so became the most important lord in eastern and central Switzerland.

Before Rudolf there had long been no generally recognised king in the empire. This period is called the **Interregnum**, “rule in between”. In 1273 the prince-electors chose Rudolf as **King of the Romans**. He was already about **55 years old** at the time. The princes probably hoped that a king who was not too powerful would not be dangerous to them.

Rudolf’s greatest opponent was King **Ottokar II of Bohemia**. He did not want to recognise Rudolf and also ruled Austria. In 1278 the battle on the **Marchfeld** east of Vienna took place. Rudolf won, and Ottokar was killed. Afterwards Rudolf gave the Duchy of **Austria** to his sons. In this way he laid the foundation for the long rule of the Habsburgs in Austria.

At that time a king only became **emperor** once the **Pope** had crowned him in Rome. Rudolf did plan a journey to Rome, but the coronation never happened. That is why he remained king. He died in 1291 and was buried in **Speyer Cathedral**, where other rulers already lay.

For the valley communities of central Switzerland Rudolf was a powerful neighbour. Shortly after his death in 1291 **Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden** concluded the well-known **Federal Charter**. Later there were many conflicts between the Swiss Confederates and the Habsburgs. The Habsburg family, however, went on ruling in Austria for centuries.

gewusst: You can still visit the small Habsburg Castle near Brugg in the canton of Aargau today.
The Federal Charter of 1291 was made only a few weeks after Rudolf’s death.

teile.einleitung: Raphael was one of the most famous painters of the Italian Renaissance. He lived from 1483 to 1520 and created large wall paintings and many well-known paintings of the Madonna in Rome.
wichtigste: Raphael was born in Urbino in 1483.
As a young painter he probably worked with Pietro Perugino.
Pope Julius II brought him to Rome around 1508.
With his workshop he painted the Stanze in the Vatican Palace.
His “Sistine Madonna” hangs in Dresden today.
Raphael is buried in the Pantheon in Rome.

abschnitte.text: **Raphael** was born in **Urbino** in Italy in **1483**. His father was **court painter** there and taught him the first basics. As a young artist Raphael probably worked in the workshop of **Pietro Perugino**. His early paintings look very similar to Perugino’s. After that he learned a great deal in **Florence** from other great artists.

Around **1508** Pope **Julius II** brought Raphael to **Rome**. He was to paint rooms in the **Vatican Palace**. These rooms are called the **Stanze**, from the Italian word “stanza” for room. With his workshop Raphael painted large **frescoes** there, that is, pictures on fresh plaster. Best known is the **“School of Athens”** with many scholars of antiquity. The same pope also gave Michelangelo large commissions.

Raphael painted many **Madonnas**, that is, pictures of Mary with the infant Jesus. Especially famous is the **“Sistine Madonna”**. In 1754 the Elector of Saxony bought the painting, and it has hung in **Dresden** ever since. At the bottom edge **two thoughtful little angels** lean on a ledge. Today they can be seen on many postcards and posters.

Raphael died in Rome in **1520**, aged only **37**. He had wished to be buried in the **Pantheon**, an ancient building in Rome. His tomb can still be seen there. Towards the end Raphael also directed building work on the new St Peter’s Basilica. His clear, harmonious paintings became a model for centuries.

gewusst: Raphael died on a Good Friday, and according to old tradition he was also born on a Good Friday.
The Pantheon in Rome is almost 2,000 years old and has a huge dome with an open hole in the middle.

teile.einleitung: Benjamin Franklin was a printer, inventor, researcher and politician from America. He is one of the founders of the United States and is still pictured on the 100-dollar note today.
wichtigste: Benjamin Franklin was born in Boston in 1706.
As a young man he learned the trade of printer.
He researched lightning and invented the lightning rod.
He is credited with bifocal spectacles for near and far.
In 1731 he founded a lending library with friends.
From 1776 he won help in France for the independence of the USA.
He is pictured on the 100-dollar note, but was never president.

abschnitte.text: Benjamin Franklin was born in 1706 in **Boston**. He had many brothers and sisters, and the family was not rich. With his older brother he learned the trade of **printer**. At 17 he moved to **Philadelphia**. There he later owned a printing shop and a newspaper of his own.

Franklin was very interested in **electricity**. According to tradition, in 1752 he flew a **kite** during a thunderstorm. In this way he wanted to show that lightning is electric current. This was very dangerous, and you must never copy it. From his research came the **lightning rod**, which protects houses from lightning.

Franklin liked to think about things of everyday life. He is credited with **spectacles for near and far**. He divided the lenses into two halves: the top for seeing into the distance, the bottom for reading. He also developed an economical stove. For many of his inventions he wanted no money, they were meant to be useful to everyone.

Books were expensive at that time. That is why in 1731 Franklin founded, with friends, a **library** from which the members could borrow books. He thought reading and learning very important. Later he also helped to found a school that became a university.

Franklin worked to make the American colonies **independent** of Britain. In 1776 he signed the **Declaration of Independence**. From 1776 he lived for some years in **France**. There he persuaded the French king to help the Americans. Franklin died in 1790 in Philadelphia.

gewusst: Benjamin Franklin was never president of the USA and is still on the 100-dollar note.
For years Franklin published a popular almanac with sayings and advice.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Legnica took place in 1241 in Silesia. A Mongol army defeated an army under Duke Henry II of Silesia there.
wichtigste: The battle took place in April 1241 at Legnica in Silesia.
The Mongols defeated the army of Duke Henry II the Pious.
Henry II fell in the battle.
His mother was Saint Hedwig of Silesia.
Only two days later the Mongols won at Mohi in Hungary.
Legnica, in German Liegnitz, is in Poland today.

abschnitte.text: In the 13th century the **Mongols** conquered a huge empire in Asia. In 1241 their armies advanced as far as Central Europe. One part marched through Poland to **Silesia**, while another part attacked **Hungary** at the same time. The Mongol riders were very fast and skilled with bow and arrow.

On 9 April 1241 **Duke Henry II the Pious** of Silesia faced the Mongols with his army at **Legnica**. The Mongols won, and Henry **fell** in the battle. Only **two days later** the Mongols also defeated the Hungarian army in the **Battle of Mohi**. After that, however, they did not advance further west but withdrew again in 1242.

Henry’s mother was **Hedwig of Silesia**. She was honoured for her piety and her help for the poor and was later declared a saint. A monastery was built at the site of the battle; the place is now called Legnickie Pole, in German Wahlstatt. The town of **Liegnitz** is now called **Legnica** and lies in **Poland**.

gewusst: Saint Hedwig is still an important saint in Poland and Silesia today.

teile.einleitung: The warhorse was the horse on which a knight rode into battle. It was strong, well trained and very valuable.
wichtigste: A warhorse was the strong fighting horse of a knight.
A good warhorse was very expensive.
Warhorses were mostly stallions.
It learned to stay calm in the noise of battle.
With spurs the knight urged his horse on, and the stirrups gave him support.
Some warhorses wore armour of their own or a colourful cloth with the coat of arms.
On journeys the knight rode a different horse to spare the warhorse.

abschnitte.text: A **warhorse** was a knight’s most important horse. It had to be strong, brave and fast. They were mostly **stallions**, because these were thought to be stronger and more spirited. A good warhorse was **very expensive**, much more than an ordinary horse. That is why only rich people could afford such a horse.

A warhorse was trained for many years. It learned to **stay calm in the noise of battle**, when weapons clashed and people screamed. It had to make quick turns and respond to small signals from the rider. A frightened horse would have been dangerous in battle.

With the **spurs** on his heels the knight urged his horse on. The **stirrups** gave him a firm seat. In this way he could stay on the horse in the **lance charge**, even when he hit his opponent with full force. A high saddle with a backrest also helped with this.

Some warhorses wore **armour of their own**, for example protection for the head and chest. Often a **colourful cloth** lay over the horse. On it the knight’s **coat of arms** could be seen. In this way people could tell in battle or at a tournament who was sitting on the horse.

On journeys a knight mostly did not ride his warhorse but another, more comfortable horse. In this way the warhorse was **spared** and stayed fresh for battle. For the luggage there were separate **packhorses**. A squire often led the warhorse alongside him.

gewusst: Warhorses were probably not as huge as is often thought. They were mainly strong and agile.
Another word for warhorse is “destrier”.

teile.einleitung: A **moated castle** is a castle surrounded by water. Instead of on a mountain, it protected itself with ditches, a lake or a river. A well-known moated castle in Switzerland is Hallwyl Castle in Aargau.
wichtigste: A moated castle is surrounded by water.
Moated castles were often built on flat land.
The water kept attackers away.
Attackers could hardly dig a tunnel under the wall.
Hallwyl Castle in the canton of Aargau stands on two islands.

abschnitte.text: Many castles stood high on a mountain or rock. On **flat land**, however, there was no mountain for protection. So there the castle was protected with **water**. Around the castle people dug **moats** or built it in a lake or river. You got in over a **drawbridge**. If the bridge was pulled up, the castle was cut off by the water.

In a siege attackers sometimes tried to dig a **tunnel** under the castle wall. In this way they wanted to bring the wall down or get in secretly. With a moated castle this hardly worked. Water ran into every tunnel at once. Ladders and siege towers also found it hard to get up to the wall because of the water.

A well-known moated castle in Switzerland is **Hallwyl Castle** in the canton of **Aargau**. It stands on **two islands** and is surrounded by moats. The castle lies near **Lake Hallwil**. For a long time it belonged to the Hallwyl family. Today it is a museum that shows how people lived there in the past.

gewusst: Bottmingen Castle in the canton of Basel-Landschaft is also a moated castle.
Many moated castles were later converted into water palaces, in which it was more comfortable to live.

teile.einleitung: **Timbuktu** is a city in the West African country of Mali. It lies on the edge of the Sahara, close to the River Niger. In the Middle Ages Timbuktu was a rich trading city and famous for its scholars and books.
wichtigste: Timbuktu lies in Mali on the southern edge of the Sahara.
Tuareg nomads founded the place around the year 1100.
Merchants came through the desert with camel caravans.
Mansa Musa had the Djinguereber Mosque built.
The old mosques are built mainly of mud.
In 2012 many old manuscripts were rescued to Bamako.

abschnitte.text: Around the year **1100** **Tuareg nomads** used the place as a camp near water. From it grew an important trading city. Timbuktu lay on the southern edge of the **Sahara** and near the River **Niger**. Here the **camel caravans** from the north arrived. A caravan is a long line of camels and merchants. Their goods, for example **salt**, were loaded onto **river boats**, and in the other direction **gold** came from the south.

In the Middle Ages many **scholars** lived in Timbuktu. Around the **Sankore Mosque** they taught and studied law, religion, mathematics and astronomy. That is why this place is often called a university. In Timbuktu many books were written by hand and collected. Many of these **manuscripts** are still kept today.

The ruler **Mansa Musa** of the Mali Empire made a famous pilgrimage to Mecca. Afterwards he had the **Djinguereber Mosque** built in Timbuktu. It still stands today. The old mosques are built mainly of **mud**, with wooden beams sticking out of the walls. After the rainy season the inhabitants renew the mud together. The mosques are part of the **UNESCO World Heritage**.

In **1591** an **army from Morocco** with firearms conquered the Songhai Empire and with it Timbuktu. Afterwards the city lost much of its wealth. In **2012** armed groups occupied the city. Brave librarians smuggled hundreds of thousands of old manuscripts to the capital, **Bamako**. In this way most of the manuscripts were saved.

gewusst: In Europe Timbuktu long counted as a legendary, almost unreachable city.
The wooden beams in the mud walls also serve as scaffolding when the mud is renewed.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages knights were meant not only to fight well but also to have good qualities. These are called knightly virtues. They were an ideal that not all knights lived up to.
wichtigste: A virtue is a good quality in a person.
Loyalty meant staying true to your lord and to your word.
A knight was supposed to protect the weak and the poor.
Bravery meant acting courageously in danger.
Moderation, in the Middle Ages “mâze”, meant not going to extremes.
Generosity meant giving and sharing gladly.
Anyone who was cowardly or broke his word lost his honour.

abschnitte.text: A **virtue** is a **good quality** in a person. In the Middle Ages a picture of the ideal knight developed. He was to be brave, loyal, moderate and generous. Poets told of this in songs and stories, for example about King Arthur and his knights. In reality, by no means all knights lived by these ideals.

**Loyalty** meant always staying true to your lord and your **word**. A loyal knight did not abandon his lord. **Honour** was also very important. Anyone who was **cowardly** or lied was no longer respected by the others. He lost his honour, and for a knight that was terrible.

abschnitte.titel: Courage and protection for the weak
abschnitte.text: **Bravery** means acting courageously in danger. This virtue was very important for knights. A good knight, however, was supposed to use his strength for others. He was to protect **the weak and the poor**, widows and orphans. This was part of the ideals of chivalry, which were also encouraged by the Church.

**Moderation**, called **“mâze”** in the Middle Ages, meant not going to extremes in eating, drinking and anger. **Generosity** meant being open-handed and giving something to others. At a prince’s **court** you had to behave well. That is why the German word for polite, **“höflich”**, comes from the word “Hof” (court). Good manners at table and towards guests were part of the ideal knight.

gewusst: When we say today that someone is “chivalrous”, we mean that he is helpful and decent.
The German words “höflich” (polite) and “höfisch” (courtly) still recall life at the courts of the Middle Ages.

teile.einleitung: The year 1960 is called the Africa Year. In this year 18 African colonies became independent. Most of them had previously belonged to France.
wichtigste: In 1960 18 African colonies became independent, 14 of them from France.
Nigeria became independent from Britain on 1 October 1960.
Madagascar declared independence on 26 June 1960.
Upper Volta became independent in 1960 and has been called Burkina Faso since 1984.
The poet Léopold Sédar Senghor became the first president of Senegal.
Ghana had already become independent in 1957.
In 1963 African states founded the Organisation of African Unity.

abschnitte.text: In the 19th century European states had divided up almost all of **Africa** among themselves. These territories were called **colonies**. After the Second World War more and more Africans demanded **independence**. The breaking away of the colonies is called **decolonisation**. In the year **1960** as many as **18** colonies became free, which is why people speak of the **Africa Year**.

As early as **1957** the British colony of the Gold Coast became independent as **Ghana**. It was one of the first countries south of the Sahara. Its leader **Kwame Nkrumah** became a model for other independence movements. He also campaigned for the unity of Africa. Ghana's path encouraged many other colonies.

Of the 18 colonies that became free in 1960, **14 belonged to France**. These include **Senegal**, **Mali** and **Cameroon**. The first president of Senegal was the well-known poet **Léopold Sédar Senghor**, who governed until 1980. The island nation of **Madagascar** became independent on 26 June 1960, and it is the largest island of Africa. The colony of **Upper Volta** became free on 5 August 1960 and has been called **Burkina Faso** since 1984.

On **1 October 1960** **Nigeria** became independent from Britain. Today it is the most populous country in Africa. The **Congo** became free from Belgium in the same year, but soon fell into a serious crisis. **British Somaliland** and **Italian Somaliland** joined together on 1 July 1960 to form **Somalia**. That is why people sometimes count 17 instead of 18 new states.

The new states wanted to work together. In 1963 they founded the **Organisation of African Unity** in **Addis Ababa** in Ethiopia. It was meant to promote cooperation and support decolonisation. In 2002 it was replaced by the **African Union**. Many young states, however, had to struggle for a long time with borders, poverty and conflicts left over from the colonial period.

gewusst: Many borders in Africa were drawn by the colonial powers with a ruler, without regard for the peoples on the ground.
Senghor was not only president, but later also became the first African to be admitted to the Académie française.

teile.einleitung: Albert Einstein was one of the most famous physicists of all time. His theory of relativity changed our picture of space, time and gravity. He spent some of his most important years in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Einstein was born in 1879 in Ulm in Germany.
In 1896 he passed the Matura at the cantonal school in Aarau in the canton of Aargau.
He studied at the ETH in Zurich.
In 1901 he became a Swiss citizen and remained one all his life.
From 1902 he worked at the Patent Office in Bern.
In 1905 he published the special theory of relativity and the formula E = mc².
He liked to play the violin.

abschnitte.text: Albert Einstein was born in **1879** in **Ulm** in **Germany**. He grew up in Munich. Even as a child he played the **violin**, and music later helped him to think. He was interested early in mathematics and the natural sciences. But he did not like the strict school in Munich.

Einstein attended the **cantonal school in Aarau** in the canton of **Aargau** and passed the **Matura** there in **1896**. Afterwards he studied at the **ETH in Zurich**, which was then called the Polytechnic. He became a teacher of mathematics and physics. In **1901** he received **Swiss citizenship**. He kept it all his life, even when he later took on other citizenships.

From **1902** Einstein worked at the **Patent Office in Bern**. There he examined inventions. In his free time he researched physics. **1905** is regarded as his **miracle year**, because he published several groundbreaking papers. In Bern you can visit the **Einstein House** today, where he lived at the time.

In 1905 Einstein published the **special theory of relativity**. It shows that time and space do not pass in the same way for everyone when they move very fast. In the same year came the formula **E = mc²**. It shows that **mass and energy** are connected. Ten years later followed the **general theory of relativity**, which explains **gravity** in a new way.
