In 1921 Einstein received the Nobel Prize for Physics.

abschnitte.titel: Later life and a famous photo
abschnitte.text: In 1933 Einstein left Germany because the Nazis came to power. Afterwards he lived in the **USA** and did research in Princeton. He died there in 1955. A photo from **1951** is world famous: on his birthday he **stuck out his tongue** at a photographer. The picture shows his humour and can still be seen on many posters today.

gewusst: As a teenager Einstein gave up German citizenship and was stateless for some years before he became Swiss.
Einstein did not receive the Nobel Prize for the theory of relativity, but for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.

teile.einleitung: “Ora et labora” is Latin and means “Pray and work”. This short phrase sums up how monks are meant to live in a monastery: prayer and work alternate throughout the day.
wichtigste: “Ora et labora” means “Pray and work”.
The motto fits the Rule of Benedict of Nursia.
Benedict lived in Italy and founded the monastery of Monte Cassino around 529.
Around the year 540 he wrote a rule for life in a monastery.
Monks who live by this rule are called Benedictines.
The monks prayed together several times a day and worked in between.
In Switzerland Benedictines live, for example, in Engelberg Abbey in the canton of Obwalden.

abschnitte.text: **Benedict of Nursia** was born in Nursia in Italy. Around 529 he founded the monastery of **Monte Cassino** on a mountain. Around 540 he wrote a **rule**, that is, a collection of regulations for life together in a monastery. It says when the monks pray, eat, sleep and work. Anyone who lives by this rule is a **Benedictine**.

The monks met in the church **several times a day** for prayer together. The first prayer was already in the night or very early in the morning. These fixed times of prayer are called the **Liturgy of the Hours**. The monks mostly sang psalms from the Bible. The bell called them together each time.

Between prayers they worked: in the **field**, in the **garden**, in the kitchen or in the **writing room**. There monks carefully copied books by hand. Benedict wrote that **idleness**, that is, laziness, was an enemy of the soul. That is why every monk was to do something useful every day. In this way a monastery could largely provide for itself.

There are Benedictine monasteries in Switzerland to this day. **Engelberg Abbey** in the canton of Obwalden was founded in the year **1120**. **Einsiedeln Abbey** in the canton of Schwyz, an important place of pilgrimage, is also well known. The monks there still live by the motto “Pray and work”. Many monasteries run schools or offer guests a place to stay.

gewusst: The phrase “Ora et labora” does not appear word for word in Benedict’s rule. It is a later, short summary.
In the Middle Ages many monasteries preserved old books, because the monks copied them again and again.

teile.einleitung: The Cistercians are a Catholic order of monks that came into being in 1098 in the monastery of Cîteaux in France. They wanted to live simply, in poverty and by strict rules. They also founded important monasteries in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Robert of Molesme founded the monastery of Cîteaux, in Latin Cistercium, in 1098.
The order takes its name from the place Cîteaux.
Bernard of Clairvaux was the most influential Cistercian of his time.
The Carta Caritatis joined all the monasteries together.
Lay brothers, the conversi, did a lot of the fieldwork.
Cistercian churches have only a roof turret instead of a bell tower.
Wettingen monastery in Aargau was a Cistercian abbey from 1227 to 1841.

abschnitte.text: In 1098 the abbot **Robert of Molesme** left his monastery with a few monks. In Burgundy they founded the monastery of **Cîteaux**, in Latin **Cistercium**. The order takes its name from this place. The monks wanted to follow the **Rule of St Benedict** strictly again. Prayer, work and a simple life stood at the centre.

The most important Cistercian was **Bernard of Clairvaux**. He entered Cîteaux around 1113 and soon became abbot of the new monastery of Clairvaux. He was a famous preacher and adviser to popes and kings. On behalf of the pope he preached in **Vézelay** in 1146 for the **Second Crusade**. Through him the order grew very quickly.

The constitution of the Cistercians is called the **Carta Caritatis**, the “Charter of Charity”. It regulated the relationship of the **daughter houses** to their **mother houses**. Every year the abbots met for the **General Chapter** at Cîteaux. In **visitations** abbots visited other monasteries and checked whether the rules were being kept. In this way the many monasteries stayed closely connected.

The Cistercians often founded their monasteries in remote valleys. They cleared land, laid out ponds and built mills. A large part of the fieldwork was done by the **conversi**. These were **lay brothers** who worked mainly on the farms, the **granges**. In this way the monasteries could farm large estates themselves.

The Cistercians rejected **splendour** in churches. Instead of tall towers their churches carried only a small **roof turret**. Pictures and coloured windows were at first hardly allowed either. In Switzerland several abbeys came into being, such as **Hauterive** near Fribourg, **Kappel am Albis** and **St Urban**. The monastery of **Wettingen** was founded in 1227 and settled with monks from Salem. In 1841 the canton of **Aargau** dissolved the monastery.

gewusst: Because of their light-coloured habits the Cistercians were also called “white monks”.
Hauterive Abbey in the canton of Fribourg is lived in by Cistercians again today.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Agincourt took place on 25 October 1415 in northern France. A small English army under King Henry V defeated a much larger French army.
wichtigste: The battle was part of the Hundred Years’ War between England and France.
It took place on the feast day of Saints Crispin and Crispinian.
Before that, Henry V had conquered the port city of Harfleur.
The English army wanted to march to Calais.
A muddy field hindered the heavily armoured French knights.
Henry’s order to kill many prisoners is still disputed today.
Shakespeare made the battle famous in his play “Henry V”.

abschnitte.text: In the **Hundred Years’ War** England and France fought for a long time over land and over the French crown. In 1415 the English king **Henry V** landed in Normandy. He besieged and conquered the port city of **Harfleur**. Afterwards his weakened army wanted to march **to Calais**, which belonged to the English at the time. At **Agincourt** a large French army blocked its way.

On **25 October 1415** the armies faced each other. After heavy rain the field was a **soaked, muddy ploughed field**. The heavily armoured French knights could only struggle forward in it. The English **longbowmen** shot many arrows at them. Although the French had many more warriors, the English won.

During the battle Henry V ordered many **prisoners to be killed**. He probably feared a new attack and did not want the prisoners to take up arms again. Even at the time this order was against the rules of war. To this day it is **disputed** among historians.

At Agincourt the French prince **Charles of Orléans** was also taken prisoner. He afterwards stayed in England for about **25 years**. During this long time he wrote many **poems**. Today he is regarded as one of the most important French poets of the Middle Ages.

The poet **William Shakespeare** wrote the play **“Henry V”** about 180 years later. In it the battle plays a central role. Before the fight the king gives a famous speech to his soldiers on the feast day of Saints **Crispin and Crispinian**. The play has been filmed several times.

gewusst: Crispin and Crispinian are regarded as the patron saints of shoemakers.
The war between England and France to which Agincourt belongs actually lasted more than a hundred years, from 1337 to 1453.

teile.einleitung: Zähringen towns are towns that were founded or expanded by the Dukes of Zähringen. In Switzerland they include Bern, Fribourg, Burgdorf and Thun.
wichtigste: The Zähringers were a powerful noble family in south-western Germany and in Switzerland.
They founded several towns, including Bern and Fribourg.
With Berchtold V the Dukes of Zähringen died out in 1218.
Their inheritance around Burgdorf and Thun fell to the Counts of Kyburg.
The Kyburg possessions later passed to Habsburg.

abschnitte.text: The **Dukes of Zähringen** ruled over territories in the Black Forest and the Swiss Central Plateau in the 12th century. To secure their power they founded **towns**. These include **Freiburg im Breisgau**, **Fribourg** and **Bern**. They also expanded **Burgdorf** and **Thun**. Towns brought trade, taxes and protection.

Many Zähringen towns have a similar layout. They often lie on a river, which protects the town. Through the middle run one or more broad **main streets** on which markets were held. In Bern you can still see this in the old town today. The **Zähringen Fountain** in Bern recalls the founders.

With **Berchtold V** the Dukes of Zähringen died out in **1218**. Their inheritance was divided up. The possessions around **Burgdorf and Thun** fell to the **Counts of Kyburg**. Their possessions later passed to **Habsburg**. Bern, on the other hand, became an imperial city and later built up a large territory of its own.

gewusst: According to tradition Bern was founded in 1191 by Duke Berchtold V.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Hastings in 1066 changed the history of England. The Norman William defeated the English king Harold and became king himself.
wichtigste: The battle took place on 14 October 1066.
The Normans under William landed at Pevensey in September.
Shortly before, the English had fought the Norwegians at Stamford Bridge.
The English fought in a shield wall.
The Normans had mounted knights, which the English lacked.
With a pretended retreat the Normans lured the English out of their position.
King Harold is said to have died from an arrow in the eye.

abschnitte.text: At the beginning of 1066 the English king Edward the Confessor died without children. **Harold Godwinson** became king as **Harold II**. But **William**, the Duke of **Normandy** in France, also wanted the crown. He said it had been promised to him. In addition the Norwegian king Harald Hardrada claimed England.

In September 1066 the **Norwegians** landed first in the north of England. Harold defeated them at **Stamford Bridge**. Only a few days later William landed with his army in the south, **at Pevensey**. Harold had to march south by forced marches with his tired troops.

On **14 October 1066** the armies met. The English stood on a hill and formed a **shield wall**: the warriors held their shields close together like a wall. The Normans had archers and above all **mounted knights**, which the English lacked. For a long time the shield wall held.

The Normans pretended several times to **flee**. Some English left their position and pursued them. In this way the shield wall grew weaker. In the evening King Harold fell. According to tradition **an arrow in the eye** struck him, but whether it happened exactly like this is uncertain. Without their king the English gave up.

William was crowned King of England at Christmas 1066. Since then he has been called **William the Conqueror**. The Normans brought new nobles, castles and many French words to England. On the battlefield William had an **abbey** built. The battle is also shown on the famous **Bayeux Tapestry**, an embroidery about 70 metres long.

gewusst: The battle did not take place in Hastings itself but some kilometres away. The place there is now simply called “Battle”.
The Bayeux Tapestry is actually not a tapestry but a strip of embroidered linen.

teile.einleitung: Polynesia is a huge world of islands in the Pacific. The name comes from Greek and means “many islands”. Its inhabitants are among the greatest seafarers in history.
wichtigste: Hawaii, New Zealand and Easter Island form the Polynesian Triangle.
The ancestors of the Polynesians came from the region of Taiwan and South-East Asia.
They sailed over long distances in double-hulled canoes.
Stars, waves and birds helped them to find their way.
New Zealand was settled last, around 1250 to 1300.
The Māori call New Zealand Aotearoa.

abschnitte.text: The corners of the **Polynesian Triangle** are **Hawaii** in the north, **New Zealand** in the south-west and **Easter Island** in the east. The triangle covers a huge part of the Pacific. All the islands within it were settled by people with **related languages**. These also include, for example, Tahiti, Samoa and Tonga.

Languages and genes show that the ancestors of the Polynesians came from the region of **Taiwan and South-East Asia**. Over many generations they moved from island to island towards the east. **New Zealand**, as one of the last large landmasses in the world, was only settled in the **13th century**. The ancestors of the **Māori** reached it around 1250 to 1300. The Māori call their land **Aotearoa**, often translated as “land of the long white cloud”.

The Polynesians travelled in **double-hulled canoes**. Two hulls joined by a platform made the boats stable. With sails they carried people, animals and plants far across the sea. They had no compass. The navigators found their way by the **stars**, the **waves** of the sea and by **seabirds** and clouds, which showed where land lay.

In 1976 the replica canoe **Hōkūleʻa** sailed without instruments from Hawaii to **Tahiti**. The navigator **Mau Piailug** guided it using only traditional knowledge. The voyage proved that such journeys could be made deliberately. The **sweet potato** comes from South America but was already growing on Polynesian islands before Columbus. This points to early contacts between Polynesians and South America.

gewusst: The Polynesian Triangle is much larger than the whole of Europe but consists mostly of sea.
Polynesian navigators memorised the rising points of many stars on the horizon.

teile.einleitung: The astrolabe is an old measuring instrument. Seafarers used a simple form of it to work out their position at sea from the Sun or the stars.
wichtigste: With the astrolabe people measured how high the Sun or stars stood in the sky.
In this way seafarers could find out how far north or south they were.
The seafarer's astrolabe was a round ring of metal.
It was mostly made of brass or bronze and was therefore heavy.
A rotating pointer in the middle was used for sighting.

abschnitte.titel: An instrument with a long history
abschnitte.text: Greek scholars already knew the **astrolabe** in antiquity. Later researchers in the **Islamic world** developed it further. These instruments were often artistically decorated and showed the starry sky. With them scholars could tell the time and calculate the movement of the stars.

In the 15th century Portuguese seafarers in particular sailed far out to sea. They needed a simple and robust instrument. Their **astrolabe** was a round **ring** of **brass** or **bronze** with a **scale of degrees**. Because it was heavy, it swayed less in wind and waves. In the middle a pointer with two small holes for sighting turned.

The seafarer held the astrolabe up by a ring so that it hung vertically. Then he pointed the pointer at the **Sun** or a bright **star**. On the scale he read off how high the heavenly body stood above the horizon. From this angle he could work out how far north or south he was. This is called the **latitude**.

On a rocking ship measuring was difficult and often inaccurate. In time better instruments such as the **octant** were invented. How far east or west a ship was could not be determined with the astrolabe. For that, very accurate clocks were needed later.

gewusst: The word astrolabe comes from Greek and means roughly “star taker”.
In old shipwrecks bronze astrolabes have been found that lay in the sea for centuries.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages not every larger settlement was automatically a town. Only with **town rights** did a place gain special rights and freedoms. These rights changed people’s lives greatly.
wichtigste: A place only became a proper town with town rights.
Town rights were granted by a king or a prince.
The right to hold a market and the right to a town wall were often part of them.
The rights of a town were set out in a charter with a seal.
An imperial city was directly subject to the king or emperor.
Under the principle “Town air makes you free”, an unfree person became free after a year and a day in the town.

abschnitte.text: **Town rights** were a collection of rights granted to a place. They were given by the ruler of the land, that is, a **king** or a **prince**. The rights were written down in a **charter** and confirmed with a seal. The citizens kept this charter carefully, for it was the proof of their freedoms. The ruler also had an advantage: a rich town paid him taxes and dues.

Together with town rights a town often received the **right to hold a market**. With it the town could hold markets regularly. This attracted merchants and brought money into the town. The right to build a **town wall** was also important. The wall protected the inhabitants and their property. Because there were hardly any soldiers of its own, the men of the town had to keep watch themselves and defend the wall in case of danger.

In the countryside many people lived as **serfs**. They depended on a lord and were not allowed to simply move away. In many towns, however, the principle “Town air makes you free” applied. Anyone who lived **a year and a day** in the town without his lord taking him back was free. That is why many people moved from the countryside to the towns. In this way the towns grew strongly in the Middle Ages.

Some towns had no prince over them but were directly subject to the king or emperor. They were called **imperial cities**. They could largely govern themselves, with a **council** of their own. **Zurich** and **Bern** were also such towns. Imperial cities were often especially proud of their freedom and defended it against neighbouring nobles.

In the area of present-day Switzerland the noble family of the **Zähringers** founded several towns. Duke **Berchtold V of Zähringen** founded the town of **Bern** in **1191**. The Zähringers also founded **Fribourg**. With new towns nobles wanted to secure their power and promote trade. Many Swiss towns have their roots in this period.

gewusst: When the Zähringers died out, Bern became an imperial city.
The principle “Town air makes you free” was one of the reasons why towns grew so fast in the Middle Ages.

teile.einleitung: The English Parliament grew out of assemblies that the king summoned in the Middle Ages. It became one of the oldest parliaments in the world and a model for many others.
wichtigste: In 1265 Simon de Montfort for the first time also invited representatives of the towns.
Edward I’s “Model Parliament” of 1295 is seen as a model for later parliaments.
Since the 14th century there have been two houses: the House of Lords and the House of Commons.
The most important means of pressure was the granting of taxes.
The Good Parliament of 1376 saw the first impeachment.
The chairman of the House of Commons is called the Speaker.

abschnitte.text: English kings consulted nobles and high clergy from early on. In 1265 **Simon de Montfort**, the leader of the barons in the revolt against King Henry III, summoned a **parliament**. For the first time, besides knights of the shires, **citizens from the towns** also came. In 1295 King **Edward I** invited the nobility, the clergy and representatives of the shires and towns. This **Model Parliament** became the pattern for later parliaments.

Since the 14th century Parliament has been divided into two **houses**. In the **House of Lords**, the upper house, sat the high nobility and high clergy. In the **House of Commons**, the lower house, sat **knights of the shires and citizens of the towns**. Each shire sent two knights, and many towns two citizens. This division into two has lasted to this day.

The king needed a lot of money for wars, for example in the **Hundred Years’ War** against France. New **taxes** had to be approved by Parliament. This approval was its most important **means of pressure**. Often Parliament only gave the money if the king dealt with complaints. In this way it gradually gained more influence.

abschnitte.titel: The Good Parliament and the Speaker
abschnitte.text: In 1376 the **Good Parliament** met. There the Commons accused several advisers of King Edward III of bribery and mismanagement. This is how the procedure of **impeachment**, a charge brought by Parliament, came about. Since the late 14th century the House of Commons has had a **Speaker**, who presented the concerns of the Commons to the king. The first Speaker officially given that title is considered to be **Thomas Hungerford** in 1377.

gewusst: The British House of Commons still has a Speaker today, who chairs its sittings.
Switzerland also has two houses in its parliament: the National Council and the Council of States.

teile.einleitung: Adolf Hitler was a dictator who ruled Germany from 1933 to 1945. He was the leader of the Nazis, began the Second World War and is responsible for the Holocaust, the murder of millions of Jews and other people. His story shows how important democracy and human rights are.
wichtigste: Adolf Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 in Braunau am Inn in Austria.
In Vienna he was rejected by the Academy of Art and lived in poor circumstances.
In 1919 he joined the German Workers' Party, which became the NSDAP.
His attempted coup in Munich in 1923 failed at the Feldherrnhalle.
On 30 January 1933 Paul von Hindenburg appointed him Reich Chancellor.
He set up a dictatorship and began the Second World War in 1939.
Under his rule about six million Jews were murdered.
On 30 April 1945 he took his own life in Berlin.

abschnitte.text: Adolf Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 in **Braunau am Inn** in Austria. He wanted to become a painter, but was rejected by the Academy of Art in Vienna. Between about 1907 and 1913 he lived in Vienna in poor circumstances. In the First World War he fought as a soldier in the German army.

In September 1919 Hitler joined the **German Workers' Party** in Munich, which was soon called the NSDAP. He became its leader and gave speeches full of hatred, above all against Jews. On 8 and 9 November 1923 he attempted a **coup**, which the police stopped at the Feldherrnhalle. In prison at Landsberg his book “Mein Kampf” was partly written.

After the **Great Depression** many people were unemployed and dissatisfied. In 1932 Hitler lost the election for Reich President to Paul von Hindenburg. All the same, Hindenburg appointed him **Reich Chancellor** on 30 January 1933. After Hindenburg's death on 2 August 1934 Hitler combined both offices and called himself the “Führer”.

Hitler abolished democracy, banned other parties and had opponents arrested. Jews were stripped of their rights and persecuted step by step. In the **Holocaust** about six million Jewish men, women and children were murdered, many in **extermination camps** such as Auschwitz. Sinti and Roma, people with disabilities and many others were also persecuted and killed.

On 1 September 1939 Hitler had Poland invaded, and with that the **Second World War** began. In the war about 60 million people died worldwide. When the Red Army captured Berlin in 1945, Hitler took his own life in the bunker on 30 April 1945. A week later Germany surrendered.

During the war Switzerland was surrounded by Germany and its allies and remained **neutral**. It took in some refugees, but also turned many Jewish refugees away at the border. Today memorials and school lessons recall the victims. In Germany the symbols of the Nazis are banned today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ruler who governs alone and allows no criticism.
The ideology of Hitler and the NSDAP, full of racism and hatred of Jews.
A violent attempt to overthrow the government.
The mass murder of the European Jews by the Nazis.
The head of government in the German Reich.

gewusst: Until 1932 Hitler was not even a German citizen, but first Austrian and then stateless.
In Berlin a large memorial with 2,711 concrete blocks recalls the murdered Jews of Europe today.
The name Holocaust comes from Greek, and in Hebrew the genocide is called the Shoah.

teile.einleitung: The Battle of Tannenberg in 1410 was one of the largest battles in medieval Europe. A Polish-Lithuanian army defeated the Teutonic Order.
wichtigste: The battle took place on 15 July 1410.
The Teutonic Order fought against Poland and Lithuania.
The Lithuanian grand duke Vytautas led the Lithuanian troops.
Grand Master Ulrich von Jungingen fell in the battle.
In Poland it is called the Battle of Grunwald.
Heinrich von Plauen afterwards successfully defended Marienburg.

abschnitte.text: The **Teutonic Order** was a military order. Its members were monks and knights at the same time. On the Baltic Sea it had built up a state of its own, with **Marienburg** as its headquarters. It repeatedly quarrelled over land with its neighbours **Poland** and **Lithuania**. In 1409 a great war broke out.

On **15 July 1410** the armies met between the villages of Tannenberg and Grunwald. The Polish army was led by King Władysław II Jagiełło, the Lithuanians by the grand duke **Vytautas**. After a long fight the Poles and Lithuanians won. The Grand Master of the Order, **Ulrich von Jungingen**, fell, as did many knights of the Order.

After the victory the Polish-Lithuanian army besieged **Marienburg**. **Heinrich von Plauen** defended the castle successfully, and the besiegers withdrew again. In the **First Peace of Thorn** in 1411 the Order lost only a little land. It had to pay a lot of money, however, and became weaker and weaker afterwards.

In **Poland** the battle is called the **Battle of Grunwald**, in Lithuania the Battle of Žalgiris. For both countries it is still an important event in their history. A large monument stands on the battlefield, and every year the battle is re-enacted there.

gewusst: The Polish painter Jan Matejko painted the battle in a huge picture, which hangs today in the National Museum in Warsaw.

teile.einleitung: Anne Frank was a Jewish girl who had to hide with her family in Amsterdam during the Second World War. In hiding she wrote a diary that is now one of the best-known books in the world.
wichtigste: Anne Frank was born in Frankfurt am Main in 1929.
Her family moved to Amsterdam in the Netherlands.
From 1942 eight people hid in the “Secret Annex”.
Anne wrote her diary letters to an invented friend called Kitty.
The helper Miep Gies kept the diary safe after the arrest.
Her father Otto Frank had the diary printed in 1947.
The Anne Frank Fonds has its seat in Basel.

abschnitte.text: Anne Frank was born in 1929 in **Frankfurt am Main**. When the **Nazis** came to power in Germany, they persecuted Jews more and more. The Jewish Frank family therefore moved to **Amsterdam** in the Netherlands. But in 1940 the German army occupied the Netherlands too. Now the Franks were no longer safe there either.

In July 1942 the family went into hiding. The hiding place lay in the rear part of Otto Frank's company building. Anne called it the **Secret Annex**. Eight people lived there: the four members of the Frank family, the van Pels family of three and the dentist Fritz Pfeffer. During the day everyone had to be very quiet so that the workers in the building would not notice anything.

For her 13th birthday Anne received a **diary**. In it she wrote what she experienced, thought and felt. Many entries are letters to an invented friend called **Kitty**. Anne wanted to become a writer later. So she revised her texts herself, so that a book could be made of them after the war.

Some employees of the firm helped the people in hiding. One of them was **Miep Gies**, who brought food and news. In August 1944 the people in hiding were discovered and arrested. They were taken to concentration camps. Anne died in early 1945 in the camp of **Bergen-Belsen** of an illness. After the arrest Miep Gies had gathered up Anne's writings and kept them.

abschnitte.titel: The diary goes around the world
abschnitte.text: Of the family only **Otto Frank** survived. He had the diary printed in 1947. Today it is translated into very many languages. Otto Frank later lived near **Basel** and founded the **Anne Frank Fonds** there in 1963. In Amsterdam the Secret Annex is now a museum that many people visit.

gewusst: The diary of Anne Frank has been translated into over 70 languages.
Anne Frank was only 15 years old.

teile.einleitung: The Visigoths were a Germanic people who travelled through half of Europe in late antiquity. They defeated a Roman army, plundered Rome and later founded kingdoms of their own in Gaul and Spain.
wichtigste: In 378 the Goths defeated an Eastern Roman army at Adrianople, and Emperor Valens fell.
Under King Alaric I the Visigoths plundered the city of Rome in 410.
From 418 they settled in Aquitaine, and their capital was Toulouse.
Later Toledo in Spain became their capital.
In the 4th century Bishop Wulfila translated the Bible into Gothic.
The Goths were at first Arian Christians.
From 711 Muslim Arabs and Berbers conquered the Visigothic kingdom.

abschnitte.text: In the 4th century the **Huns** pushed into Europe from the east. Many Goths therefore fled across the Danube into the Roman Empire. Soon a quarrel with the Romans broke out. In 378 the Goths defeated an Eastern Roman army at **Adrianople**, present-day Edirne in Turkey. Emperor **Valens** lost his life there. This defeat showed how vulnerable the great empire had become.

Under their king **Alaric I** the Visigoths moved through the Balkans and into Italy. In 410 they captured Rome and plundered the city for three days. For many centuries Rome had not been taken by enemies. The event shook the whole Roman world. Alaric died soon afterwards in southern Italy.

From 418 the Visigoths were allowed to settle in **Aquitaine** in the south-west of Gaul. Their capital was **Toulouse**, which is why people speak of the **Kingdom of Toulouse**. In 507 they lost most of Gaul to the Franks. After that their centre lay in Spain, and in the 6th century **Toledo** became the capital. The kingdom covered almost the whole Iberian Peninsula.

In the 4th century the bishop **Wulfila** translated the Bible into the Gothic language. For this he created a **Gothic alphabet** of his own. A famous copy is the **Codex Argenteus**, the “Silver Bible”, which today lies in Uppsala in Sweden. The Goths followed **Arianism** at first, a teaching that the Roman imperial church rejected as heresy. This led to tensions with the Catholic population. In 589 King Reccared and his people converted to the Catholic faith.

In 711 Muslim troops from North Africa crossed over to Spain. They were **Arabs and Berbers**. They defeated the Visigothic king **Roderic**. Within a few years they conquered almost the whole Iberian Peninsula. With that the Visigothic kingdom fell, and only in the north did small Christian territories hold out.

gewusst: Wulfila's Gothic Bible is among the oldest texts in a Germanic language.
The Silver Bible is so called because it is written in silver ink on purple parchment.

teile.einleitung: Auguste Piccard was a Swiss physicist and adventurer from Basel. He was the first person to rise into the stratosphere in a balloon and later built a submersible for the deep sea.
wichtigste: Auguste Piccard was born in Basel in 1884.
He was a physicist and professor.
In 1931 he was the first person to rise into the stratosphere in a balloon.
He sat in a closed sphere of aluminium.
His second flight started in 1932 at Dübendorf near Zurich.
He was the model for Professor Calculus in “The Adventures of Tintin”.

abschnitte.text: Auguste Piccard was born in 1884 in **Basel**. He had a twin brother called Jean. Auguste studied at the ETH in Zurich and became a **physicist**. Later he worked as a professor in Brussels in Belgium. Among other things he wanted to research **radiation from space**.

The **stratosphere** is a layer of the atmosphere high above the clouds. There the air is so thin that you cannot breathe. So Piccard built an airtight **sphere of aluminium** that hung from a huge gas balloon. On 27 May 1931 he took off from **Augsburg** in Germany. He reached almost 15,800 metres, about **16 kilometres**. That was a world record.

A year later, in 1932, Piccard set off on a second flight. This time it began from **Dübendorf airfield** near Zurich. He rose a little higher than the first time. The flights made him famous all over the world.

Piccard did not only want to go high, but also deep. He developed a submersible for the deep sea, a so-called **bathyscaphe**. The idea was similar to the balloon: a strong sphere for the people and a large buoyancy body. With his son **Jacques** he dived to over 3,000 metres in 1953.

The Belgian artist **Hergé** knew Piccard from Brussels. He made him the model for **Professor Calculus** in the comics “The Adventures of Tintin”. The Piccard family also stayed adventurous: his grandson **Bertrand Piccard** later flew around the Earth in a balloon and in a solar aeroplane.

gewusst: Jacques Piccard, the son of Auguste, dived into the Mariana Trench in 1960, the deepest place in the world's oceans.
Auguste's twin brother Jean also became a natural scientist and made balloon flights to great heights.

teile.einleitung: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was a cloth merchant from Delft in the Netherlands. With microscopes that he made himself, he discovered in the 17th century a world of tiny living things that nobody had seen before.
wichtigste: Leeuwenhoek lived from 1632 to 1723 in Delft in the Netherlands.
By trade he was a cloth merchant and sold fabrics.
He built small microscopes himself, mostly with only one lens.
In a drop of water he saw tiny living things that he called “little animals”.
In the plaque on teeth he discovered bacteria.
He described the red blood cells very precisely.

abschnitte.text: Leeuwenhoek was a **cloth merchant**. To test the quality of fabrics he looked at the threads with magnifying glasses. In this way he began to take an interest in lenses. He learned to grind very small lenses himself. He had never attended a university.

A **microscope** makes small things look large. Leeuwenhoek's microscopes were hardly bigger than a hand. They mostly had only **a single lens**, which was ground very well. Even so, some magnified more than 200 times. That was better at the time than many microscopes with several lenses.

abschnitte.titel: Life in a drop of water
abschnitte.text: Leeuwenhoek looked at water from ponds and rain barrels. In it he saw countless tiny living things swimming about. He called them “little animals”. Today such living things are called **microorganisms**. He wrote down his observations in letters to the **Royal Society** in London, a famous society of researchers.

Once Leeuwenhoek scraped plaque from his teeth and put it under the microscope. He saw tiny living things that we now call **bacteria**. He also examined blood and described the **red blood cells**, which give blood its colour. That is why he is often called the father of **microbiology**, the science of the smallest living things.

gewusst: Leeuwenhoek was born in the same year and in the same town as the painter Jan Vermeer.
In the course of his life he made hundreds of lenses.

teile.einleitung: Scholasticism was a way of thinking and learning in the Middle Ages. Scholars tried to understand and justify the Christian faith with reason.
wichtigste: Scholasticism was the science and teaching method at the schools and universities of the Middle Ages.
Anselm of Canterbury is regarded as the “father of scholasticism”.
His motto “fides quaerens intellectum” means “faith seeking understanding”.
Peter Abelard set contradictory statements against each other in “Sic et non”.
The “Sentences” of Peter Lombard were a textbook for centuries.
William of Ockham advised making no unnecessary assumptions.

abschnitte.text: The word **scholasticism** comes from the Latin word for school. It describes the way teaching was done in the monastery and cathedral schools and later at the **universities**. The scholars wanted to think through the **faith** with **reason**. They asked questions, collected reasons for and against and then looked for an answer. An important method was the debate, the **disputation**.

**Anselm of Canterbury** lived in the 11th century and is regarded as the **“father of scholasticism”**. His motto was **“fides quaerens intellectum”**, “faith seeking understanding”. **Peter Abelard** wrote the work **“Sic et non”**, “Yes and No”. In it he set statements of the Church Fathers against each other that contradicted one another. Readers were to think for themselves about how the contradictions could be resolved.

**Peter Lombard** wrote the **“Sentences”** in the 12th century. In them he arranged teachings about the faith by topic. For centuries this book was the basis of theological study. Later **Thomas Aquinas** became very well known. He combined Christian teaching with the thinking of the Greek philosopher **Aristotle**.

The Franciscan **William of Ockham** lived in the 14th century. He is known for one principle: you should make **no unnecessary assumptions**. If two explanations fit equally well, the simpler one is to be preferred. This principle is called **“Ockham’s razor”**, because it cuts away what is superfluous. Researchers still use it today.

gewusst: The first university in Switzerland was founded in Basel in 1460. There too, teaching at first followed the method of scholasticism.
Universities such as Paris and Oxford arose in the Middle Ages and still exist today.

teile.einleitung: Monks and nuns are people who devote their whole lives to God. In the Middle Ages many of them lived in monasteries, where they prayed, worked and preserved knowledge.
wichtigste: Monks wear a long robe, the habit.
Nuns cover their hair with a veil.
Many monks wore a tonsure.
Monks and nuns took vows, for example to live in poverty.
They lived unmarried and did not marry.
A monastery had a cloister and a dining hall, the refectory.

abschnitte.text: **Monks** and **nuns** wanted to give their whole lives to God. That is why they moved into a **monastery**. When they entered, they took a **vow**, a solemn promise. They promised to **live in poverty**, that is, without any possessions of their own. They lived unmarried and did not start a family. They also promised to obey the abbot or abbess.

Monks wear a long, simple robe with a hood. It is called a **habit** or **cowl**. Nuns covered their hair with a **veil**. It showed that they had given their lives to God. Many monks had a circle shaved bald on top of their heads. This hairstyle is called a **tonsure**.

In the monastery every day followed a fixed order. Several times a day a **bell** called everyone to **prayer**. Then they all went to the church. In between they worked: in the garden, in the fields or in the writing room. Many monasteries lived by the rule of Saint **Benedict**: “Pray and work”.

Around an inner courtyard lay the **cloister**, a covered walkway. There the monks walked, prayed and read. In the **refectory**, the dining hall, everyone ate together. Often they stayed silent while eating, and someone read aloud from a book.

In the Middle Ages monasteries were places of learning. Monks copied books by hand. The monastery of **St Gallen** is famous for its old **Abbey Library**. It is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The monastery of **Einsiedeln** is still inhabited today.

gewusst: The Abbey Library of St Gallen holds manuscripts that are more than a thousand years old.
The Plan of St Gall from the 9th century shows what an ideal monastery should look like.

teile.einleitung: The Middle Ages are the period between antiquity and modern times. They lasted about 1,000 years, roughly from 500 to 1500 AD. During this time castles, monasteries and towns appeared, and so did the beginnings of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Middle Ages lie between antiquity and modern times.
They lasted from about 500 to 1500, so around 1,000 years.
A kingdom was usually headed by a king.
Nobles and the Church owned most of the land.
Christianity was the most important religion in Europe.
Mainly monks and nuns could read and write.
The beginnings of Switzerland lie in the Middle Ages, and the Federal Charter bears the date 1291.
At the end of the Middle Ages, printing made books cheaper.

abschnitte.text: The Middle Ages are divided into three parts: the **Early Middle Ages**, the High Middle Ages and the Late Middle Ages. They began roughly with the end of the Western Roman Empire in the 5th century. They ended around 1500, when America was discovered and printing spread. A famous ruler was **Charlemagne**, who was crowned emperor in Rome in the year 800.

A kingdom was usually headed by a **king** or an emperor. He gave land to nobles, who in return had to serve him faithfully and go to war with him. This system is called **feudalism**. Most people were peasants and had to hand over part of their harvest to their lords.

**Christianity** shaped the whole of life, from Sundays to the many feast days. The Church owned a lot of land and was very powerful. **Monasteries** were home to monks and nuns, who prayed, worked and copied books. The monastery of St Gallen was already a famous centre of learning in the Early Middle Ages.

People mostly wrote with a **quill**, often a goose feather, which they dipped in ink. Valuable books were written on **parchment**, which was made from animal skin. Every book was copied by hand, which could take months. Only the printing press of Johannes Gutenberg around 1450 made books much cheaper.

In the Middle Ages Uri, Schwyz and Unterwalden joined together in an alliance. The **Federal Charter** bears the date 1291 and is now kept in the Museum of the Federal Charters in Schwyz. The Swiss Confederates won battles such as Morgarten in 1315 and Sempach in 1386. Little by little more places such as Lucerne, Zurich and Bern joined.

In the Middle Ages there was no **electric light**. In the evening candles, oil lamps or the fire in the hearth gave light. Most people lived in the countryside, in simple houses made of wood and clay. Diseases such as the plague were dangerous because nobody knew their causes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time of the ancient Greeks and Romans before the Middle Ages.
The period after the Middle Ages, from about 1500 until today.
A writing material made from treated animal skin.
A system in which land was granted in return for loyalty and service.
A place where monks or nuns live, pray and work together.

gewusst: A large book on parchment needed the skins of many animals, sometimes of more than a hundred sheep or calves.
The Abbey Library of St Gallen keeps manuscripts that are more than 1,000 years old.
The word “Middle Ages” was only invented by scholars of modern times; the people of that age did not call their time that.

teile.einleitung: The Ottoman Empire was a great power for more than 600 years. It began around 1300 as a small principality in Anatolia and later stretched over parts of Asia, Europe and Africa.
wichtigste: The empire is named after **Osman I**.
The traditional founding year is about 1299.
It arose in north-west Anatolia, in present-day Turkey.
In 1453 the Ottomans conquered Constantinople, today’s Istanbul.
Under Suleiman I, the Magnificent, the empire was especially powerful.
Twice, in 1529 and 1683, the Ottomans besieged Vienna without success.
After the end of the empire the Republic of Turkey was created in 1923.

abschnitte.text: Around 1300 **Osman I** led a small principality in **north-west Anatolia**, on the border of the Byzantine Empire. The year **1299** is traditionally regarded as the founding year, but it is not precisely documented. His successors called themselves **Ottomans** after him. In 1326 they conquered the city of **Bursa** and made it their first capital. The tombs of the first sultans are there.

In the 14th century the Ottomans pushed into Europe. The city of **Edirne**, formerly Adrianople, was conquered in 1362 and then became the capital. In 1453 Sultan **Mehmed II** took Constantinople. The city, today **Istanbul**, became the new capital. The sultans lived in the **Topkapı Palace** for about 400 years; today it is a museum.

**Suleiman I** ruled from 1520 to 1566. Under him the empire reached a peak of power and size. He issued many laws and promoted magnificent buildings. In 1529 his army besieged **Vienna** but had to withdraw. A second siege of Vienna in 1683 also failed. After that the Ottomans did not advance any further into Central Europe.

The **Janissaries** were the elite soldiers of the sultans. They formed an infantry force that served the sultan directly. The empire was very large, so there were many provinces with their own governors. People of different languages and religions lived in it. At the head stood the **sultan**, supported by the grand vizier.

In the 19th century the empire became weaker and lost many territories. After the First World War it fell apart, and in 1922 the rule of the sultans ended. In 1923 a treaty was signed in the Swiss city of **Lausanne** that fixed the borders of the new **Turkey**. The **Treaty of Lausanne** is regarded as the founding document of present-day Turkey. In the same year the republic was proclaimed.

gewusst: The Ottoman Empire lasted more than 600 years, longer than most empires in history.
The Topkapı Palace in Istanbul is today one of the most visited museums in Turkey.

teile.einleitung: The tithe was an important levy in the Middle Ages. Peasants had to hand over a tenth of their harvest, originally to the Church. In Switzerland old tithe barns still recall it today.
wichtigste: The word tithe comes from ten.
The tithe was a tenth of the harvest.
Originally it went to the Church.
Mostly grain was handed over, often also young animals.
On grain the Great Tithe was paid, on fruit and vegetables the Small Tithe.
The tithe was collected in the tithe barn.

abschnitte.text: The word **tithe** comes from the word for **ten**. A tenth is one part of ten equal parts. If a farmer harvests 10 sacks of grain, he hands over **1 sack**. With 30 sheaves it is **3 sheaves**, because 30 divided by 10 is 3. In this way the tithe was easy to work out.

The tithe was originally a levy for the **Church**. The idea is already found in the Bible. With the tithe **priests**, churches and help for the poor were paid for. Charlemagne made it compulsory in his empire. Later the tithe rights often came into the hands of monasteries, nobles or towns.

Most peasants had hardly any money. So they handed over a part of their **harvest**, above all **grain**. This was called the **Great Tithe**. On fruit, vegetables and herbs the **Small Tithe** was paid. From young animals such as calves, lambs or piglets, too, a part had to be handed over.

The grain that was handed over was stored in large buildings, the **tithe barns**. They were often the largest houses in the village. In **Switzerland** a few old tithe barns still stand today. Many are now used as halls, museums or homes.

In time many peasants felt the tithe was unfair. After the French Revolution it was abolished in many countries. In Switzerland it was replaced in the **19th century**. The peasants often had to **buy themselves out** with money. Today people pay **taxes** to the municipality, the canton and the Confederation instead.

gewusst: Many buildings and streets in Switzerland still carry the word “Zehnt”, meaning tithe, in their names.
Because the tithe was so widespread, it is among the best-known levies in the whole history of Europe.

teile.einleitung: In the 19th century millions of people emigrated from Europe to America. They fled from hunger, poverty or persecution and hoped for a better life. Many people from Switzerland also set out.
wichtigste: In 1816 and 1817 the “Year Without a Summer” set off a wave of emigration from Switzerland.
The famine in Ireland from 1845 to 1849 drove millions of people to America.
After 1848 political refugees, the Forty-Eighters, fled to the USA.
Emigrants from Glarus founded New Glarus in Wisconsin in 1845.
The Homestead Act of 1862 promised settlers land.
From 1892 many immigrants arrived through Ellis Island near New York.

abschnitte.text: In 1815 the volcano **Tambora** erupted in Indonesia. Its ash cooled the climate, and 1816 became the **Year Without a Summer**. In eastern Switzerland the harvests failed, and bitter hardship followed. Many families emigrated. In **Ireland** between 1845 and 1849 a fungus destroyed the potato harvest several times. About a million people died, and millions emigrated.

Not everyone fled from hunger. After the failed **revolution of 1848** in Germany many liberals and democrats were persecuted. They are called **Forty-Eighters**. One of them was **Carl Schurz**, who became a politician in the USA. Many Forty-Eighters there campaigned against **slavery**.

Important emigrant ports were, for example, **Bremerhaven** and Le Havre. By **sailing ship** the journey often took six weeks or more. The passengers lived crowded together in steerage. From the second half of the 19th century **steamships** sailed, which were much faster. The crossing then took only a few days to about two weeks.

From 1892 the island of **Ellis Island** near New York was the central immigration station of the USA. There the arrivals were examined and registered. Until 1954 about 12 million people came through Ellis Island. Many moved on to the west. The **Homestead Act** of 1862 promised settlers about 160 acres of land if they farmed it for five years.

abschnitte.titel: A piece of Switzerland in America
abschnitte.text: In 1845 emigrants from the canton of **Glarus** founded the settlement of **New Glarus** in the state of Wisconsin. They were fleeing poverty and unemployment in the textile industry. Some Swiss municipalities even paid for poor families' journeys. New Glarus still keeps up Swiss traditions today.

gewusst: On Ellis Island there is a museum about immigration today.
In Bremerhaven the German Emigration Centre recalls the people who travelled overseas from there.

teile.einleitung: The **University of Bologna** in Italy is regarded as the oldest university in Europe. In the Middle Ages it was famous above all for the study of law. Students from all over Europe travelled there.
wichtigste: The founding year of the University of Bologna is traditionally given as 1088.
It is regarded as the oldest university in Europe.
In the Middle Ages Bologna was famous above all for law.
The jurist Irnerius taught Roman law there.
Emperor Frederick I Barbarossa protected travelling students with the “Authentica Habita”.
In Bologna the students themselves ran the university.

abschnitte.text: The University of Bologna came into being in the late 11th century. There is no exact founding date. In **1888** the university celebrated its **800th anniversary** and so fixed **1088** as its founding year. It is regarded as the **oldest university in Europe**. Its Latin motto is **Alma Mater Studiorum**, which means “nourishing mother of studies”.

In the Middle Ages Bologna was famous above all for **jurisprudence**. The jurist **Irnerius** taught the old **Roman law** there, which had been rediscovered. Students from all over Europe came to learn from him and his successors. Many later became judges, advisers to kings or high officials of the Church. In this way Roman law spread across the whole of Europe.

Travelling students were often without protection in foreign towns. In the 12th century Emperor **Frederick I Barbarossa** placed them under imperial protection with the privilege **“Authentica Habita”**. A privilege is a special right. Students and teachers received their own legal rights. This strengthened the young university greatly.

In Bologna the **students** joined together in a community, a **corporation**. They ran the university: they elected the **rector** and even employed the teachers. In **Paris** it was different, there the teachers, the masters, formed the corporation. Bologna became the model for many later universities in southern Europe.

In **1999** education ministers of many European countries signed a joint declaration in Bologna. From it came the **Bologna Process**. **Switzerland** took part too. Since then people at Swiss universities study in two stages, first the **Bachelor's** and then the **Master's**. This makes it easier to continue studying in other countries.

gewusst: The University of Bologna is still one of the largest universities in Italy today.
The students in Bologna joined together in groups according to where they came from, the so-called nations.

teile.einleitung: The labour movement is the joining together of workers who have fought since the 19th century for better wages, shorter working hours and more rights. It arose when, with industrialisation, many people worked in factories under harsh conditions. Many things that are taken for granted today, such as holidays or the AHV, go back to its efforts.
wichtigste: The labour movement arose in the 19th century during industrialisation.
The many problems of the workers such as poverty, illness and bad housing were called the social question.
Trade unions are associations of employees for better working conditions.
In a strike the workers lay down their work together.
The Swiss Federation of Trade Unions was founded in 1880, the Swiss Social Democratic Party in 1888.
In November 1918 the General Strike took place in Switzerland, led by Robert Grimm.
1 May is regarded worldwide as Labour Day.

abschnitte.text: With **industrialisation** large factories arose in the 19th century, for example spinning mills and engineering works. People often worked 12 to 14 hours a day, six days a week. Children also had to work in the factories. Wages were low, homes were cramped and damp, and anyone who fell ill earned nothing any more. These many problems were called the **social question**.

A single worker could do little against the factory owner. So the workers joined together in **trade unions** to demand better wages and working conditions together. Their strongest means was the **strike**: everyone lays down work at the same time until an agreement is reached. In Switzerland the **Swiss Federation of Trade Unions** was founded in 1880.

In 1848 Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published the **Communist Manifesto**. It ends with the famous call “Workers of the world, unite!”. The workers who owned nothing except their labour were called proletarians. In many countries workers' parties arose, in Switzerland in 1888 the **Social Democratic Party** (SP). As early as 1838 the Grütli Society had been founded in Geneva, an early association of craftsmen and workers.

After the First World War many families in Switzerland were poor, because prices had risen sharply. In November 1918 the **Olten Action Committee** under Robert Grimm called a **general strike**, and about 250,000 people laid down their work. The Federal Council sent soldiers, and in Grenchen soldiers shot three young workers. After three days the strike was called off. All the same many demands were later met: in 1919 and 1920 the 48-hour week, in 1919 proportional elections for the National Council and in 1948 the **AHV**.

**1 May** is Labour Day and has been celebrated in many countries since 1890. It recalls protests in Chicago in 1886, in which workers demanded the eight-hour day. On this day trade unions march through the streets with flags and banners. In some Swiss cantons, for example in Zurich, 1 May is a full or partial public holiday.

Many achievements of the labour movement are part of everyday life today. They include paid **holidays**, accident insurance, the AHV and rules against child labour. In 1877 the Federal **Factory Act** introduced a working day of at most 11 hours. Since 1937 employers and trade unions in Switzerland have often settled disputes by negotiation instead of strikes. This way is called **industrial peace**.

begriffe.erklaerung: An association of employees that campaigns for better wages and working conditions.
The workers stop working together in order to push through demands.
The many problems of the workers in the 19th century, such as poverty, illness and bad housing.
A worker who owns nothing except his labour.
A contract between trade unions and employers that regulates wages and working hours for a whole sector.

gewusst: In the General Strike of 1918 women's suffrage was already demanded, among other things, but it was only introduced in Switzerland in 1971.
The Federal Factory Act of 1877 banned factory work for children under 14.
The AHV, which was demanded in 1918, only came into force 30 years later, on 1 January 1948.

teile.einleitung: Benito Mussolini was an Italian politician and dictator. He founded the fascist movement and ruled Italy from 1922 to 1943 with ever more violence and without democracy. At Hitler's side he led his country into the Second World War, which ended in catastrophe for Italy.
wichtigste: Mussolini was born in 1883 in Predappio in northern Italy.
From about 1902 to 1904 he lived in Switzerland as a young emigrant.
In 1919 he founded the “Fasci di combattimento” in Milan, the beginning of Fascism.
After the March on Rome he became prime minister in October 1922.
After the murder of Giacomo Matteotti in 1924 he built up a dictatorship.
From 1935 Italy waged a cruel war in Abyssinia, present-day Ethiopia, also using poison gas.
On 28 April 1945 Mussolini was shot by partisans.

abschnitte.text: Benito Mussolini was born on 29 July 1883 in **Predappio** in the region of Emilia-Romagna. His father was a blacksmith, his mother a teacher. He himself first became a teacher too. Around 1902 he went to **Switzerland**, where he got by with odd jobs, took part with socialists and was arrested and expelled several times. Back in Italy he became a well-known journalist of the Socialist Party and edited its newspaper “Avanti!”.

When the First World War began, Mussolini demanded that Italy should join the fighting. For this he was expelled from the **Socialist Party** at the end of 1914. He founded a newspaper of his own and later served as a soldier himself. On 23 March 1919 he founded the “Fasci di combattimento”, the fighting leagues, in Milan. From this came **Fascism**, a movement that glorified a strong leader, national pride and violence against opponents. His followers wore black shirts and were therefore called “Blackshirts”.

In October 1922 tens of thousands of Fascists marched towards the capital in the **March on Rome**. King Victor Emmanuel III gave way and appointed Mussolini prime minister. In June 1924 the socialist deputy **Giacomo Matteotti** was murdered by Fascists because he had denounced election fraud. After this crisis Mussolini banned other parties, abolished freedom of the press and had himself called “Duce”, which means leader. In 1929 he concluded the Lateran Treaties with the pope, through which the state of Vatican City came into being.

From December 1935 Italy systematically used poison gas in the war against **Abyssinia**, present-day Ethiopia, a serious war crime. In 1936 Italian troops captured the capital Addis Ababa. Mussolini allied himself ever more closely with Adolf Hitler and in 1938 also introduced laws against Jews in Italy. In June 1940 Italy entered the **Second World War** at Germany's side. Many campaigns, for example in Greece and North Africa, ended in heavy defeats.

In July 1943, after the Allied landing in Sicily, Mussolini was deposed and arrested. German soldiers freed him in September 1943 from a hotel on the Gran Sasso. In northern Italy he then led a puppet state with German help, the so-called Republic of **Salò**. In April 1945 he tried to flee towards Switzerland in disguise, but was caught by **partisans** on Lake Como. On 28 April 1945 he was shot together with his lover Clara Petacci.

begriffe.erklaerung: A movement that wants an all-powerful leader, extreme nationalism and violence against opponents.
Rule in which one person or group has all the power and the people are not allowed to vote freely.
Italian for leader, which is what Mussolini had himself called.
Armed fighters who do not belong to a regular army and fight against occupiers or dictators.

gewusst: The word Fascism comes from the Latin “fasces”, a bundle of rods with an axe, which was a sign of power in ancient Rome.
In Lausanne the young Mussolini is said to have slept at times under a bridge because he had no money.
Mussolini was Hitler's model: the March on Rome inspired Hitler in 1923 to his failed coup in Munich.

teile.einleitung: **Thomas Aquinas** was an Italian scholar and monk in the 13th century. He is regarded as one of the most important thinkers of the Middle Ages. He wanted to show that faith and reason fit together.
wichtigste: Thomas Aquinas lived in the 13th century and was a Dominican.
His most important teacher was Albert the Great.
His main work is the unfinished Summa Theologiae.
With the “five ways” he wanted to show that God exists.
As a Doctor of the Church he bears the honorary title Doctor Angelicus.

abschnitte.text: Thomas was born around **1225** in southern Italy, near the town of Aquino. That is where his name comes from. Against the will of his family he joined the **Dominican order**. His most important teacher was **Albert the Great**, a universal scholar. With him Thomas studied in **Paris** and **Cologne**. Later he taught himself at the University of Paris and in Italy. He died in **1274**.

The main work of Thomas is called the **Summa Theologiae**. In it he sets out the whole of **theology** in an orderly way. Theology is the study of God and of faith. The work is built up as questions and answers. Thomas first lists objections, then gives his answer and explains it. In **1273** he broke off the work, shortly before his death, which is why it remained unfinished.

Thomas studied the Greek philosopher **Aristotle** closely. He was convinced that with the mind one can find out a great deal about the world and about God. At the start of the Summa stand the **five ways**, in Latin **Quinque viae**. They reason from observations, such as motion and cause, to God as the first origin. This way of joining faith with careful thinking is called **scholasticism**.

The Catholic Church declared Thomas a saint in **1323** and later named him a **Doctor of the Church**. His honorary title is **Doctor Angelicus**, which means “the angelic teacher”. Other scholars have other nicknames: Duns Scotus is called Doctor Subtilis, Bonaventure Doctor Seraphicus. The teaching of Thomas still shapes Catholic theology today.

gewusst: Because of his quiet manner, fellow students supposedly called him the “dumb ox”.
The Summa Theologiae runs to several thousand pages, even though it is unfinished.

teile.einleitung: A mill turns grains of corn into flour. In the Middle Ages mills were very important, because without flour there was no bread.
wichtigste: In the mill, grains are ground into flour.
The person who runs a mill is called a miller.
Many mills were driven by flowing water.
A water wheel drives the millstones.
Two millstones grind the grain.
A windmill is driven by the wind.

abschnitte.text: In the **mill** the **grains of corn** are ground. This makes **flour** for bread. For this, two heavy round **millstones** lay on top of each other. The lower one stayed in place, the upper one turned. Between them the grains were ground fine.

Many mills stood on a **stream** or river. The **flowing water** pushed against a large **water wheel** and turned it. Through gear wheels the wheel drove the millstones. This meant nobody had to grind by muscle power any more. In Switzerland there used to be a mill on the stream in very many villages.

Where there was little flowing water, people built **windmills**. They have big **sails**. The wind turns them, and so the mill grinds. Windmills were found above all in flat country, for example in the Netherlands.

The man who runs the mill is called the **miller**. That is why many people are still called Miller today. Many farmers had no money. So the miller often kept a small **share of the flour** as his pay. Some people distrusted millers, because they feared that they kept too much.

Many mills belonged to a lord. The farmers of his territory were not allowed to go to just any mill. They had to have their grain ground at their lord’s mill. It was called a **banal mill**. In this way the lord earned something from every sack of grain.

gewusst: Miller is one of the most common surnames in Switzerland and Germany.
In the past water wheels also drove saws and hammers in workshops.

teile.einleitung: The plough is one of the most important tools of farming. It loosens and turns the soil so that seeds can be sown afterwards. In the Middle Ages the heavy wheeled plough brought great progress.
wichtigste: A plough loosens the soil and turns the earth.
The tip, the ploughshare, was often made of iron.
The heavy plough of the Middle Ages often had wheels at the front.
Oxen pulled the plough with a wooden yoke.
Horses were faster but more expensive to keep.
The grooves that the plough makes are called furrows.

abschnitte.text: A **plough** tears open the earth and **turns** it. In doing so weeds are buried and the soil becomes loose. Afterwards farmers can sow. The plough draws long grooves in the field, called **furrows**. Without a plough it would be very hard work to cultivate large fields.

abschnitte.titel: From the scratch plough to the wheeled plough
abschnitte.text: Older ploughs were simple **scratch ploughs**. They only scratched the soil but did not turn it. In the Middle Ages the heavy **wheeled plough** spread. It had **wheels** at the front so that it could be steered better. Its tip, the **ploughshare**, was made of **iron**, because iron is hard and cuts well into the earth. A slanting board turned the clod of earth over.

An **ox** is a male bovine that is calmer than a bull and well suited to work. Oxen are **very strong** and have great stamina. So that two oxen could pull together, a **yoke** was laid over their heads or necks. The yoke is a heavy, shaped piece of wood. In this way the animals could pull the heavy plough for a long time.

**Horses** pulled the plough faster than oxen. But they were **more expensive** and needed more and better feed, for example oats. With the **horse collar**, a padded ring around the neck, horses could pull heavy loads without having their breathing cut off. Even so, oxen remained the most important draught animals in many places for a long time. Today tractors usually pull the plough.

gewusst: With the heavy plough, heavy, wet soils could also be farmed better in the Middle Ages.
The expression “to be under the yoke” means to be oppressed, and recalls draught animals.

teile.einleitung: The Republic of Genoa was a city-state on the coast of north-west Italy. Through sea trade it became rich and powerful in the Middle Ages and founded trading bases as far as the Black Sea.
wichtigste: Genoa was a maritime republic and a great trading power in the Mediterranean.
In 1261 Genoa gained access to the Black Sea in the Treaty of Nymphaeum.
Caffa in Crimea was the most important Genoese trading base there.
In the War of Chioggia Genoa lost to its rival Venice in 1381.
In 1407 the Casa di San Giorgio was founded, one of the oldest banks in Europe.

abschnitte.text: **Genoa** lies on the coast of Liguria in north-west Italy. In the Middle Ages the city became a **republic** ruled by rich families. With its ships it traded across the whole **Mediterranean**. Its greatest rivals were the maritime republics of **Pisa** and **Venice**. The famous seafarer **Christopher Columbus** came from Genoa.

In 1261 Genoa gained access to the **Black Sea** in the **Treaty of Nymphaeum**. The most important base there was **Caffa** on the **Crimean** peninsula, today’s Feodosia. Caffa was a trading centre for grain, furs, silk and also for slaves. From there the **plague** probably came to Europe in 1347. Genoa had many more trading colonies in the East.

Genoa and Venice fought for a long time for dominance in trade. In the **War of Chioggia** the Genoese occupied the town of **Chioggia** in the lagoon of Venice. There, however, they were besieged and had to surrender. The war ended in **1381** with a victory for **Venice**. After that Genoa was no longer the stronger naval power.

In **1407** Genoa founded the **Casa di San Giorgio**. It managed the **public debt** and the government bonds of the republic. In return it received tax revenue and even colonies. At times it was more powerful than the government itself. It is regarded as **one of the oldest banks in Europe**. The Republic of Genoa lasted until 1797, when Napoleon dissolved it.

gewusst: Genoa bore the proud nickname “La Superba”, the Magnificent.
The island of Corsica belonged to Genoa for a long time before it passed to France in 1768.

teile.einleitung: The Republic of Venice was an independent city-state in a lagoon on the Adriatic for more than a thousand years. Through sea trade it became one of the richest powers in Europe and ruled islands and coasts in the eastern Mediterranean.
wichtigste: At its head stood the doge, elected for life.
Its heraldic animal is the winged lion of Saint Mark.
In 1204 crusaders, at Venice’s urging, conquered Constantinople.
In the Arsenal galleys were built in large numbers.
Since the Serrata of 1297 only old patrician families governed.
From 1310 the Council of Ten oversaw state security.
Crete belonged to Venice until 1669.

abschnitte.titel: Doge and lion of Saint Mark
abschnitte.text: The head of the republic was called the **doge**. He was elected for life and lived in the **Doge’s Palace** on St Mark’s Square. The patron saint of Venice is the Evangelist **Mark**. His symbol, the **winged lion**, is the heraldic animal of the city. It can still be seen today on many buildings and on flags.

The **Great Council** was important. With the reform of **1297**, the **Serrata del Maggior Consiglio**, it was restricted to the old **patrician families**. “Serrata” means “closing”. From then on membership was practically hereditary. In 1310, after a conspiracy, the **Council of Ten** was created. It oversaw state security and was feared for its secret proceedings.

Venice lived from **sea trade** with the East. In the **Arsenal**, the great state shipyard, **galleys** were built almost as on an assembly line. It was one of the largest enterprises in Europe. German merchants lived and stored their goods in the **Fondaco dei Tedeschi** by the Rialto Bridge. In this way spices, silk and other goods from the Orient travelled via Venice to the north, including to Switzerland.

In the **Fourth Crusade** Venice steered the crusader army to **Constantinople**, which was conquered and plundered in **1204**. Afterwards Venice acquired the claims to the island of **Crete**. Crete became its most important colony in the eastern Mediterranean. Only in **1669** did the Ottomans conquer the capital, Candia. The Republic of Venice itself ended in **1797** at the hands of Napoleon.

Every year on **Ascension Day** a special ceremony took place. The doge sailed out in the state barge **Bucintoro** and threw a **golden ring** into the sea. In this way Venice symbolically “married” the **Adriatic**. The ceremony showed that Venice ruled the sea. Today it is staged again as a festival.

gewusst: The four bronze horses on St Mark’s Basilica were brought by the Venetians from Constantinople in 1204.
Venice stands on more than a hundred small islands that are linked by canals and bridges.

teile.einleitung: The Vikings were outstanding seafarers. With their ships they sailed across seas and rivers, traded and conquered. Their ships are still regarded as masterpieces of boatbuilding.
wichtigste: The fast warship of the Vikings is called a longship.
A longship had a large, square sail and oars.
The ships were made of wood, often oak, with iron rivets.
Because they sat shallow in the water, they could also sail on rivers.
The broad merchant ship was called a knarr.
In the museum at Roskilde in Denmark you can see real Viking ships.

abschnitte.text: The **longship** was long, narrow and fast. It had a mast with **one large, square sail**. When no wind blew, the men rowed. They often hung the round **shields** in a row along the **side of the ship**. At the front some ships carried a carved head, for example a dragon.

The Vikings built their ships of **wood**, often oak. The planks overlapped like roof tiles. This way of building is called **clinker construction**. The planks were joined with **iron rivets**. This made the ships light, strong and a little flexible in high waves.

Longships sat only a little way into the water, they lay **shallow**. So they could also sail into shallow **rivers** and land directly on a beach. In this way the Vikings got far inland. They sailed to England, France and Iceland, along rivers to Eastern Europe and even to North America.

For trade there was the **knarr**. It was broader and higher than a longship. In it there was room for many **goods and animals**. The knarr travelled mainly under sail and needed fewer rowers. With such ships settlers brought cattle and supplies to Iceland and Greenland.

In **Roskilde** in **Denmark** stands the Viking Ship Museum. There ships are shown that were recovered from the **fjord** in the 20th century. The Vikings had once sunk them deliberately to block the entrance. In the museum replicas are also built and sailed. Further famous ships from graves stand in Oslo in Norway.

gewusst: On Viking ships the steering oar sat at the back on the right-hand side. That is where the word “starboard” comes from.
Replicas of Viking ships have shown that they could sail across the Atlantic.

teile.einleitung: Norse mythology covers the myths about the gods of the Germanic peoples in northern Europe, especially the Vikings. Many of these stories were written down in Iceland in the Middle Ages.
wichtigste: Odin is the father of the gods.
He has only one eye and two ravens, Huginn and Muninn.
His horse Sleipnir has eight legs.
Thor is the god of thunder with the hammer Mjölnir.
Thursday is named after the thunder god.
According to the myths, fallen warriors went to Valhalla.

abschnitte.text: **Odin** is the highest god in the Norse myths. He is thought to be wise and clever. According to the myth he gave up an **eye** to drink from a spring of wisdom. That is why he has only one eye left. His two **ravens**, **Huginn** and **Muninn**, fly over the world every day and tell him everything in the evening.
Odin rides a special horse. It is called **Sleipnir** and has **eight legs**. Sleipnir is faster than any other horse. According to the myth it can even run through the air and over the sea.

**Thor** is the **god of thunder**. The Vikings believed that his hammer made lightning and thunder. The hammer is called **Mjölnir**. According to the myth it returns to Thor’s hand after every throw. Thor protects gods and humans from the giants.

Among the Germanic peoples in the south the thunder god was called **Donar**, in the north **Thor**. **Thursday** is named after him. In German the day is called “Donnerstag”, thunder’s day, and in English “Thursday”, Thor’s day. Other days of the week also remind us of old gods, for example the English “Wednesday” of Odin, who was called Wodan in the south.

According to the myth, brave fallen warriors went to **Valhalla**. This is the great hall of Odin. There they were to feast and prepare for a last great battle at the end of the world. Many of these stories are found in the **Edda**, a collection from Iceland.

gewusst: The stories of the Edda were only written down in the 13th century, long after the time of the Vikings.
Many films and comics about Thor are loosely based on these old myths.

teile.einleitung: The Donation of Pepin was a promise by the Frankish king Pepin to the Pope. Pepin agreed to hand over territories in Italy to him. From this the Papal States arose.
wichtigste: In 754 at Quierzy Pepin promised the Pope territories in Italy.
The Pope was Stephen II, who travelled across the Alps for this.
The Lombard king Aistulf had occupied the territories.
Pepin marched into Italy twice, in 754 and 756.
The most important territory was the Exarchate of Ravenna.
From this the Papal States arose, which lasted until 1870.

abschnitte.text: The Lombard king **Aistulf** had conquered **Ravenna** in 751 and was threatening Rome. Pope **Stephen II** sought help from the Frankish king **Pepin**. In 753 and 754 he travelled across the **Alps** into the Frankish kingdom. He was the first pope to visit the Frankish kingdom. Pepin was the father of **Charlemagne**.

In **754** Pepin promised at **Quierzy** to hand over to the Pope the territories occupied by the Lombards. This promise is called the **Donation of Pepin**. In the same year the Pope anointed Pepin and his sons at **Saint-Denis**. He gave Pepin the title **“Patricius Romanorum”**, protector of the Romans.

After the first campaign in **754** Aistulf did not keep the agreement. So in **756** Pepin marched into Italy a **second time**. Only then were the territories handed over. Among them was the **Exarchate of Ravenna**, formerly a Byzantine administrative region. Pepin did not give it back to Byzantium but to the Pope.

The territories handed over formed the basis of the **Papal States**. There the Pope was also a worldly ruler. The Papal States lasted until **1870**. Another document, the **Donation of Constantine**, claimed that a Roman emperor had already given power to the Pope. It was probably created in the 8th or 9th century. The humanist **Lorenzo Valla** proved in 1440 that it is a **forgery**.

gewusst: Of the former Papal States only Vatican City is left today, the smallest state in the world.
The Pontifical Swiss Guard has protected the Pope in the Vatican since the year 1506.

teile.einleitung: The Amsterdam Stock Exchange is regarded as the oldest modern securities exchange in the world. It came into being in the 17th century, when shares of the Dutch East India Company began to be traded. Many ideas of today's financial world were tried out there for the first time.
wichtigste: From 1602 shares of the VOC were traded in Amsterdam.
In 1609 the city founded the Amsterdam Exchange Bank.
Isaac Le Maire is regarded as the originator of the first documented short sales.
Hendrick de Keyser built the first exchange building, used from 1611.
The book “Confusión de Confusiones” of 1688 is regarded as the oldest work on share trading.
The Beurs van Berlage was built from 1898 to 1903.
Since the year 2000 the exchange has belonged to Euronext.

abschnitte.text: In **1602** the **Dutch East India Company**, **VOC** for short, was founded. It traded in spices from Asia. Many people bought **parts** of the company, so-called **shares**.
