Soon after the founding, regular **trading** in these shares began. That is why Amsterdam is regarded as the home of the oldest modern **securities exchange**.

In Amsterdam coins from many countries came together. This made paying difficult. That is why the **Amsterdam Exchange Bank** was founded in **1609**, in Dutch the Amsterdamsche Wisselbank. It accepted coins of different origins and kept **accounts** in a stable unit of account. In this way it made international **trade** easier.

Soon traders tried to earn money from rising or falling prices. The merchant **Isaac Le Maire** sold VOC shares for future delivery in 1609 that he did not yet own. He was betting on **falling prices**. Such deals are called **short sales**. The authorities banned them as early as **1610**. In 1688 **Joseph de la Vega** described in the book **“Confusión de Confusiones”**, in the form of dialogues, the dealings on the exchange, including options and futures.

At first the traders met in the open air. From **1611** they used a building of their own on the **Rokin**, which the architect **Hendrick de Keyser** had designed. It had an open **courtyard** with arcades. From 1898 to 1903 the **Beurs van Berlage** was built. **Hendrik Petrus Berlage** designed it with clear brick shapes. It is regarded as an important building of early **modernism** in the Netherlands.

In **2000** the exchanges of **Amsterdam, Paris and Brussels** joined together to form **Euronext**. The most important Amsterdam share index is called the **AEX**. Today trading is done almost entirely electronically on computers. In Switzerland, too, there is a large exchange: the **SIX Swiss Exchange** in Zurich.

gewusst: The VOC is regarded as one of the first companies whose shares could be freely bought and sold.
No more trading takes place in the Beurs van Berlage today, and the building is used for concerts and events.

teile.einleitung: Albrecht Dürer was one of the most important artists of the German Renaissance. He lived in Nuremberg and was a painter, draughtsman and master of printmaking. Works such as the “Young Hare” or the “Praying Hands” are known all over the world.
wichtigste: In 1502 Dürer painted the “Young Hare” so realistically that you can see every hair.
The “Praying Hands” are a famous drawing by him.
Dürer was one of the first artists to paint himself again and again.
With the woodcut he could print pictures many times over.
In 1515 he drew a rhinoceros that he had never seen.
He travelled to Italy to get to know the art of the Renaissance.
As a young journeyman he worked in Basel around 1492.

abschnitte.text: Albrecht Dürer was born in **1471** in **Nuremberg**. His father was a goldsmith. Albrecht first learned this craft and then painting. Afterwards he went travelling as a young **journeyman**. Around **1492** he came to **Basel**. There he made pictures for **printed books**, because Basel was at that time an important town for printing.

Dürer wanted to get to know the new art of the **Renaissance**. He travelled across the Alps to **Venice** in **Italy**. There he learned a great deal from the Italian painters, for example about perspective and the portrayal of the human body. He was even in Italy twice. Back in Nuremberg he combined the Italian ideas with the art of the north.

In **1502** Dürer painted a **young hare**. The picture is so exact that you can see every single hair. It is one of the most famous animal pictures in the world. Just as well known is the drawing **“Praying Hands”**. You can find it today on many cards and pictures. Dürer observed nature very closely.

Dürer was one of the first artists to paint **himself** again and again. That was something new at the time. At the age of 13 he drew a self-portrait. He signed his works with his mark: a large **A** with a small **D** beneath it. This **monogram** made his pictures instantly recognisable.

In a **woodcut** a picture is carved into a block of wood. Afterwards it can be **printed** on paper again and again. In this way Dürer's works were spread all over Europe. In **1515** he made a woodcut of a **rhinoceros**, although he had never seen one. He had only a description and a sketch. That is why his rhinoceros wears a kind of **armour**.

gewusst: The real “Young Hare” is very sensitive to light and is therefore only rarely shown in a museum in Vienna.
Dürer's rhinoceros was considered correct for so long that it was still reproduced in school books centuries later.

teile.einleitung: The Berlin Wall was a heavily guarded border structure that separated West Berlin from the east from 1961 to 1989. The GDR built it to stop its citizens from fleeing to the west. It became the symbol of the division of Germany and Europe, and its fall on 9 November 1989 the symbol of freedom.
wichtigste: On 13 August 1961 the GDR began building the Wall.
As late as June 1961 Walter Ulbricht had claimed that nobody had any intention of building a wall.
The Wall enclosed West Berlin over a length of about 155 kilometres.
According to present research at least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall.
John F. Kennedy said “Ich bin ein Berliner” in West Berlin in 1963.
Ronald Reagan demanded “Tear down this wall” at the Brandenburg Gate in 1987.
On 9 November 1989 the Wall was opened after a misleading remark by Günter Schabowski.

abschnitte.text: After the Second World War two German states came into being: the Federal Republic in the west and the **GDR** in the east. By 1961 about three million people had fled from the GDR to the west, many of them through Berlin. Above all young and well-educated people left. On 15 June 1961 the GDR head of state **Walter Ulbricht** still said: “Nobody has any intention of building a wall.” Two months later, in the night of 13 August 1961, soldiers and police sealed off the border.

At first the border consisted of barbed wire, then it was built up with stones and later with concrete slabs about 3.6 metres high. Behind the actual wall lay the **death strip** with watchtowers, dog runs, ditches and bright lamps. The border guards had orders to shoot at people fleeing. The GDR officially called the Wall an “anti-fascist protection rampart” and claimed that it protected against the West. Well-known crossings were **Checkpoint Charlie** and Bornholmer Strasse.

Despite the danger many people tried to escape, for example through tunnels, in hidden cars or with home-built flying machines. On 17 August 1962 the 18-year-old **Peter Fechter** was shot near Checkpoint Charlie and bled to death in the death strip before the eyes of many onlookers. According to present research at least 140 people died at the Berlin Wall. Families and friends were separated for decades.

On 26 June 1963 US President **John F. Kennedy** visited West Berlin and said before hundreds of thousands: “Ich bin ein Berliner.” With this he showed that the USA stood by the city. On 12 June 1987 **Ronald Reagan** stood before the Brandenburg Gate and called on the Soviet leader Mikhail Gorbachev: “Tear down this wall”. Both speeches are world famous to this day.

In the autumn of 1989 more and more people in the GDR demonstrated for freedom. On the evening of 9 November 1989 the SED politician **Günter Schabowski** declared at a press conference that new travel rules would apply “immediately, without delay”, although that was not what had been planned. Thousands streamed to the border crossings until the guards opened the gates. People celebrated on the Wall and chipped pieces out of it. Less than a year later, on 3 October 1990, Germany was reunified.

abschnitte.titel: What can still be seen today
abschnitte.text: Today only a few parts of the Wall are preserved. The **East Side Gallery** is a stretch more than a kilometre long that artists from all over the world have painted. In the memorial on Bernauer Strasse you can see what the death strip looked like. In the ground a double row of cobblestones marks the former course in many places. Pieces of the Wall stand today as a reminder in many countries of the world.

begriffe.erklaerung: German Democratic Republic, the communist state in the east of Germany from 1949 to 1990.
The heavily guarded area behind the Wall in which people who were fleeing were shot at.
A well-known border crossing in Berlin for foreigners and diplomats.
The opening of the Berlin Wall on 9 November 1989.

gewusst: The Wall stood for 28 years, and on 5 February 2018 it had been gone exactly as long as it had stood.
In January 1989 the GDR leader Erich Honecker still claimed that the Wall would still stand in 50 and even in 100 years.
A piece of the Berlin Wall also stands in Switzerland, including in Geneva and Lugano.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages minstrels travelled from place to place and entertained people. They played music, sang songs and told stories.
wichtigste: Minstrels played music and entertained people in the Middle Ages.
They travelled from place to place, to markets, festivals and castles.
They often played the bagpipes.
The hurdy-gurdy is an instrument with a crank.
In their songs they often told of heroes and adventures.

abschnitte.text: **Minstrels** were entertainers of the Middle Ages. They played **music**, sang, danced or showed tricks such as juggling. They could be met at **markets**, at weddings, festivals and in **castles**. Most had no fixed home but wandered about as **travelling people**. They had few rights and were often looked down on, although people loved their entertainment.

Minstrels often played the **bagpipes**. They have an air bag and several pipes and are very loud, so they suited markets well. Another instrument was the **hurdy-gurdy**. It has a **crank** that turns a wheel. The wheel rubs against the strings, rather like a violin bow. In addition there were flutes, drums and the **fiddle**, an early violin.

In their songs minstrels often told **of heroes and adventures**. Because many people could not read, stories and also news spread from place to place in this way. Besides the minstrels there were the **Minnesänger**, who were often nobles themselves. Their songs are collected in the **Manesse Codex**, which was made around 1300 in **Zurich**.

gewusst: The hurdy-gurdy is still played today, for example in folk music and at medieval markets.

teile.einleitung: Poland-Lithuania was a union of the countries of Poland and Lithuania that began in the late Middle Ages. It lasted more than 400 years and was at times one of the largest states in Europe.
wichtigste: The Union of Krewo of 1385 laid the foundation.
The Lithuanian grand duke Jogaila was baptised in 1386.
He married the Polish queen Hedwig of Anjou.
As king he was called Władysław II Jagiełło and founded the Jagiellonian dynasty.
Lithuania was the last country in Europe to be Christianised.

abschnitte.text: In 1385 Poland and Lithuania concluded the **Union of Krewo**. In it the Lithuanian grand duke **Jogaila** promised to be baptised and to marry the young Queen of Poland. This created a **personal union**: two countries had the same ruler but remained separate states. This link later became ever closer.

**Hedwig of Anjou** was the daughter of King Louis of Hungary and Poland. She had been crowned Queen of Poland as a young girl. In 1386 she married **Jogaila**. He was baptised and crowned King of Poland as **Władysław II Jagiełło**. He founded the ruling family of the **Jagiellonians**.

**Lithuania** had remained **pagan**, that is, not Christian, until the 14th century. With Jogaila’s **baptism** in 1386 the people, too, gradually adopted Christianity. In this way Lithuania became the **last country in Europe** to be Christianised. In 1410 Polish and Lithuanian troops together defeated the Teutonic Order in the **Battle of Tannenberg**, called Grunwald in Polish.

gewusst: In 1569 Poland and Lithuania joined together even more closely in the Union of Lublin.
At the end of the 18th century Poland-Lithuania was divided up by its neighbours and vanished from the map.

teile.einleitung: Before there were engines, people had to lift heavy loads with their own strength. For this, **treadwheel cranes** were built in the Middle Ages. Workers walked inside a large wooden wheel and so lifted stones high into the air.
wichtigste: A treadwheel crane was driven by people walking inside a large wheel.
The wheel turned a shaft onto which a rope wound.
On the rope hung the load, for example a heavy block of stone.
Treadwheel cranes were built of wood.
They were used in building castles and churches and at harbours.

abschnitte.titel: Walking like in a hamster wheel
abschnitte.text: A **treadwheel crane** had a large wheel made of wood. In it one or more workers walked, rather like a hamster in its wheel. The wheel turned a **shaft**, that is, an axle. A **rope** wound itself onto this shaft. At the end of the rope hung the load that was pulled upwards. Because the wheel was large and the shaft thin, people could lift much heavier loads with it than they could carry.

The wheel, arm and frame of the crane were made of **wood**. Steel did not yet exist in such quantities. Carpenters built the cranes right on the building site. Sometimes a crane even stood on top of a wall or tower that was just being built. In this way the crane grew upwards with the building.

When building **castles** and **churches**, people used the crane to lift **heavy blocks of stone** and beams onto the walls. This was much easier and faster than carrying everything up. There were also treadwheel cranes at **harbours** to lift goods out of ships. On **Cologne Cathedral** a medieval crane stood for centuries on the unfinished tower. It became a landmark of the city.

gewusst: Even the ancient Romans knew cranes with treadwheels.
The old crane on Cologne Cathedral was only taken down in the 19th century, when the cathedral was finally completed.

teile.einleitung: The Apollo programme was a space programme of the USA. Its aim was to bring people to the Moon and safely back to Earth. Between 1969 and 1972 this succeeded six times.
wichtigste: The Apollo programme was carried out by the American space agency NASA.
Apollo 11 was the first mission to land on the Moon, in July 1969.
Neil Armstrong was the first person to set foot on the Moon.
Six missions landed on the Moon, and in all 12 people walked there.
Apollo 17 was the last mission to land on the Moon, in December 1972.
The astronauts brought rock from the Moon back to Earth.

abschnitte.text: At the start of the 1960s the USA and the **Soviet Union** were competing in space. President **John F. Kennedy** declared in 1961 that the USA should put a man on the Moon before the end of the decade. From this came the **Apollo programme** of the space agency **NASA**. Hundreds of thousands of people worked on it.

For the journey the huge **Saturn V** rocket was built. It was over 100 metres tall. At the top sat the spacecraft with three astronauts. Two of them climbed into the **lunar module** and landed on the Moon. The third stayed in the spacecraft and circled the Moon until the others came back.

In July 1969 **Apollo 11** landed on the Moon. **Neil Armstrong** was the first person to set foot on the Moon, and shortly afterwards **Buzz Aldrin** followed. Michael Collins waited in the spacecraft. Millions of people watched on television. The astronauts set up measuring instruments and collected Moon rock.

After Apollo 11 further landings followed. Six missions arrived on the Moon, each with two astronauts on the surface. So altogether there were **12 people**. On the last flights they even drove around in a **lunar rover**. **Apollo 17** landed in December 1972 as the last mission. Since then nobody has been on the Moon.

On Apollo 11 there was also an experiment from Switzerland. Researchers at the **University of Bern** had developed a **solar wind sail**, a foil that caught tiny particles from the Sun. The astronauts set it up on the Moon and brought it back. In Bern the researchers afterwards studied what the solar wind is made of.

gewusst: The Bernese solar wind sail was the only experiment on Apollo 11 that did not come from the USA.
The footprints on the Moon last a very long time because there is no wind or rain there.
Apollo 13 had to turn back because of an accident, but the three astronauts returned safely to Earth.

teile.einleitung: **Tenochtitlan** was the capital of the Aztecs in Mexico. The city lay on an island in a lake and was crossed by canals. When the Spanish arrived, they marvelled at its size.
wichtigste: According to tradition Tenochtitlan was founded in the year 1325.
The city lay on an island in Lake Texcoco.
Broad causeways connected it to the mainland.
Many goods were carried by canoe along the canals.
In the centre stood the great temple, the Templo Mayor.
Today Mexico City stands on this spot.

abschnitte.text: According to tradition the **Aztecs** founded their capital in the year **1325**. They built it on an island in **Lake Texcoco**. The city was surrounded entirely by water. Over time the Aztecs enlarged the island by piling up earth. Around the city they laid out beds on the water, the **chinampas**, on which they grew maize, beans and other plants.

Tenochtitlan had many **canals**. People travelled through the city by **canoe** and carried their goods that way. The Aztecs had no horses and no carts. Long, broad **causeways** led across the lake to the shore. On them people could reach the city on foot.

In the middle of the city stood the **Templo Mayor**. This was a large pyramid with two temples on top. They were dedicated to two important gods of the Aztecs: the war god **Huitzilopochtli** and the rain god **Tlaloc**. Around the temple lay palaces and other sacred buildings. You can visit the remains of the Templo Mayor in Mexico City today.

When the Spanish arrived in **1519**, probably about **200,000 people** lived in Tenochtitlan. There were hardly any cities that large in Europe at the time. The Spanish under **Hernán Cortés** described the city with its markets and temples in amazement. In **1521** they conquered Tenochtitlan after heavy fighting. Afterwards they built their own city on the ruins, present-day **Mexico City**.

gewusst: The lake around Tenochtitlan has almost completely disappeared today, and Mexico City stands on the old lake bed.
The Templo Mayor was built over several times, so that several temples fit inside one another like bowls.

teile.einleitung: A lightning rod protects houses in thunderstorms. It catches the lightning and leads it safely into the earth. It was invented by Benjamin Franklin around 1752.
wichtigste: Benjamin Franklin invented the lightning rod around 1752.
Franklin showed that lightning is electric current.
The lightning rod sits at the top of the roof.
It is made of metal such as copper or iron, because metal conducts electricity well.
Along a wire it leads the lightning into the earth.

abschnitte.text: In a thunderstorm the clouds become electrically charged. If the voltage grows too great, it discharges in a **flash of lightning**. In the 18th century **Benjamin Franklin** showed that lightning is a huge **electrical discharge**. That was an important discovery. Before that many people believed that lightning was a punishment from heaven.

If lightning strikes a house, it can set it on fire. In the past barns, houses and church towers often burned down in this way. Lightning mostly looks for the way through the **highest point**. These are, for example, towers, tall trees or roof ridges.

A lightning rod has three parts. On top of the roof sits a **rod** of metal. From there a thick **wire** leads down the wall of the house. At the bottom it is connected to the **earth**. If lightning strikes, the current flows along the wire into the ground. So the house stays undamaged.

A lightning rod is made of **metal** such as **copper** or iron. Metal **conducts electricity** very well. The current of the lightning therefore prefers to take the way through the metal rather than through wood or walls. In Switzerland the regulations require lightning protection for many large buildings.

gewusst: A flash of lightning is several times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
In a car you are quite safe in a thunderstorm, because the metal shell conducts the current around the outside.

teile.einleitung: The Enlightenment was an intellectual movement in Europe that reached its peak in the 18th century. Its thinkers wanted people to think for themselves and rely on their reason instead of simply believing everything. Many ideas of that time, such as human rights, separation of powers and schooling for all, shape our lives to this day.
wichtigste: The Enlightenment reached its peak in the 18th century, which is therefore also called the “Age of Enlightenment”.
Reason stood at the centre: people were to think for themselves and test claims.
Immanuel Kant declared in 1784 that enlightenment is “man's emergence from his self-imposed immaturity”.
The motto “Sapere aude” means: dare to use your own understanding.
Montesquieu demanded in 1748 the division of power into legislature, government and courts.
John Locke named life, liberty and property as the natural rights of every person.
With Voltaire, Rousseau, Haller and Pestalozzi Switzerland also played an important role.

abschnitte.text: The **Enlightenment** began around 1700 and reached its peak in the 18th century. Its followers thought that the world can be understood through **reason** and observation. Old habits, superstition and blind obedience to kings or churches were to be examined critically. The picture behind it: the light of understanding is to drive away the darkness of ignorance. That is why the period is called “Enlightenment” in English and “Siècle des Lumières”, the century of lights, in French.

The German philosopher **Immanuel Kant** of Königsberg wrote his famous essay “An Answer to the Question: What is Enlightenment?” in 1784. In it he made “Sapere aude” the motto of the movement. In France Denis Diderot and Jean-Baptiste le Rond d'Alembert published the **Encyclopédie** from 1751, a huge reference work that wanted to make the knowledge of the time accessible to everyone. In 1779 Gotthold Ephraim Lessing argued in his play “Nathan the Wise”, with the parable of the ring, for tolerance between Judaism, Christianity and Islam.

The Englishman **John Locke** wrote that every person has natural rights to life, liberty and property. A state must protect these rights, otherwise the people may resist. The Frenchman Montesquieu demanded in his book “The Spirit of the Laws” in 1748 the **separation of powers**: legislature, government and courts should be separate so that nobody has too much power. Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who was born in Geneva, wrote in 1762 about the “Social Contract” and the rule of the people.

The famous French writer **Voltaire** lived in Geneva from 1755 for many years and later in nearby Ferney, just across the border. The Bernese physician and naturalist **Albrecht von Haller** wrote the poem “The Alps”, which praised the mountain world and the simple life of mountain farmers and drew many travellers to Switzerland. Johann Heinrich **Pestalozzi** of Zurich worked for the education of poor children and founded schools, for example in Stans and Yverdon. His idea of learning with “head, heart and hand” is still well known today.

The ideas of the Enlightenment influenced the American **Declaration of Independence** of 1776 and the French Revolution of 1789. The Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen of 1789 also builds on them. Modern democracies such as Switzerland know today separation of powers, fundamental rights and freedom of opinion. Compulsory schooling and the idea that science rests on evidence also go back in large part to the Enlightenment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability to think clearly and logically and to give grounds for things.
When someone does not decide for himself but lets others think for him.
The power in the state is divided among parliament, government and courts.
Respecting other opinions and religions, even if you think differently yourself.
A large reference work that collects knowledge from many fields.

gewusst: The Encyclopédie was banned for a time because it criticised Church and king, and was nevertheless secretly printed on.
In Ferney Voltaire had a watchmaking business and workshops set up, and the small village became a lively place.
Albrecht von Haller is said to have written tens of thousands of book reviews and letters in his life.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages most people wore clothes made of wool. From the sheep to the finished tunic it was a long way with a lot of handwork. Almost every family in the countryside spun and wove for itself.
wichtigste: Wool mostly came from sheep.
A sheep is sheared, and this does not hurt it.
In spinning, the fibres are twisted into a thread with the spindle.
On the loom thread becomes cloth.
Peasants mostly wore a tunic in brown or grey.
Dyeing was done with plants, for example madder for red.
Wool keeps you warm, which is why it was so important in winter.

abschnitte.text: Sheep have a thick **fleece**. In spring it is cut off, which is called **shearing**. This does not hurt the sheep, it is like having a haircut. Afterwards the wool was washed and the fibres combed so that they lay in one direction. Only then was it ready for spinning.

In **spinning** the wool fibres are twisted into a long **thread**. The simplest tool for this is the **spindle**, a wooden stick with a small weight. When the spindle turns, it twists the fibres together. Women and girls often spun on the side, even while walking. In the later Middle Ages the **spinning wheel** came to Europe, which worked faster.

From the threads people made cloth on the **loom**. In this, lengthwise threads and crosswise threads are crossed with each other. In this way a piece of cloth comes into being row by row. In the towns weavers worked as a **craft** of their own and were organised in guilds. In Switzerland, too, weaving was important, and Fribourg was known for its woollen cloth in the 15th century.

Cloths were dyed with **plants**. From leaves, roots and flowers colours were obtained. The root of the **madder** gave red, **woad** gave blue. Bright colours were laborious and expensive. That is why peasants mostly wore cloths in natural colours such as **brown and grey**.

Peasants often wore a **tunic**, a long, simple shirt. Over it they tied a **belt**. In addition there were leggings, caps and in winter a cloak. Wool holds **warmth** well, so you freeze less in woollen clothes. Clothes were valuable and were worn for a long time and mended.

gewusst: Wool can absorb a lot of moisture without feeling wet at once.
The grease in sheep's wool is called lanolin and is still used today for ointments and creams.

teile.einleitung: A scriptorium was the writing room in a medieval monastery. There monks copied books by hand, long before printing existed.
wichtigste: In the scriptorium monks copied books by hand.
They wrote with a quill, usually from a goose.
Parchment was often made from calfskin.
They scraped away mistakes with a knife.
Work was mostly done in daylight and in silence.
Copying out a whole Bible could take more than a year.
Ink was often made from oak galls.

abschnitte.text: The word **scriptorium** comes from the Latin word for writing. It was a room in the monastery where monks **copied books by hand**. Because there was no printing yet, this was the only way to make copies of books. Work was mostly done **in daylight**, because candles gave too little light and were expensive. The monks were **silent** while writing in order to concentrate.

The monks wrote with a **quill**, usually **from a goose**. They cut the tip to shape with a small knife. Black ink was often made from **oak galls**. These are small balls that grow on oak leaves when a wasp lays its eggs there. Mixed with iron salt they made a lasting ink.

For a long time there was hardly any paper in Europe. People wrote on **parchment**, a specially treated animal skin. Often **calfskin** was used, but also the skin of sheep or goats. For a whole Bible the skins of many animals were needed. If a monk made a mistake, he carefully scraped it away with a **knife**.

Copying out a whole **Bible** could take **more than a year**. Many books were richly decorated. Large, coloured opening letters are called **initials**. Sometimes they were even decorated with gold. The finished pages were bound together. The **book covers** often consisted of **wood** covered with leather.

A famous scriptorium existed in the **monastery of St Gallen**. There many precious manuscripts were produced in the Middle Ages. Many of them can still be admired today in the **Abbey Library of St Gallen**. The Abbey District of St Gallen has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site** since 1983.

gewusst: Some scribes noted small complaints in the margins of the pages, for example that their hand hurt or that it was cold.
In the Abbey Library of St Gallen visitors put on felt slippers to protect the old wooden floor.

teile.einleitung: The Seljuks were a Turkish ruling family from the 11th to the 13th century. They founded a large empire in Persia, Mesopotamia and Anatolia.
wichtigste: The Seljuks were a dynasty of Turkish origin.
In 1055 Tughril Beg entered Baghdad and received the title of sultan from the caliph.
In 1071 the Seljuks won at Manzikert and captured Emperor Romanos IV Diogenes.
After that Turkish groups settled in Anatolia.
The vizier Nizam al-Mulk shaped the administration and founded colleges.
The Seljuks of Rum had their capital in Konya.
In 1243 they lost to the Mongols at Köse Dağ.

abschnitte.text: The **Seljuks** were a family of Turkish origin. They are named after their forefather **Seljuk**. Their people came from the steppes of Central Asia and were **Muslims**. In the 11th century they conquered large parts of Persia. In **1055** their leader **Tughril Beg** entered **Baghdad**. The caliph gave him the title **sultan**, that is, “ruler”.

In **1071** Sultan Alp Arslan defeated an army of the Byzantine Empire at **Manzikert** in eastern Anatolia. The Byzantine emperor **Romanos IV Diogenes** was taken **prisoner** but was soon released again. After this battle more and more Turkish groups settled in **Anatolia**, present-day Turkey. Later Byzantium asked the West for help, which contributed to the First Crusade.

Under Sultan **Malik Shah** the empire reached its greatest power. His Persian vizier, that is, chief minister, was called **Nizam al-Mulk**. He organised the administration and founded colleges that were named after him. The scholar **Omar Khayyam** worked for the sultan on a very precise **calendar reform**. Omar Khayyam is also famous as a poet.

In Anatolia a separate empire arose, the **Sultanate of Rum**. “Rum” meant “Rome” and referred to the territory of the Byzantine Empire. The capital was **Konya**. There the Seljuks built mosques, schools and, along the trade routes, large inns for travellers. In **1243** they lost to the **Mongols** at **Köse Dağ** and afterwards had to pay them tribute.

gewusst: The famous poet Rumi lived in Konya at the time of the Seljuks of Rum.
The large inns along the trade routes are called caravanserais. Some of them still stand today.

teile.einleitung: Antisemitism means hostility and hatred towards Jews. Such prejudices have existed for centuries, and in the 19th century modern antisemitism arose from them. It led to the Holocaust and has unfortunately not disappeared to this day.
wichtigste: Antisemitism is hostility towards Jews.
The year 1879 is often regarded as the birth year of modern antisemitism in Germany.
Modern racial antisemitism saw Jews as a “race”, so that even baptism changed nothing.
The “Protocols of the Elders of Zion” are a forgery.
From 1933 the Nazis stripped Jews of their rights step by step.
In the November pogroms of 1938 synagogues were destroyed and people were murdered.
Swiss history, too, has antisemitic chapters, for example the “J stamp” of 1938.
Today many people and laws stand up against antisemitism.

abschnitte.text: **Antisemitism** means prejudice, hatred and violence against Jews. Even in the Middle Ages there was Christian **anti-Judaism**, in which Jews were excluded because of their religion. During the plague they were wrongly blamed, and murders took place. Anyone who was baptised, however, counted as a Christian at that time.

From 1879 the term antisemitism spread in Germany, which is why this year is often regarded as the birth year of modern antisemitism. Now enemies of Jews saw Jews as a separate **“race”**, so that even baptism changed nothing. In 1879 the historian **Heinrich von Treitschke** coined the sentence “The Jews are our misfortune”. Later this sentence stood on every issue of the Nazi hate paper “Der Stürmer”.

The **“Protocols of the Elders of Zion”** are an antisemitic forgery that appeared in Russia at the beginning of the 20th century. They claim an alleged Jewish world conspiracy. At the **Bern trial** from 1933 to 1935 experts showed in court that the text is forged and copied. All the same it is still spread today.

On 1 April 1933 the Nazis called for a **boycott** of Jewish shops, doctors' surgeries and law firms. The law of 7 April 1933 made it possible to dismiss Jewish civil servants. In the **November pogroms** of 1938 synagogues were destroyed and Jewish people were murdered and arrested. In the Holocaust the Nazis murdered about six million Jews.

Only in 1866 did Jews in Switzerland receive the right to settle anywhere. The first **popular initiative** to be accepted, in 1893, banned Jewish ritual slaughter, a method of slaughtering animals, and was also accepted for antisemitic motives. In 1938 Switzerland agreed with Germany to mark the passports of German Jews with a **“J stamp”**. As a result Jewish refugees could be turned away more easily at the border.

Even today Jews experience abuse, hatred on the internet and sometimes violence. In Switzerland the **anti-racism law** has banned public incitement against people because of their religion or origin since 1995. Schools, memorials and organisations educate people about the history. What matters is to recognise prejudice and to stand up for respect.

begriffe.erklaerung: Older, religiously based hostility towards Jews.
Violent riots against a group of people.
The house of worship of Jews.
A false explanation according to which a secret group secretly steers the world.
Deliberately not buying from certain people or firms.

gewusst: In 1995 the Federal Council officially apologised for the introduction of the “J stamp”.
The ban on ritual slaughter of 1893 was the very first popular initiative accepted by the Swiss people.
In Germany tens of thousands of small memorial stones set in the ground, the Stolpersteine, recall individual victims.

teile.einleitung: Knighting is the solemn ceremony in which a squire becomes a knight. In the Middle Ages it was the high point of a long training. In Great Britain it still exists today as an honour.
wichtigste: In the knighting ceremony a squire was solemnly made a knight.
He was usually about 21 years old.
The squire knelt down before his lord.
The lord touched his shoulder with the flat of a sword.
The new knight promised his lord loyalty.
In Great Britain a man is called “Sir” after being knighted.

abschnitte.text: A boy from a noble family often came to a lord’s court as a child. First he served as a **page**, later as a **squire**. As a squire he helped a knight, looked after horses and weapons and learned to fight. At about **21 years old** he could be knighted. Before that he had to have proved himself through **courage and loyalty**.

At the **knighting** the squire **knelt** before his lord. In this way he showed his respect. The lord laid the **flat of his sword** on the squire’s shoulder. The new knight **swore** to serve his lord **loyally**. After that he was allowed to call himself a knight. Earlier the **sword-girding** was also common, in which the sword was solemnly buckled on the young man.

Only someone who was himself a **knight** or a high lord such as a **king** could knight another person. The ceremony often took place on a church feast day or before a battle. Sometimes there was a great feast or a tournament afterwards. For the family of the new knight it was an important day.

In **Great Britain** the king still knights deserving people to this day. In 2026 this is **King Charles III**. Today knighthood is an **honour for special achievements**, for example in art, sport or science. A man is afterwards called **“Sir”**, a woman **“Dame”**. One example is the musician **Sir Paul McCartney** of the Beatles.

gewusst: At the British knighting ceremony today the king touches the shoulders with a sword, just as in the Middle Ages.
The English word for a knighting, “accolade”, is today also used for a special award.

teile.einleitung: Samurai were warriors in ancient Japan. They served a lord and lived by strict rules of loyalty and honour.
wichtigste: Samurai were warriors in Japan.
They served a lord, the daimyo.
Above the lord stood the shogun, the supreme commander.
Their best-known sword is the curved katana.
The early samurai fought mainly with the bow from horseback.
Their code of honour is called bushido.
A samurai without a master was called a ronin.

abschnitte.text: The **samurai** were a warrior class in **Japan**. The word means roughly “the one who serves”. Every samurai served a **lord**, the **daimyo**. In return he received rice or land. Above the lord stood the **shogun**, the real ruler of the country. The emperor had little power at that time.

The early samurai fought mainly **with the bow from horseback**. Later the sword became more and more important. The best known is the **katana**, a slightly curved, very sharp sword. Samurai often carried two swords, a long one and a short one. The art of the swordsmith was highly developed in Japan.

In battle samurai wore **armour**. It consisted of many small plates of iron or leather joined with coloured cords. In this way the warrior could move well. In addition there was a helmet, often decorated with emblems or horns. Some suits of armour were real works of art.

abschnitte.titel: Bushido, the way of the warrior
abschnitte.text: For a samurai **loyalty and honour** were especially important. The rules for these are called **bushido**, “the way of the warrior”. They included courage, obedience to one’s lord and self-control. Many samurai also learned writing, poetry or the tea ceremony. A samurai who no longer had a lord was called a **ronin**.

In the 19th century Japan opened up to other countries and built a modern army. The samurai class was abolished in the 1870s. Wearing swords in public was banned. To this day, however, samurai are very well known from films, books and martial arts.

gewusst: The story of the 47 ronin who stayed loyal to their dead lord is still one of the best-known tales in Japan.
The Japanese art of archery, kyudo, is still practised today.

teile.einleitung: Zheng He was a Chinese admiral who led huge fleets across the Indian Ocean some 600 years ago. His treasure ships reached as far as Africa, decades before the Europeans sailed there.
wichtigste: Zheng He was a seafarer and admiral from China.
He served the emperors of the Ming dynasty.
Between 1405 and 1433 he led seven great voyages.
His large ships were called treasure ships.
He reached the east coast of Africa.
His fleet brought a giraffe to China.
Zheng He grew up in a Muslim family.

abschnitte.text: Zheng He was born around 1371 in the south of **China**. He came from a **Muslim** family, and his original name was **Ma He**. As a boy he came to the court of a prince. This prince later became emperor and gave him the name Zheng He. He became an **admiral** and led great fleets across the sea.

The largest ships of the fleet were called **treasure ships**. They carried precious gifts such as **silk** and **porcelain** to foreign countries. According to old reports they were **much bigger** than the ships in which Columbus later sailed to America. Exactly how big they were is disputed among experts. A fleet included many ships and thousands of people.

The **Ming dynasty** ruled China from 1368. Its emperors sent Zheng He on **seven** great voyages between **1405 and 1433**. They led across the **Indian Ocean** to South-East Asia, India and Arabia. Zheng He reached the east coast of **Africa**. That was decades before the Portuguese reached the Indian Ocean. His background helped him in dealings in Muslim port cities.

abschnitte.titel: A giraffe at the imperial court
abschnitte.text: The voyages were meant to show the emperor's power and to build trade and friendships. Many rulers sent envoys and gifts to China. Once even a **giraffe** from Africa came to China on a ship. The people at the imperial court were amazed. Some took it for a legendary animal that brought good luck.

After the death of Zheng He the great fleet voyages were stopped. The new rulers thought them too expensive. China turned more towards its own country. Later European seafarers sailed into the Indian Ocean. Today Zheng He is regarded in China as a great hero of seafaring.

gewusst: Zheng He died during or shortly after his seventh voyage, and where exactly he is buried is not known for certain.
The voyages of Zheng He began almost 90 years before Columbus sailed to America.

teile.einleitung: A pogrom is a violent persecution of a group of people, often a minority. In the Middle Ages Jews in Europe, including in present-day Switzerland, were repeatedly persecuted because of false accusations.
wichtigste: A pogrom is a violent campaign of hatred against a minority.
It was often based on prejudice and false accusations.
In 1294 the Jews in Bern were expelled after an invented murder charge.
During the plague of 1348 and 1349 Jews were falsely accused of poisoning wells.
In Basel Jews were murdered in January 1349.

abschnitte.text: The word **pogrom** comes from Russian and means roughly **“devastation”**. It refers to the violent persecution of people who belong to a **minority**. In the Middle Ages in Europe this often struck the **Jews**. It usually began with **prejudice**, envy and invented accusations. Today such acts are condemned as serious injustice.

In 1294 the Jews in **Bern** were accused of murdering a boy. This was a **false accusation**, a so-called **ritual murder legend**, which was widespread at the time. The city council used the mood to get rid of debts owed to Jewish moneylenders. The Jews were **expelled** from the city.

abschnitte.titel: The time of the plague, 1348 and 1349
abschnitte.text: When the **plague** reached Europe, many people looked for someone to blame. Jews were falsely accused of having **poisoned wells**. At **Chillon Castle** on Lake Geneva in 1348 Jews were forced by torture into **false confessions**. These forced statements were sent to other cities, where they served as supposed proof. In **Basel** in January 1349 the Jews were killed on an island in the Rhine, even before the plague had reached the city. Similar persecutions struck many towns at that time.

gewusst: Only in 1866 did Jews in Switzerland receive the right to settle freely anywhere.

teile.einleitung: Otto the Great was a king and emperor of the Middle Ages. He ruled over the East Frankish Kingdom, from which Germany later emerged, and was crowned emperor in Rome in 962.
wichtigste: Otto’s father was King **Henry I**, and Otto became king after his death in 936.
In 955 Otto defeated the Hungarians on the Lechfeld near Augsburg.
In 962 the Pope crowned him emperor in Rome.
In 951 he married Adelaide of Burgundy.
In 968 he founded the Archbishopric of Magdeburg.
In governing, he relied heavily on bishops and abbots.
Otto died in 973 and is buried in Magdeburg Cathedral.

abschnitte.text: Otto was the son of **Henry I**, who was king of the East Frankish Kingdom from 919. After his father’s death in 936, Otto was crowned king in Aachen. At first he had to assert himself against rebellious dukes and even against his own relatives. In 962 the Pope crowned him **emperor** in Rome. Because of his successes he was later called “the Great”.

The **Hungarians** were a nation of horsemen who for decades carried out raids into the East Frankish Kingdom. In 955 they besieged the city of **Augsburg**. On the **Lechfeld**, a plain on the River Lech south of Augsburg, Otto defeated their army. After that the Hungarian invasions stopped. The victory made Otto very famous.

Otto’s first wife **Edith** came from England. After her death he married **Adelaide of Burgundy** in 951, the widow of the King of Italy. In this way Otto gained influence in Italy. Adelaide later also helped to found the monastery of **Payerne** in the present-day canton of Vaud. Otto’s son **Otto II** married the Byzantine princess **Theophanu** in Rome in 972 to improve relations with the East.

In governing, Otto relied especially on **bishops and abbots**. Clergy had no heirs of their own, so they could not pass their offices on to family members. Otto gave them land and rights and so won loyal helpers. In 968 he founded the **Archbishopric of Magdeburg**, from where the lands east of the Elbe were to be converted to Christianity. Magdeburg was his favourite place.

Otto the Great died in **973**. He was buried in **Magdeburg Cathedral**, where his first wife Edith is also buried. His son Otto II followed him as emperor. The whole ruling dynasty is named after Otto: the **Ottonians**. The imperial crown that he renewed lasted for many more centuries.

gewusst: Otto deliberately had himself crowned in Aachen, the city of Charlemagne.
The monastery of Payerne in Vaud, which Adelaide helped to found, has one of the largest Romanesque churches in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages many towns were surrounded by a high wall. It protected the inhabitants from enemies. In Switzerland some town walls still survive today.
wichtigste: The town wall protected the town from enemies.
In front of some walls lay a moat, the town ditch.
Towers stood on the wall at regular intervals.
In Murten you can still walk along a long stretch of the old wall today.
The Museggmauer in Lucerne has nine towers.

abschnitte.text: A **town wall** protected the inhabitants **from enemies**. It was thick and high so that attackers could not easily get in. At the top ran a **wall walk** along which the watchmen could go. Through narrow openings defenders could look out and fight back. The wall also showed that a town was rich and important.

**Towers** stood on the wall at regular intervals. From there you could see far across the land. You could only enter the town through the **town gates**. They were **closed at night**, and anyone who wanted to come in was checked. In front of some walls lay a moat, the **town ditch**. It made it even harder to get close to the wall.

In **Murten** in the canton of Fribourg the medieval **town wall** is almost completely preserved. You can still walk along a long stretch of the covered **wall walk** today. From the top there is a beautiful view over the roofs of the old town and over Lake Murten.

In **Lucerne** stands the **Museggmauer** with **nine towers**. It is among the best-preserved town fortifications in Switzerland. Some towers can be visited in summer. In the **Zytturm** is the oldest clock in the town.

When towns grew larger, the walls were often in the way. With new weapons such as cannons they also lost their value as protection. In the 19th century many towns tore down their walls, for example **Zurich**. Often only individual gates remained standing, such as the **Spalentor** in **Basel**.

gewusst: The clock in the Zytturm in Lucerne is the only clock in the town that is allowed to strike a minute earlier than all the others.
Where town walls once stood there are often wide roads or parks today.

teile.einleitung: A **coat of arms** is a coloured badge of identity. It belongs to a family, a town, a canton or a country. Coats of arms came into being in the Middle Ages on the shields of knights.
wichtigste: A coat of arms is a coloured badge of identity.
Knights painted coats of arms on their shields so that they could be recognised.
That is why coats of arms mostly have the shape of a shield.
The Swiss coat of arms shows a white cross on red.
Bern has a bear, Uri a bull's head and Basel-Stadt a Basel crozier on its coat of arms.
The most common heraldic animal is the lion.

abschnitte.titel: How coats of arms came into being
abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages knights wore **armour** and a **helmet**. In them one knight looked like the next. So that they could be recognised in battle and at tournaments, they painted a sign on their **shield**. From this the **coats of arms** developed. Later they were passed on within the family. That is why coats of arms still mostly have the **shape of a shield** today.

Coats of arms have clear, strong colours so that they can be recognised from far away. Red, blue, black and green are common, together with gold and silver, which are often painted as yellow and white. On the shield there are figures such as animals, crosses or stars. The most common **heraldic animal** is the **lion**. It stands for courage and strength. The study of coats of arms is called **heraldry**.

The **Swiss coat of arms** shows a **white cross on a red ground**. The same sign can be seen on the Swiss flag. It goes back to the coat of arms of the canton of **Schwyz**, which is also red. Today the Swiss cross is found on passports, coins and many products. It is one of the best-known signs in the world.

abschnitte.titel: Coats of arms of the cantons
abschnitte.text: Every canton has a coat of arms of its own. In the **Bernese coat of arms** a **black bear** walks over a yellow stripe. The bear is the heraldic animal of the town and canton of Bern. The coat of arms of **Uri** shows a **black bull's head** on a yellow ground, the bull of Uri. The coat of arms of **Basel-Stadt** shows a **black Basel crozier** on white. The crozier recalls the bishop of Basel, who formerly ruled over the town.

Not only cantons but almost all **municipalities** in Switzerland have a coat of arms of their own. You see them on municipal buildings, on flags or on letters from the municipality. Many families also have a **family coat of arms**. In Switzerland, colourful **heraldic panes** used to be popular. These are windows of painted glass with a coat of arms.

gewusst: In heraldry right and left are described from the point of view of the shield bearer, that is, exactly the other way round from how you see the picture.
The coat of arms of Zurich is divided diagonally, white above and blue below.

teile.einleitung: Reconquista means “reconquest” in Spanish. This is the name for the centuries during which Christian kingdoms on the Iberian Peninsula conquered the territories under Muslim rule. It ended in 1492 with the fall of Granada.
wichtigste: From 711 a large part of the Iberian Peninsula came under Muslim rule.
The Battle of Covadonga around 722 is traditionally seen as the beginning of the Reconquista.
In 1085 Alfonso VI of Castile conquered Toledo.
El Cid conquered Valencia in 1094.
In 1212 the Christian kingdoms won at Las Navas de Tolosa.
In 1492 Granada, the last Muslim state, fell to the Catholic Monarchs.

abschnitte.text: From **711** Muslim armies conquered a large part of the **Iberian Peninsula**, that is, present-day Spain and Portugal. The Muslim territory was called **al-Andalus**. Only in the north did small Christian kingdoms remain. In **Asturias** around **722** the nobleman **Pelayo** won the **Battle of Covadonga**. In Spanish tradition this is seen as the start of the reconquest.

In **1085** King **Alfonso VI of Castile** conquered the city of **Toledo**, the old capital of the Visigoths. Later Toledo became famous for translators who rendered Arabic writings into Latin. The Castilian knight **Rodrigo Díaz de Vivar** conquered **Valencia in 1094**. He was called **“El Cid”**, from the Arabic word for “lord”. His deeds are sung in the epic poem “Cantar de mio Cid”.

In **1212 Castile, Aragon and Navarre** fought together against the **Almohads**, a Muslim ruling dynasty from North Africa. At **Las Navas de Tolosa** they won a decisive victory. After that the Christian kingdoms quickly conquered great cities such as **Córdoba** and **Seville**. In the south only the kingdom of **Granada** remained.

In **Granada** the **Nasrids** ruled. They built the magnificent palace complex of the **Alhambra**, today a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**. **Isabella I of Castile** and **Ferdinand II of Aragon** had married in 1469 and so united their kingdoms. In **1492** they conquered Granada, and with this the Reconquista ended. In 1496 Pope Alexander VI gave them the honorary title **“Catholic Monarchs”**.

gewusst: From Covadonga to Granada the Reconquista lasted almost 800 years.
In the same year, 1492, in which Granada fell, Columbus sailed west on behalf of the Catholic Monarchs.

teile.einleitung: The palas is the residential building of a medieval castle. The family of the lord of the castle lived here, and feasts were held in the great hall.
wichtigste: The palas was the home of the castle’s lord and family.
The word is related to “palace” and comes from the Latin “palatium”.
The great hall was usually on the upper floor.
Today this hall is often called the knights’ hall.
It was heated with an open fireplace.
Tapestries kept out the cold of the stone walls.

abschnitte.text: A castle consisted of several buildings: walls, towers, stables and the **palas**. In the palas lived the **family of the lord of the castle**. Servants and animals lived in other buildings. The palas was built for living in and was therefore the most comfortable. It had larger rooms and more windows than the towers. The word comes from the Latin **“palatium”** and is related to **palace**.

In the palas there was a **great hall**, which today is often called the **knights’ hall**. It was usually on the **upper floor**, and sometimes a separate staircase led up to it from outside. In the hall the lord and his guests ate and celebrated. Here there were **feasts and banquets**, music and storytelling. Tournaments, however, took place outside.

The thick **stone walls** often made castles cold and damp. That is why a large fire burned in the hall, in an **open fireplace**. Even so, it was cool in winter in many places. **Tapestries** were hung on the walls. They kept out the cold and were at the same time a beautiful decoration. Windows were small and often closed only with wooden shutters.

gewusst: In Switzerland you can visit an old knights’ hall in several castles, for example in Lenzburg Castle in Aargau.
Glass for windows was very expensive in the Middle Ages, so only rich castles had glazed windows.

teile.einleitung: Romanesque is a building style of the Middle Ages. Thick walls, small windows and round arches are typical. Many churches and monasteries in Europe, including in Switzerland, were built in this way.
wichtigste: Romanesque architecture was widespread in Central Europe from about 1000 to 1250.
The round arch over windows and doors is typical.
Romanesque churches look massive, with thick walls and small windows.
The name recalls the building art of the ancient Romans.
Beneath the choir there is often an underground room, the crypt.
Speyer Cathedral is regarded as the largest surviving Romanesque church in the world.
The church of St Martin in Zillis is famous for its painted wooden ceiling.

abschnitte.text: The name **Romanesque** was only invented by scholars in the 19th century. It means roughly “in the manner of the Romans”. For the builders of the Middle Ages took over forms from Roman architecture, for example the **round arch** and thick columns. After the Romanesque came the **Gothic** with pointed arches and large windows.

Romanesque churches look like **fortresses of God**. Their walls are very thick, because they had to carry the heavy roof and the stone **vaults**. Large windows would have weakened the walls, so they are small. Inside it is therefore often rather dark. Many churches have mighty towers.

Beneath the **choir**, the area with the altar, many Romanesque churches have an underground room. It is called a **crypt**. There saints or important people were buried, or relics were kept. The crypt often has low columns and small vaults.

**Speyer Cathedral** in Germany is regarded as the largest surviving Romanesque church in the world. It was built in the 11th century. In its crypt several emperors and kings lie buried. Since 1981 the cathedral has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

There are also beautiful Romanesque buildings in Switzerland. Especially famous is the church of **St Martin in Zillis** in the canton of the Grisons. Its painted **wooden ceiling** from the 12th century consists of 153 panels that show stories from the Bible and fabulous creatures. The All Saints’ Minster in **Schaffhausen** and the abbey church of **Payerne** are also Romanesque.

gewusst: The wooden ceiling of Zillis is among the oldest surviving painted church ceilings anywhere.
Romanesque churches were originally often painted in bright colours inside, even if the walls are mostly grey or white today.

teile.einleitung: The Ottonians were a ruling dynasty that provided the kings and emperors of the East Frankish Kingdom in the 10th and early 11th centuries. They are named after Otto I, the Great.
wichtigste: Otto I was crowned king in Aachen in 936.
In 962 Pope John XII crowned him emperor in Rome.
In the Privilegium Ottonianum Otto I confirmed the Papal States.
With the “Renovatio imperii Romanorum” Otto III wanted to renew the Roman Empire.
The monastery of Reichenau on Lake Constance was a centre of book painting.
With Henry II the Ottonians died out in the male line in 1024.

abschnitte.text: It began with **Henry I**, who was king from 919. He was buried in 936 in the convent of **Quedlinburg**, which his widow Matilda made into an important place of remembrance. He was followed by **Otto I**, **Otto II** and **Otto III**. The last ruler was **Henry II**, who died in 1024. He was followed by a king from the House of **Salian**.

Otto I had himself crowned **in Aachen in 936**, the palace city of Charlemagne. In this way he linked up with the tradition of the Carolingians. On 2 February **962** Pope John XII crowned him **emperor** in Rome. In the same year Otto confirmed the Papal States in the **Privilegium Ottonianum**. A newly elected pope was to swear an oath of loyalty to the emperor before his consecration.

**Otto III** was born in 980 and became king as a child. He followed the programme of the **“Renovatio imperii Romanorum”**, the renewal of the Roman Empire. That is why he wanted to make **Rome** the centre, and he lived there for a time. In January 1002 he died north of Rome, aged only about **21**.

Under the Ottonians magnificent churches and manuscripts were created. The monastery of **Reichenau** on an island in **Lake Constance** was a centre of **Ottonian book painting**. There precious books with gold and glowing colours were made for the rulers. Several of these manuscripts are now part of the **Memory of the World**. The collegiate church of Quedlinburg is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

gewusst: Reichenau lies very close to the Swiss border, opposite Thurgau.
Henry II and his wife Kunigunde were later declared saints by the Church.

teile.einleitung: The Saxon Wars were long wars waged by Charlemagne against the Saxons. In the end the Saxons belonged to the Frankish Empire and became Christians.
wichtigste: The Saxon Wars lasted more than 30 years, from 772 to 804.
The Saxons lived in the north-west of present-day Germany.
In 772 Charlemagne destroyed the Saxon sanctuary Irminsul.
The most important leader of the Saxons was called Widukind.
In 782 Charlemagne had many captured Saxons executed, which is called the Massacre of Verden.
A strict law threatened with death every Saxon who refused baptism.

abschnitte.text: The **Saxons** were a Germanic people. They lived in the **north-west of present-day Germany**, roughly in present-day Lower Saxony and Westphalia. They had no king but several leaders. Unlike the Franks they were not yet Christians and worshipped their own gods. Again and again there were quarrels and raids on the border with the Frankish Empire.

In the year **772** **Charlemagne** marched against the Saxons. Right at the start he destroyed the **Irminsul**, an important sanctuary of the Saxons. What the Irminsul looked like exactly is not known; perhaps it was a large tree trunk or a pillar. This began a war that was to last **more than 30 years**, until about 804.

The best-known leader of the Saxons was **Widukind**. He led several uprisings against the Franks. In **785** he gave up and was baptised. Charlemagne became his godfather. Even so, other Saxons went on fighting for many more years.

The war was fought very harshly. In **782** Charlemagne had many captured Saxons executed at Verden on the Aller. This event is called the **Massacre of Verden**. In addition Charlemagne issued a strict law, the **Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae**. It threatened Saxons who refused **baptism** with the death penalty. Later the laws became somewhat milder.

In the end Saxony belonged to the **Frankish Empire**. Bishoprics were founded, for example in **Paderborn**, Münster and Bremen. In this way the Saxons gradually became Christians. Today historians judge the violence of these wars critically, but they also see in them a step towards the later German empire.

gewusst: Only a good hundred years later, with Henry I, a Saxon became king of the East Frankish Kingdom.
The name “Saxons” is often derived from the seax, a short sword of the Germanic peoples.

teile.einleitung: In the assassination at Sarajevo on 28 June 1914 the Austrian heir to the throne Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie were shot dead. The assassin was the young Bosnian Serb Gavrilo Princip. The assassination set off a crisis at the end of which the First World War began.
wichtigste: On 28 June 1914 the heir to the throne Franz Ferdinand was murdered in Sarajevo.
His wife Sophie Chotek died with him.
The assassin Gavrilo Princip belonged to the group Mlada Bosna (Young Bosnia).
The assassins were supported by the Serbian secret society “Black Hand” under Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, called “Apis”.
Before the fatal shots another assassin had thrown a bomb at the convoy of cars.
Because the driver took a wrong turn and stopped next to Princip while turning, he was able to shoot.
A month later, on 28 July 1914, Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia.

abschnitte.text: **Franz Ferdinand** was the nephew of Emperor Franz Joseph I and was to become the next emperor of **Austria-Hungary**. His wife **Sophie Chotek** came from a Bohemian noble family that was regarded at court as not of equal rank. In June 1914 Franz Ferdinand visited army manoeuvres in Bosnia. On 28 June the couple drove through Sarajevo in an open car.

Bosnia and Herzegovina had been annexed by Austria-Hungary in 1908, that is, taken into its own empire. But many Serbs wanted Bosnia to belong to a common state of the South Slavs with **Serbia**. That is why Austria-Hungary was hated by them. In addition, 28 June was the anniversary of the **Battle of Kosovo** of 1389, an important day of remembrance for the Serbs. Many therefore felt the visit on this day to be a provocation.

Several young men of the group **Mlada Bosna** waited along the route beside the River Miljacka. They were supported by the Serbian secret society **Black Hand**, whose leading figure was Colonel Dragutin Dimitrijević, called “Apis”. The assassin Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a **bomb** at the convoy of cars. It bounced off the heir's car and injured people in the car behind. Franz Ferdinand was unhurt and drove on to the town hall.

After the reception at the town hall Franz Ferdinand wanted to visit the injured in hospital. The driver knew nothing of the changed route and took a wrong turn at the **Latin Bridge**. As he tried to turn, the car stopped right next to **Gavrilo Princip**. The 19-year-old fired twice with a pistol and fatally hit Franz Ferdinand and Sophie.

Princip was arrested at once and put on trial in October 1914. Because he was still a **minor** at the time of the deed, he could not be sentenced to death under the law of the time. He received 20 years of hard imprisonment. Princip died in 1918 in the prison of **Theresienstadt** of tuberculosis.

Austria-Hungary held Serbia responsible for the assassination. In the so-called **July Crisis** it set Serbia a harsh ultimatum. On 28 July 1914 Austria-Hungary declared war on Serbia. Because the great powers were linked by **alliances**, Russia, Germany, France and Britain soon joined in. In this way the assassination became the trigger of the **First World War**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A murderous attack on an important person, often for political reasons.
The person who is to become king or emperor after the present ruler.
When a state simply declares a foreign territory to be its own.
A final demand with a deadline, after which consequences such as war are threatened.
The weeks after the assassination in the summer of 1914 in which the dispute turned into war.

gewusst: The car in which Franz Ferdinand was shot stands today in the Museum of Military History in Vienna.
Franz Ferdinand and Sophie were not buried in the Imperial Crypt in Vienna, but at Artstetten Castle in Lower Austria.
Exactly one month lay between the assassination and the declaration of war on Serbia.

teile.einleitung: The **Knights Templar** were a religious order of knights from the time of the Crusades. Its members were knights and monks at the same time. The order became rich and powerful until it was dissolved in the 14th century.
wichtigste: The Order of the Templars was founded in Jerusalem around 1120.
The founder and first master was Hugues de Payens.
The name comes from the Temple of Solomon.
The Templar knights wore a white mantle with a red cross.
King Philip IV of France had the Templars arrested in 1307.
Pope Clement V dissolved the order in 1312.

abschnitte.text: Around **1120** the French knight **Hugues de Payens** and a few companions joined together in **Jerusalem**. They wanted to protect the **pilgrims** who travelled to the Holy Land. Hugues de Payens is regarded as the founder and first master of the order. The knights were given quarters on the **Temple Mount**. There people believed the old **Temple of Solomon** had stood, and that is where the name Templars comes from.

At the **Council of Troyes** in **1129** the order was officially recognised and given a rule of its own. The Templars lived like monks but also fought as knights. The Cistercian abbot **Bernard of Clairvaux** promoted the order with his writing “In Praise of the New Knighthood”. In this way the Templars became known all over Europe. Their badge was the **white mantle with the red cross**.

Many people gave the order land and money. Before long the Templars owned castles, farms and houses in many countries of Europe. They also kept money safe for others and lent money out. For this reason they are regarded as early **bankers**. Even kings borrowed money from them. This made the order powerful, but also envied.

The French king **Philip IV the Fair** was in debt to the order and wanted its wealth. On **Friday 13 October 1307** he had the Templars in France arrested. They were accused of false things, and confessions were forced out of them. Under pressure from the king, Pope **Clement V** dissolved the order in **1312** at the **Council of Vienne**. Most of its property went to the **Hospitallers**, another order of knights.

The last grand master was called **Jacques de Molay**. He withdrew his forced confessions and said the order was innocent. For this he was executed in **1314** in Paris, on an island in the Seine. Many legends and secrets have grown up around the Templars to this day. Most of them, however, are invented.

gewusst: Many people see Friday the 13th as an unlucky day, but it has not been proved that this is connected with the arrest of the Templars.
Bernard of Clairvaux described the Templars as knights who are at the same time monks.

teile.einleitung: In the past the night watchman walked through the streets of the town at night. He called out the hours and made sure that no fire broke out.
wichtigste: The night watchman made his rounds at night.
He called out the time every hour.
Above all he warned of fire.
A lantern helped him in the dark.
With a horn he could raise the alarm.
In Lausanne a watchman still calls out the hours every night.

abschnitte.text: When everyone was asleep, the **night watchman** walked through the streets. He made sure that everything stayed quiet. Most people had no clock. That is why the night watchman called out the **time** every hour. A well-known song begins with the words “Hear, gentlemen, and let me tell you” (in German, “Hört, ihr Herrn, und lasst euch sagen”).

Houses were often made of wood and stood close together. A **fire** was especially dangerous at night. A fire could quickly destroy a whole street. If the night watchman saw smoke or flames, he woke everyone at once. With a **horn** he blew a loud alarm.

There were no street lamps at that time. That is why the night watchman carried a **lantern**. A candle or an oil light burned inside it. He often also had a **halberd** with him. This is a long staff with a point and an axe blade. With it he could defend himself.

In **Lausanne** this old profession still exists today. Every night a watchman calls out the hours from the tower of the **cathedral**. In French he is called “le guet”. He calls from **10 pm to 2 am**. This tradition is one of the oldest of its kind in Europe.

gewusst: After every stroke of the hour the watchman of Lausanne calls “C’est le guet, il a sonné l’heure”, which means “This is the watchman, the hour has struck”.
In some towns today you can join a night watchman tour.

teile.einleitung: In Japan a shogunate was a rule by military leaders, the shoguns. For many centuries they governed the country while the emperor had hardly any real power.
wichtigste: The shogun was the supreme military ruler of Japan.
Minamoto no Yoritomo became the first shogun of the Kamakura shogunate in 1192.
In the time of the shoguns the emperor had hardly any real power.
In 1274 and 1281 Japan repelled attacks by the Mongols.
The storms that destroyed the enemy fleets at that time were called kamikaze.
In 1600 Tokugawa Ieyasu won the Battle of Sekigahara.
From 1603 the Tokugawa shogunate had its seat in Edo.

abschnitte.text: The title **shogun** means roughly “supreme commander”. Officially the **emperor** appointed the shogun. In reality, however, the shogun held the power. He commanded the **samurai** and decided on laws and taxes. The emperor lived in Kyoto and performed mainly religious and ceremonial duties.

In **1192** **Minamoto no Yoritomo** became the first shogun with firm rule. He governed from the city of **Kamakura**, which is why this period is called the Kamakura shogunate. In this time the **Mongols** attacked Japan twice, in **1274** and **1281**. Both times the enemy fleets were badly hit by violent storms. The Japanese called these storms **kamikaze**, “divine wind”.

Later the Ashikaga shogunate ruled. Its power, however, grew weaker and weaker. In the 15th and 16th centuries many princes fought against each other. Only in **1600** did **Tokugawa Ieyasu** win the great battle of **Sekigahara**. This cleared the way to power over the whole of Japan.

In 1603 Tokugawa Ieyasu became shogun. His family ruled from **Edo**, today’s **Tokyo**. For more than 250 years there was now peace in the country. During this time Japan closed itself off strongly from other countries. In 1867 and 1868 the time of the shoguns ended, and the emperor took over the government again.

gewusst: Edo, the seat of the Tokugawa shoguns, was already one of the largest cities in the world in the 18th century.
The name Tokyo means “eastern capital”.

teile.einleitung: The **wall walk** is a passage along the top of a castle wall or town wall. From here watchmen kept a lookout and defended the wall. In some Swiss towns you can still walk along an old wall walk today.
wichtigste: The wall walk is the passage along the top of the wall.
It lay behind the battlements.
Watchmen kept a lookout from the wall walk.
Many wall walks had a roof for protection.
The curtain wall runs all the way around the castle.
Through a machicolation people dropped stones on attackers.

abschnitte.text: Around a castle there was often a **curtain wall**. On top of it lay the **wall walk**. On it the defenders could run along the wall. On the outside the **battlements** protected them. These are the teeth of the wall behind which one could hide. Between the battlements there were gaps through which one could look out and shoot.

On the wall walk **watchmen** paced to and fro. They kept a lookout to see whether enemies were approaching. In an attack soldiers defended the castle from there. Many wall walks were covered with a **wooden roof**. The roof protected against rain and snow, but also against arrows falling from above.

On some walls there was a small projection that stuck out from the wall. It is called a **machicolation**. In its floor it had a hole. Through this opening people dropped **stones** on attackers who stood right at the foot of the wall or at the gate. That is why machicolations were often built over gates.

Not only castles but also towns had walls with wall walks. In **Murten** in the canton of Fribourg the old **curtain wall** is well preserved. Its wall walk is covered, and you can walk along it around part of the old town. In **Lucerne**, too, a long stretch of the old town fortifications with several towers still stands in the **Museggmauer**.

gewusst: From the wall walk in Murten you can see over the roofs of the old town to Lake Murten.
The German word Wehrgang comes from “sich wehren”, which means to defend oneself.

teile.einleitung: The Agricultural Revolution is the name for the great changes in English farming in the 18th century. New methods of cultivation, tools and ideas about breeding greatly raised yields. This also helped industrialisation.
wichtigste: The Norfolk rotation replaced the three-field system with fallow.
Clover takes nitrogen from the air and so fertilises the soil.
Charles Townshend got the nickname “Turnip” because of fodder turnips.
Jethro Tull is credited with a horse-drawn seed drill around 1701.
With enclosures, common land became fenced private land.
Robert Bakewell became known for the deliberate breeding of sheep and cattle.
Farm workers who were no longer needed moved to the towns as labourers.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages the **three-field system** was often used. One field lay **fallow** each year so that the soil could recover. In England in the 18th century the **Norfolk rotation** took hold. In it **wheat, turnips, barley and clover** alternated over four fields. So no field lay fallow any more, and more was harvested.

**Clover** improved the soil. On its roots live **nodule bacteria** that take **nitrogen** from the air. This fertilises the soil for the next plant. At the same time clover and **turnips** served as **fodder** for cattle, even in winter. The politician **Charles Townshend** promoted growing turnips so keenly that he was nicknamed **“Turnip”**.

Around 1701 **Jethro Tull** is said to have invented a **horse-drawn seed drill**. It placed the seed in even rows and at even depths. As a result less seed was lost, and yields rose. **Robert Bakewell** became known for the **deliberate breeding** of sheep and cattle. He chose animals with desired qualities, and his **Leicester sheep** put on meat quickly.

Formerly the villagers used some pastures and fields **in common**. In the 18th century these areas were often turned by acts of Parliament into **fenced private land**. This is called **enclosure**. The large estates could in this way farm more modernly. But many **smallholders** lost their grazing rights and their livelihood.

Higher yields fed **more people**. At the same time **fewer workers** were needed in the countryside. Many farm workers therefore moved to the **towns** and looked for work in the new **factories**. In this way the Agricultural Revolution promoted **industrialisation**. In Switzerland, too, people looked for better methods: in Bern citizens founded the **Economic Society** in 1759, which spread new ideas for agriculture.

gewusst: The potato, which comes from South America, also helped against hunger in Europe in the 18th century.
The term “Agricultural Revolution” is disputed among experts, because much changed not suddenly but over a long time.

teile.einleitung: The **Umayyads** were the first ruling family to make the office of caliph hereditary. From 661 to 750 they ruled a huge Islamic empire from Damascus. A branch of the family afterwards ruled in Spain for a long time.
wichtigste: Muawiya I founded the Umayyad dynasty in 661.
The capital of the empire was Damascus in present-day Syria.
The Dome of the Rock in Jerusalem was completed around 691 under Abd al-Malik.
The empire stretched from Spain to the Indus.
The Umayyads had their own gold coins minted, the dinar.
Abd ar-Rahman I founded the Emirate of Córdoba in Spain in 756.

abschnitte.text: A **caliph** is a successor of the Prophet Muhammad as head of the Muslims. **Muawiya I** had previously been governor in Syria. In **661** he became caliph and made the office **hereditary** in his family. His capital was **Damascus**. The dispute over the correct succession to Muhammad shaped this period. The **Shiites** regard Ali as the rightful successor, and the name comes from “Shiat Ali”, the party of Ali. Most other Muslims are called **Sunnis**.

Under the Umayyads the empire grew greatly. Around **711** armies under **Muhammad ibn Qasim** conquered the region of **Sindh** in present-day Pakistan and reached the river **Indus**. In the same year troops crossed over to **Spain**. So around 750 the empire stretched from Spain in the west to the Indus in the east. In **717 and 718** the Umayyads besieged **Constantinople**, but Emperor Leo III defended the city successfully, also with **Greek fire**.

Under the caliph **Abd al-Malik** the **Dome of the Rock** in **Jerusalem** was completed around **691**. It is regarded as the oldest surviving major building of Islam, and its golden dome shapes the city. Abd al-Malik also had Islamic **coins** minted without pictures. The gold coin was called the **dinar**. Arabic became the language of administration throughout the empire.

abschnitte.titel: Fall and a new start in Spain
abschnitte.text: In **750** the Umayyads were overthrown in the east by the **Abbasids**. A prince of the family, **Abd ar-Rahman I**, was able to escape. He came to Spain and founded the **Emirate of Córdoba** there in **756**. Later it became a caliphate of its own. The Umayyads in Spain made Córdoba one of the most magnificent cities in Europe.
