gewusst: The Great Mosque of Córdoba was begun under Abd ar-Rahman I.
The word dinar lives on to this day as the name of currencies in several countries.

teile.einleitung: Abraham Lincoln was the 16th President of the USA. He led the country through the Civil War and worked for the end of slavery. He is regarded as one of the most important presidents in American history.
wichtigste: Lincoln was elected in 1860 and took office in 1861.
He was the first president of the Republican Party.
On 1 January 1863 he issued the Emancipation Proclamation.
In 1863 he gave a famous short speech at Gettysburg.
He came from Illinois, but was born in Kentucky.
His nickname was “Honest Abe”.
In April 1865 he was shot in a theatre by John Wilkes Booth.

abschnitte.text: Abraham Lincoln was born in 1809 in **Kentucky**. He came from **simple circumstances** and grew up in a log cabin. He went to school very little and taught himself a great deal. Later he lived and worked for a long time as a **lawyer** in **Illinois**. That is why Illinois still calls itself the “Land of Lincoln”. Because he was regarded as especially honest, he was called **“Honest Abe”**.

Lincoln was a member of the **Republican Party**. It was against the spread of **slavery** into new territories. In 1860 he was elected **16th President** of the USA and took office in 1861. He was the first president of his party. Soon after his election several Southern states left the Union.

In 1861 the **American Civil War** between the Northern and Southern states began. Lincoln wanted to keep the country united. On **1 January 1863** he issued the **Emancipation Proclamation**. With it he declared the slaves in the rebel Southern states to be free. Slavery was only abolished completely in **1865**, by an amendment to the Constitution.

In November 1863 Lincoln dedicated a soldiers' cemetery at **Gettysburg**. His speech, the **Gettysburg Address**, lasted only about **two minutes**. He spoke of a government **“of the people, by the people, for the people”**. These words are among the most famous sentences about democracy. Many schoolchildren in the USA learn the speech by heart.

In April 1865 the war ended with the victory of the North. A few days later Lincoln visited **Ford's Theatre** in Washington. There **John Wilkes Booth**, an actor and supporter of the South, shot at him. Lincoln died the next morning. Booth was tracked down and killed a few days after the deed.

gewusst: At about 1.93 metres Lincoln was one of the tallest presidents of the USA.
His face is carved into Mount Rushmore and appears on the five-dollar note.

teile.einleitung: Apartheid was a system of racial segregation in South Africa from 1948 until the early 1990s. The white minority ruled and took almost all rights from the black majority. Only with the first free elections in 1994 and Nelson Mandela as president did this period end.
wichtigste: Apartheid is a word from Afrikaans and means separateness.
The National Party under Daniel François Malan began the policy of apartheid in 1948.
Laws assigned every person to a “race” and separated residential areas, schools and marriages.
Pass laws controlled where black people were allowed to be and to work.
At Sharpeville in 1960 the police shot 69 demonstrators.
In the Soweto uprising of 1976 schoolchildren protested against Afrikaans as the language of teaching.
Nelson Mandela was freed in 1990 after 27 years in prison.
In 1994 the first free elections took place, and Mandela became president.

abschnitte.text: The word **apartheid** comes from Afrikaans and literally means separateness. Afrikaans is a language that developed out of Dutch. After its election victory in 1948 the **National Party** under Daniel François Malan began to put racial segregation into laws. Only white people were allowed to vote, although they were a small minority.

The first law of 1949 banned marriages between people of different “races”. The **Population Registration Act** of 1950 officially assigned every person to a “race”. The **Group Areas Act** of 1950 laid down separate residential areas. The Bantu Education Act of 1953 provided a state-controlled, poorer education for black people.

Black people had to carry a **pass** that stated where they were allowed to be and to work. With the **homeland policy** black people were to be pushed out into areas called Bantustans. The aim was to take away their South African citizenship. Hendrik Verwoerd, who was stabbed to death in Parliament in 1966, is regarded as the “architect of apartheid”.

On 21 March 1960 the police shot 69 people at **Sharpeville** during a protest against the pass laws. On 16 June 1976 schoolchildren in **Soweto** protested against Afrikaans as the language of teaching, and many were killed. Steve Biko of the Black Consciousness Movement died in 1977 after mistreatment in police custody. **Nelson Mandela** of the African National Congress spent 27 years in prison, for a long time on the prison island of Robben Island.

Because of protests in the country and sanctions from abroad the government came under pressure. President **Frederik Willem de Klerk** freed Mandela in February 1990 and abolished the apartheid laws. In 1993 Mandela and de Klerk jointly received the Nobel Peace Prize. In the first free elections in April 1994 everyone was allowed to vote, and Mandela became president.

For a long time Switzerland did not take part in the economic sanctions against South Africa. Swiss banks and firms continued to do business with the apartheid state. Later the Federal Council had these relations examined by experts in a **research programme**. At the same time many people in Switzerland also protested against apartheid.

begriffe.erklaerung: When people are separated and treated unequally because of their skin colour.
A language in South Africa that developed out of Dutch.
Punitive measures by states, for example a ban on trade.
An area to which black people were to be pushed out under apartheid.
Unfair disadvantage of people because of a characteristic.

gewusst: Mandela's birthday, 18 July, is recognised today by the UN as Nelson Mandela International Day.
16 June is a public holiday in South Africa today, Youth Day, in memory of the Soweto uprising.
The prison island of Robben Island is a museum today and part of the UNESCO World Heritage.

teile.einleitung: In the Middle Ages a Pfalz, or imperial palace, was a large residence for the king. Because the king was constantly travelling through his realm, there were many such palaces in different places.
wichtigste: A royal palace was a residence for the travelling king.
The king had no fixed capital and governed on the move.
Every palace had a chapel or church.
In the royal hall the king received guests and held assemblies.
The farmers of the surrounding area had to supply food for the court.
In Zurich a palace stood on the Lindenhof.
The word Pfalz comes from the Latin “palatium”.

abschnitte.text: In the Middle Ages the king had **no fixed capital**. He travelled through the realm with his **court**, that is, many advisers, servants and warriors. In this way he could dispense justice everywhere and show who ruled. On the way he lived in **palaces** (in German, *Pfalzen*). This way of ruling is called **itinerant kingship**.

A palace had a large **royal hall**. There the king held feasts and assemblies and received important guests. Almost always there was a **chapel** or church for prayer. In addition there were living quarters, stables, storehouses and often a wall. The farms of the surrounding area had to supply **bread, meat and other food** when the king came.

In **Zurich** in the Middle Ages a royal palace stood on the hill called the **Lindenhof**. Kings lived here when they came to Zurich. Today the Lindenhof is a square with trees and a view of the old town. In **Goslar** in Germany stands a famous **imperial palace** with a large imperial house from the 11th century. It is a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

The word **Pfalz** comes from the Latin **“palatium”**. This was the name of a hill in Rome on which the Roman emperors lived. The word **palace** came from the same word. The German region called the Palatinate (Pfalz) also bears this name. The word **palas** for the residential building of a castle is also related to it.

gewusst: Charlemagne had a particularly important palace in Aachen, where his cathedral still stands today.
A fort already stood on the Lindenhof in Zurich in Roman times.

teile.einleitung: The **Tang dynasty** ruled China from 618 to 907. This period is regarded as a golden age of Chinese culture, above all of poetry. The capital, Chang'an, was one of the largest cities in the world at the time.
wichtigste: The Tang dynasty ruled China from 618 to 907.
The capital Chang'an is present-day Xi'an.
Wu Zetian is the only woman to have ruled China as empress in her own right.
The An Lushan Rebellion from 755 to 763 greatly weakened the empire.
The Diamond Sutra of 868 is regarded as the oldest dated printed book.
Li Bai and Du Fu are the best-known poets of the Tang period.

abschnitte.text: The capital of the Tang was called **Chang'an**, today it is called **Xi'an**. It was the starting point of the **Silk Road**, a long trade route to the west. In the 8th century probably about a million people lived there. Merchants, scholars and monks from many countries came to the city. Chang'an was carefully planned, with straight streets and separate districts.

Emperor **Taizong**, whose birth name was Li Shimin, ruled from **626 to 649**. He came to the throne after a struggle for power against his brothers and is regarded as one of the ablest rulers of China. Later **Wu Zetian** came to power. In the year **690** she proclaimed a Zhou dynasty of her own and ruled until 705. She is the only woman who officially ruled China as empress in her own right.

The Tang period is regarded as the **golden age of Chinese poetry**. The two best-known poets are **Li Bai** and **Du Fu**. They lived in the 8th century, and children in China still learn their poems today. In this period **woodblock printing** also developed. The **Diamond Sutra** of the year **868** is regarded as the oldest surviving printed book with a date. It was found in the caves of **Dunhuang**.

In **751** a Tang army lost to an army of the **Abbasids** at the river **Talas** in Central Asia. After that Chinese influence there was limited. From **755 to 763** the **An Lushan Rebellion** shook the empire. The general An Lushan temporarily captured both capitals, and the war cost a great many lives. Afterwards regional military governors grew ever more powerful, and the imperial court lost strength.

**Buddhism** was widespread in the Tang period, and there were many rich monasteries. Around **845** Emperor **Wuzong** had Buddhism persecuted. Thousands of monasteries were dissolved, and monks and nuns had to give up monastery life. There were economic reasons behind this too, because the monasteries owned a lot of land. In the year **907** the Tang dynasty ended.

gewusst: Chang'an was probably one of the largest cities in the world in the 8th century.
The Diamond Sutra of 868 is about 600 years older than the books that Gutenberg printed in Europe.

teile.einleitung: The attack on Pearl Harbor was a surprise attack by Japan on the American naval base in Hawaii. It took place on 7 December 1941 and cost about 2,400 Americans their lives. Afterwards the USA entered the Second World War.
wichtigste: Japan attacked Pearl Harbor in Hawaii on 7 December 1941.
The plan came from Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto.
A complete oil embargo by the USA in the summer of 1941 had sharpened the conflict.
About 2,400 Americans lost their lives.
The US aircraft carriers were not in the harbour and were spared.
The battleship USS Arizona exploded and is a memorial today.
On 11 December 1941 Germany and Italy declared war on the USA.

abschnitte.text: **Pearl Harbor** is a natural harbour on the island of Oʻahu, which belongs to Hawaii. There the American **Pacific Fleet** lay with many battleships. Hawaii lies in the middle of the Pacific, about 6,000 kilometres from Japan. For the USA the base was very important.

In the 1930s Japan conquered large parts of China and wanted to dominate South-East Asia. The USA responded in the summer of 1941 with a complete **oil embargo**. But Japan needed oil for its ships and aircraft. The Japanese leadership therefore decided to knock out the American fleet in one blow.

The plan was developed by Admiral **Isoroku Yamamoto**. On the morning of 7 December 1941, a Sunday, hundreds of Japanese aircraft attacked from aircraft carriers. They bombed ships and airfields in two waves. The battleship **USS Arizona** was destroyed when its ammunition magazines exploded, and over 1,000 sailors died.

For Japan the attack was not a complete military success. The American **aircraft carriers** were not in the harbour and stayed undamaged. Fuel stores and shipyards were also hardly hit. As early as June 1942 the USA defeated Japan in the naval Battle of Midway.

President **Franklin D. Roosevelt** called 7 December “a date which will live in infamy” in his speech to Congress, a day of shame. On 8 December the USA declared war on Japan. On 11 December 1941 Germany and Italy declared war on the USA. With that the Second World War finally became a **world war**.

Over the wreck of the USS Arizona stands a white **memorial** today. Every year millions of people visit the place. Oil still seeps from the wreck in small drops to this day. 7 December is a national day of remembrance in the USA.

begriffe.erklaerung: A harbour in which warships are stationed.
A ban on delivering certain goods to a country.
A large warship from which aircraft can take off and land.
The official announcement that a state is at war with another.

gewusst: The oil that seeps from the USS Arizona is called “black tears” by some visitors.
Some survivors had themselves buried with their comrades in the wreck of the USS Arizona after their death.
The attackers came unnoticed because the Japanese fleet sailed on a remote route through the North Pacific.

teile.einleitung: The **Fourth Crusade** was really meant to lead to the Holy Land. But the crusaders never reached their goal. Instead, in 1204 they conquered and plundered the Christian city of Constantinople.
wichtigste: Pope Innocent III called for the Fourth Crusade in 1198.
The original goal was Egypt.
The Venetian doge Enrico Dandolo strongly shaped its course.
In 1202 the crusaders conquered the city of Zara for Venice.
In 1204 they conquered Constantinople and founded the Latin Empire.
The Quadriga from Constantinople came to Venice.

abschnitte.text: Soon after his election Pope **Innocent III** called for a new crusade in **1198**. The goal was **Egypt**, the centre of power of the **Ayyubids**. From there people wanted later to win back Jerusalem. Many knights, above all from France, joined in. For the crossing they needed ships from **Venice**.

The **doge** of Venice, **Enrico Dandolo**, provided the fleet. A doge was the head of the Republic of Venice. Dandolo was already very old and almost blind, but he accompanied the army himself. The crusaders could not pay for the crossing. So in **1202** they conquered the Christian city of **Zara** on the Adriatic, present-day **Zadar**, for Venice. The pope excommunicated them for it.

A Byzantine prince promised the crusaders money and help if they would help him to the throne in **Constantinople**. So the army did not march to Egypt but there. The arrangements failed, and a quarrel broke out. In **1204** the crusaders conquered Constantinople and **plundered** the city. The pope had not wanted this conquest.

The crusaders founded the **Latin Empire** and chose **Baldwin of Flanders** as emperor. It lasted until **1261**. Many treasures came to Western Europe. The most famous piece of loot is the **Quadriga**, four ancient bronze horses from the Hippodrome of Constantinople. The originals now stand in the museum of **St Mark's** in Venice, and there are copies on the facade. The conquest deepened the gulf between the Western and the Eastern Church.

gewusst: Venice became even richer and more powerful in the Mediterranean through the Fourth Crusade.
The Quadriga of St Mark's is the only surviving ancient four-horse team made of bronze.

teile.einleitung: The Mongol invasion is the name given to the Mongol attacks on Eastern Europe in the 13th century. Their mounted armies advanced as far as Poland and Hungary and struck fear into the whole of Europe.
wichtigste: In 1223 the Mongols defeated an army of the Rus and Cumans at the Kalka.
From 1236 Batu Khan led the great campaign to the west.
Batu was a grandson of Genghis Khan.
Novgorod was spared in 1238.
In 1241 Poland and Hungary were attacked.
King Béla IV of Hungary fled as far as the Adriatic.

abschnitte.text: As early as **1223** a Mongol army appeared in the west. It was a **reconnaissance expedition** led by the generals **Subutai** and **Jebe**. At the **Kalka** they defeated an army of the **Rus** and the **Cumans**. After that the Mongols withdrew to the east for the time being.

From **1236** the great campaign began. It was led by **Batu Khan**, a grandson of **Genghis Khan**, together with Subutai. The campaign was directed against the **Volga Bulgars**, the principalities of the Rus, and later against **Poland** and **Hungary**. The Mongol riders were fast and well organised.

Many cities of the Rus were conquered. The rich trading city of **Novgorod** in the north was spared in **1238**. Because of the **thaw** and the **marshes**, the Mongols turned south again before reaching the city. Later, however, Novgorod recognised the overlordship of the Mongols and paid **tribute**, that is, regular payments.

In **1241** the Mongols also defeated the Hungarian army. King **Béla IV** barely escaped. He fled as far as **Dalmatia** on the Adriatic coast. After the Mongols withdrew, he had many **stone castles** built in Hungary. They were meant to protect the country better in case of a new attack.

gewusst: The Mongols never reached the area of present-day Switzerland.
After their withdrawal the Golden Horde remained a power in Eastern Europe for a long time.

teile.einleitung: Robin Hood is a famous hero from old English stories. He lives in the forest with his friends, takes money from the rich and gives it to the poor.
wichtigste: Robin Hood is a legendary figure from England.
He lives with his companions in Sherwood Forest near Nottingham.
He takes money from the rich and gives it to the poor.
He is an excellent archer.
His great opponent is the Sheriff of Nottingham.
His friends include Little John, Friar Tuck and Marian.

abschnitte.text: The stories of Robin Hood are set in **England**. The oldest known songs, so-called **ballads**, date from the late Middle Ages. Whether Robin Hood really existed, nobody knows for certain. He is probably an invented figure who grew together out of many tales. Over the centuries new adventures kept being added.

Robin Hood lives in **Sherwood Forest**, a large forest near the town of Nottingham. There he hides with his band, the **Merry Men**. His clothes are mostly **green**, so that he is well hidden in the forest. With **bow and arrow** he is more skilful than anyone else.

abschnitte.titel: From the rich to the poor
abschnitte.text: In the stories Robin Hood takes money from **the rich**, above all from unjust lords, and gives it to the poor. That is why he is regarded as a fighter for justice. His great enemy is the **Sheriff of Nottingham**, who plagues people with high payments. The sheriff tries again and again to catch Robin, but Robin is cleverer.

Robin’s best friend is **Little John**. The name is a joke, because Little John is in fact very big and strong. **Friar Tuck** is a fat, cheerful monk who can fight well. **Marian** is Robin’s sweetheart; she is often called “Lady Marian” or “Maid Marian”.

Robin Hood is still very popular today. There are many **books, films and series** about him. In a well-known Disney cartoon from 1973 Robin Hood is a clever fox. Children, too, like to play Robin Hood with homemade bows.

gewusst: In Sherwood Forest stands an ancient, huge oak, the “Major Oak”. According to legend Robin Hood hid in it.
Someone who takes from the rich today to give to the poor is sometimes called “a Robin Hood”.

teile.einleitung: The Wars of the Roses were struggles for the English crown in the 15th century. Two branches of the same royal family fought for decades over who was to rule.
wichtigste: The Wars of the Roses lasted from about 1455 to 1485.
The houses of Lancaster and York, two lines of the House of Plantagenet, fought.
The House of York is linked with a white rose, Lancaster with a red one.
Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick, became known as the “Kingmaker”.
King Richard III fell in 1485 at the Battle of Bosworth.
After that the Tudor dynasty took the throne.
Henry VII married Elizabeth of York and so united the houses.

abschnitte.titel: A quarrel in the royal family
abschnitte.text: The houses of **Lancaster** and **York** both belonged to the House of **Plantagenet**, which ruled England for a long time. Both descended from King Edward III and believed they had a right to the crown. When King Henry VI of the House of Lancaster ruled weakly, the quarrel broke out into the open. From about 1455 there were battles again and again.

The House of York had a **white rose** as its emblem, and the House of Lancaster is linked with a **red rose**. The name “Wars of the Roses” was only given to these conflicts by later writers. The poet William Shakespeare also wrote plays about this period. The wars were not one continuous battle but many individual fights with pauses in between.

**Richard Neville, Earl of Warwick**, was one of the most powerful nobles in England. He first helped the House of York and Edward IV to the throne. Later he changed sides and put Henry VI back on the throne as king. That is why he was called the **Kingmaker**. He fell in 1471 at the Battle of Barnet.

In 1485 King **Richard III** of the House of York and **Henry Tudor** met at **Bosworth**. Richard III fell in the battle. Henry Tudor became King of England as **Henry VII**. With him began the rule of the **Tudors**, to which Queen Elizabeth I later belonged.

Henry VII belonged to the Lancaster side. To end the quarrel he married **Elizabeth of York**, the daughter of Edward IV. In this way the two enemy houses were joined. As a sign of this the **Tudor rose** was created, which combines red and white petals. It is still a symbol of England today.

gewusst: The remains of Richard III were found under a car park in Leicester in 2012 and reburied in Leicester Cathedral in 2015.
The Tudor rose can still be seen today on some British coins and badges.

teile.einleitung: The Medieval Climate Anomaly was a time when some parts of the world were comparatively warm. It lasted roughly from 950 to 1250.
wichtigste: The warm phase lay roughly between 950 and 1250.
It was especially mild around the North Atlantic.
The warming was not equally strong everywhere, nor at the same time.
Around 985 Vikings under Erik the Red settled Greenland.
Longer growing seasons brought better harvests.

abschnitte.text: Between about **950 and 1250** it was comparatively warm around the **North Atlantic**. This is called the **Medieval Climate Anomaly**. In the past people also said “Medieval Warm Period”. The warming, however, was **different from region to region**. It was not warmer everywhere on Earth at the same time.

The milder temperatures brought **longer growing seasons**. This is the time of year when plants grow. Harvests became more reliable. Farming was also possible at higher altitudes. The population grew, new villages appeared and **towns** became bigger.

In this warm phase **Erik the Red** led settlers from Iceland to **south-west Greenland** around **985**. There they kept livestock and lived from hunting and fishing. When it turned cooler again in the Late Middle Ages, life became harder. In the **15th century** the settlements were abandoned.

gewusst: The warm phase was followed by the “Little Ice Age”, in which many Alpine glaciers also grew.

teile.einleitung: Runes are old characters of the Germanic peoples. They were carved into wood, metal, bone or stone. Especially well known are the Viking rune stones in Scandinavia.
wichtigste: Runes are old writing characters of Germanic peoples.
The row of runes is called the futhark, after its first characters.
The older row of runes had 24 characters.
In the Viking Age the row of runes had only 16 characters.
Runes consist almost only of straight lines so that they were easy to carve.
Large stones with inscriptions are called rune stones.
According to an old legend the god Odin found the runes.

abschnitte.text: Runes are the oldest writing characters of the **Germanic peoples**. They were used from about the 2nd century AD. Each character stood for a sound, like our letters. Each rune also had a name, for example for an animal or an object. They were used mainly for short texts, such as names or dedications.

The row of runes is called the **futhark**. The name is made up of the sounds of the first six characters: f, u, th, a, r and k. The **older futhark** had **24 characters**. In the Viking Age people used the **younger futhark** with only **16 characters**. As a result one character sometimes had to stand for several sounds.

Runes consist almost only of **straight lines**. Round shapes hardly occur. There is a good reason for this: the characters were **carved** into wood with a knife. Horizontal lines would hardly have been recognisable along the grain of the wood, so the lines mostly run vertically or diagonally.

Especially well known are the **rune stones**, above all in Sweden, Denmark and Norway. They often commemorate a dead person. A famous example stands in **Jelling** in Denmark. King **Harald Bluetooth** had it put up in the 10th century. It says that Harald won Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christians. The Jelling stones are today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In an old Norse **legend** the god **Odin** found the runes. He is said to have hung on a tree for nine nights until he recognised the characters. That is why runes were also seen as mysterious. With Christianity the Latin alphabet later took over. In Switzerland, too, a few objects with runes have been found, for example a clothes clasp from Bülach in the canton of Zurich.

gewusst: The symbol for the wireless technology “Bluetooth” is made up of the runes for H and B, the initials of Harald Bluetooth.
The name “Bluetooth” is the English translation of the Danish “Blåtand”.

teile.einleitung: **Vinland** was the name the Vikings gave to a land in the west that they reached around the year 1000. It lay in North America, about 500 years before Columbus came to America. Finds on the island of Newfoundland prove that they really were there.
wichtigste: Vikings reached North America around the year 1000.
Icelandic sagas tell of the voyages.
Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad found the settlement of L'Anse aux Meadows in 1960.
L'Anse aux Meadows lies on Newfoundland and is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
In the year 1021 Vikings demonstrably felled wood there.

abschnitte.text: We know of the voyages to Vinland from **Icelandic sagas**. These are old stories, above all the **“Saga of the Greenlanders”** and the **“Saga of Erik the Red”**. They were only written down about 200 years after the journeys. According to the sagas **Leif Eriksson** sailed west from Greenland and discovered new coasts. Later **Thorfinn Karlsefni** tried to found a lasting settlement with settlers, cattle and supplies. Because of quarrels with the local people they returned after a few years.

For a long time nobody knew whether the sagas were true. The Norwegian couple **Helge and Anne Stine Ingstad** searched deliberately for traces. In **1960** they found the remains of a Viking settlement at **L'Anse aux Meadows** on the island of **Newfoundland** in Canada. Anne Stine Ingstad afterwards led the excavations. They found the foundations of houses made of **turf**, a **smithy** and objects such as a bronze pin. Since **1978** the site has been a **UNESCO World Heritage Site**.

In **2021** researchers managed an exact dating. In pieces of wood from the settlement they found the trace of a **solar storm** from the year **993**. Such a storm leaves a mark in one of a tree's growth rings. By counting the **growth rings** out to the bark they arrived at the year **1021**. In this year Vikings on Newfoundland demonstrably felled wood with metal tools.

gewusst: Vinland probably means “wine land”, because the sagas tell of wild grapes.
L'Anse aux Meadows is the only securely proven Viking site in North America.

teile.einleitung: The 1968 movement is the name for the protest movements of young people at the end of the 1960s. Students in many countries questioned the state, society and authorities. In Switzerland, too, there was unrest in 1968.
wichtigste: A main cause of the protests was the Vietnam War.
The death of Benno Ohnesorg in Berlin on 2 June 1967 radicalised the student movement.
Rudi Dutschke was badly wounded in an assassination attempt in April 1968.
In France in May 1968 student protests joined with a general strike.
In Zurich the Globus riot took place in June 1968.
In West Germany the opposition outside the Bundestag called itself the APO.
Herbert Marcuse became one of the movement's leading thinkers.

abschnitte.text: In the late 1960s young people protested in many countries. A main cause was the **Vietnam War**. Television pictures of the war outraged many, and protests against the American conduct of the war linked movements on several continents. The young people also criticised rigid rules at universities, in families and in politics. Philosophers such as **Herbert Marcuse** of the Frankfurt School supplied ideas. In his book “One-Dimensional Man” he wrote in 1964 that consumer society suppresses critical thinking.

abschnitte.titel: The student movement in West Germany
abschnitte.text: In West Germany a **Grand Coalition** governed from 1966, and in the Bundestag there was hardly any opposition left. So the **extra-parliamentary opposition**, or **APO** for short, came into being. Among other things it fought against the **emergency laws** of 1968. On **2 June 1967** the student **Benno Ohnesorg** was shot dead by a policeman at a demonstration against the Shah of Persia. His death set off protests across the country. In April 1968 the spokesman **Rudi Dutschke** was badly wounded in an assassination attempt.

In France the protests began at the University of **Nanterre** and at the **Sorbonne** in Paris. In **May 1968** there were street fights with the police. Millions of workers went on **general strike**. The country stood still. President **Charles de Gaulle** dissolved parliament, but in the new elections his party won.

In Switzerland, too, young people took to the streets. In **Zurich** they demanded an **autonomous youth centre**. They wanted to use the empty **Globus Provisorium** for it. On **29 June 1968** there were serious clashes with the police, the **Globus riot**. The events set off discussions all over Switzerland about young people, the police and having a say.

abschnitte.titel: New ways of living and consequences
abschnitte.text: Some young people looked for new forms of living together. In West Berlin the **Kommune I** came into being in 1967, which attacked middle-class ways of life with provocative actions. The movement is still disputed today. Some see in it a breakthrough to more freedom and participation. Others criticise violence and radical groups that later came out of it. What is certain is that the 68ers strongly influenced society and politics in many countries.

gewusst: The year 1968 also brought the “Prague Spring”, in which more freedom was allowed in Czechoslovakia until Warsaw Pact troops marched in.
Many songs and posters from this time are still well known today.

teile.einleitung: The estates system was the idea of how society should be organised in the Middle Ages. People were divided into three estates: clergy, nobility and peasants. Which estate you belonged to was usually decided at birth.
wichtigste: According to medieval thinking there were three estates.
The clergy were to pray, the nobility to protect and fight, the peasants to work.
As a rule you became a member of an estate by birth.
The peasants made up the great majority of the population.
The peasant estate was also called the “nourishing estate” because it fed everyone.
In the Late Middle Ages the townspeople no longer fitted well into the threefold division.
The estates system was regarded as willed by God.

abschnitte.text: According to the old teaching each estate had a special task. The **clergy** prayed for all people. The **nobility** was to protect the land and fight. The **peasants** worked and in this way fed the whole of society.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the idea come from?
abschnitte.text: Around the year 1000 bishops such as Adalbero of Laon described society as divided into three. In Latin the groups were those who pray, those who fight and those who work. Later, in German, people spoke of the **teaching estate**, the defending estate and the **nourishing estate**. It was believed that God had willed this order.

The peasants made up the great majority, probably more than nine tenths of the people. Many were **serfs** and belonged to a landlord. They had to pay dues, for example the **tithe**, that is, a tenth of the harvest. In addition there were days of labour on the lord’s fields.

Nobles lived in castles and owned a lot of land. They served the king as knights and in return could demand dues from the peasants. The clergy, that is, priests, monks and nuns, did not have to pay taxes. High clergy such as bishops and abbots often came from the nobility themselves.

In the High and Late Middle Ages the towns grew. There lived craftsmen and merchants who were neither peasants nor nobles. These **citizens** became rich and self-confident and no longer fitted well into the old threefold division. In the Swiss Confederation citizens and peasants even governed without a prince.

abschnitte.titel: The end of the estates system
abschnitte.text: The estates system lasted in altered form long beyond the Middle Ages. Only the **French Revolution** of 1789 declared that all people have equal rights. In Switzerland the Helvetic Republic brought equality before the law from 1798. Today birth no longer decides which profession you take up.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of people with the same rights, duties and way of life.
Another name for the peasants, because they fed everyone.
A payment of a tenth of the harvest to the Church or the lord.
A noble or monastery that owned the land that peasants farmed.
People who work for the Church, such as priests, monks and nuns.

gewusst: A farmer’s son could move into the clerical estate by entering a monastery; this was one of the few ways to rise.
Clothing showed a person’s estate, and in some towns dress codes laid down exactly who was allowed to wear which fabrics.
The Swiss Confederation was special in the Middle Ages because there peasants and citizens governed without princes.

teile.einleitung: Many people think of helmets with horns when they think of Vikings. Real Viking helmets looked quite different, however. The best known is the Gjermundbu helmet from Norway.
wichtigste: Real Viking helmets had no horns.
The few helmets that have been found are made of iron.
They had a round cap on top.
Only a very few almost complete Viking helmets are known.
The Gjermundbu helmet was found in Norway in 1943.
It dates from the 10th century and is about a thousand years old.

abschnitte.text: In 1943 a grave with a helmet was found on the farm of **Gjermundbu** in Norway. The helmet dates from the **10th century** and is therefore about a thousand years old. It is the best-known Viking helmet of all. At the front it has a guard for the eyes and nose that looks a little like **spectacles**. Today it lies in a museum in Oslo.

Real Viking helmets were made of **iron**. Iron protected the head well from blows. The helmets had a **round cap** on top. That way sword blows slid off more easily. Iron was valuable then, so probably not all warriors had a metal helmet.

Of the Vikings we know many swords, axes and pieces of jewellery. But only **very few** almost complete helmets have been found. Usually only small **fragments** survive. Iron rusts in the ground over time. That is why well-preserved helmets are a great stroke of luck for research.

The picture of the Viking with a **horned helmet** only came into being in the 19th century. For the operas of **Richard Wagner** in 1876, costumes with horns and wings on the helmets were drawn. These pictures became very well known. Later books, films and comics took over the horns. In fights horns would rather have been a hindrance.

gewusst: Helmets with horns did exist, but much earlier: in Denmark horned helmets from the Bronze Age have been found that are about 3,000 years old.
The Gjermundbu helmet was found in many fragments and put back together.

teile.einleitung: Bertha Benz was the wife of the car inventor Carl Benz. In 1888 she made the first longer car journey in the world with the motor car and showed everyone that the car really works.
wichtigste: Bertha Benz was married to Carl Benz and supported him with money and courage.
In August 1888 she secretly set off with the motor car.
Her two sons Eugen and Richard accompanied her.
She drove from Mannheim to her home town of Pforzheim.
The outward journey was about 106 kilometres long.
She bought petrol at a chemist's shop in Wiesloch.

abschnitte.text: **Bertha Benz** was born in 1849 in **Pforzheim**. She married **Carl Benz** and believed firmly in his inventions. With her money she helped to pay for his workshop. But many people thought the motor car a loud, unsafe toy. Hardly anyone wanted to buy it.

In **August 1888** Bertha Benz secretly set off early in the morning. Her husband Carl knew nothing about it. With her were her two sons **Eugen** and **Richard**. The destination was **Pforzheim**, where her mother lived. The outward journey was about **106 kilometres** long. For a car of that time this was an enormous trip.

There were no **filling stations** then. When the fuel ran short, Bertha Benz bought it at the town chemist's in **Wiesloch**. There it was sold as a cleaning agent. That is why this chemist's shop is called the first filling station in the world today. Water to cool the engine the three fetched along the way from streams and inns.

On the way Bertha Benz repaired many things herself. A blocked **fuel line** she cleaned with her long **hatpin**. When the brakes weakened, she had a cobbler fit **leather** to the brake blocks. That made the car brake better. That is why she is regarded as the inventor of the **brake lining**. On steep hills the sons had to push.

In the evening the three arrived in Pforzheim and sent Carl a telegram. The journey showed that the motor car can also manage long distances. Bertha also brought her husband ideas for improvement, for example an extra gear for slopes. Today the **Bertha Benz Memorial Route** recalls her journey.

gewusst: The town chemist's in Wiesloch is regarded as the first filling station in the world.
Her son Eugen was only 15 years old on the journey.

teile.einleitung: In the 1880s the German Empire under Chancellor Otto von Bismarck introduced the first state social insurance schemes in the world. They protected workers in case of illness, accident and in old age. These laws are called Bismarck's social legislation.
wichtigste: The Imperial Message of 1881 announced the social insurance schemes.
Health insurance came in 1883, accident insurance in 1884.
In 1889 followed disability and old-age insurance, and the pension was first paid from the age of 70.
With the Anti-Socialist Law of 1878 Bismarck at the same time suppressed the Social Democrats.
People therefore speak of “carrot and stick”.
In Switzerland the AHV came into force in 1948.

abschnitte.text: With **industrialisation** more and more people worked in factories. Anyone who fell ill, had an accident or was too old to work earned nothing any more. Many families fell into great hardship in this way. The workers joined together and supported **social democracy**, which demanded better conditions.

Chancellor **Otto von Bismarck** saw the Social Democrats as a danger to the state. In 1878 he had the **Anti-Socialist Law** passed. It banned Social Democratic associations and newspapers, and this was the “**stick**”. At the same time he wanted to win the workers over to the state with **social insurance**, and this was the “**carrot**”. The **Imperial Message** of Emperor William I announced these insurance schemes in November 1881.

In 1883 came **health insurance**. The workers paid two thirds of the contributions, the employers one third. In 1884 followed **accident insurance**, which the employers alone paid for. In return they hardly had to be liable themselves for accidents at work. In 1889 came **disability and old-age insurance**. An old-age pension was first paid from the age of 70, which only a few reached. In 1916 the limit was lowered to 65 years.

Switzerland went its own way. As early as 1877 the Federal **Factory Act** limited working time in factories to 11 hours a day. It also banned factory work for children under 14. In 1918 **Suva** began its work, the accident insurance for many workers. The **AHV**, the old-age and survivors' insurance, was accepted by the people in 1947 and came into force on 1 January 1948.

gewusst: Germany was the first country in the world with state health, accident and pension insurance.
The constitutional article for the AHV was accepted in Switzerland as early as 1925, and the law only came more than 20 years later.

teile.einleitung: Absolutism is the name for a form of government in which one ruler governs alone and without control. It shaped Europe above all in the 17th and 18th centuries. The most famous example is the French king Louis XIV, the “Sun King”.
wichtigste: In absolutism one ruler governs alone and without control.
The word comes from the Latin “legibus absolutus”, released from the laws.
Absolute kings justified their power by the divine right of kings.
They kept a standing army that existed even in peacetime.
With mercantilism they wanted to export more goods than they imported.
In France the Estates General were not summoned from 1614 to 1789.
In enlightened absolutism rulers carried out reforms based on ideas of the Enlightenment.
In England the Bill of Rights limited the king's power in 1689.

abschnitte.text: In **absolutism** the ruler has all the power in the state. He makes the laws, is the highest judge and leads the army. The word comes from the Latin expression **legibus absolutus**, which means “released from the laws”. No parliament and no court could control the king.

**Louis XIV** ruled France from 1643 to 1715, longer than any other French king. He called himself the Sun King because everything was to revolve around him like the planets around the sun. He had the magnificent **Palace of Versailles** built, where the nobility had to live at court. The sentence “I am the state” is attributed to him.

Absolute kings said that their power came directly from God, which is called the **divine right of kings**. In France there were three estates: the clergy, the nobility and the third estate, to which citizens and peasants belonged. The assembly of the estates, the **Estates General**, was not summoned from 1614 to 1789. Only its summoning in 1789 led to the French Revolution.

The kings kept a **standing army**, that is, an army that existed even in peacetime. This cost a great deal of money. With **mercantilism** they wanted to export more goods than they imported so that money flowed into the country. For this they promoted **manufactories**, large businesses with division of labour in which work was still mostly done by hand.

In the 18th century the ideas of the **Enlightenment** spread. Some rulers now carried out reforms, but still governed alone. **Frederick II of Prussia** called himself the “first servant of the state” and, for example, largely abolished torture. Emperor Joseph II in Austria is also regarded as an enlightened ruler.

The English thinker **Thomas Hobbes** defended a very strong state in 1651 in his book “Leviathan”. England, however, went another way: the **Bill of Rights** of 1689 strengthened Parliament against the king. The Swiss Confederacy had no king, but in towns such as Bern a few rich families, the patricians, governed. Many Swiss served as mercenaries and as guards of the French kings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of government in which one ruler governs alone and without control.
The idea that a king has received his power from God.
An economic policy meant to bring as much money as possible into one's own country.
A large business with division of labour, but mostly still with handwork.
An army that exists even in times of peace.

gewusst: The Lion Monument in Lucerne recalls Swiss guards who died for the French king in 1792 during the storming of the Tuileries in Paris.
Louis XIV became king at the age of four.
In the Palace of Versailles there is a famous Hall of Mirrors with 357 mirrors.

teile.einleitung: In the **Treaty of Verdun** in 843, three brothers divided the great Frankish Empire among themselves. They were grandsons of Charlemagne. From the parts, France and Germany later developed.
wichtigste: In 843 at Verdun the sons of Louis the Pious divided the Frankish Empire.
Lothair I received the Middle Kingdom and the title of emperor.
Louis the German received the East Frankish Kingdom.
Charles the Bald received the West Frankish Kingdom, from which France developed.
In 842 Louis and Charles swore the Oaths of Strasbourg to each other.
Lorraine is named after Lothair II.

abschnitte.text: Emperor **Louis the Pious** was a son of Charlemagne. As early as **817** he laid down in the **Ordinatio imperii** how things should go on after his death. His eldest son **Lothair** was to be chief heir and co-emperor, and the younger brothers were to be subordinate to him. Later this led to quarrels. After the death of Louis in **840**, his sons **Lothair**, **Louis** and **Charles** fought over the inheritance.

In **841** Louis and Charles defeated their brother Lothair at the **Battle of Fontenoy**. The battle was very costly in lives. In **842** the two allied themselves at **Strasbourg** with an oath, the **Oaths of Strasbourg**. Each king swore in the language of his brother's army, in **Old French** and **Old High German**, so that the soldiers understood him. The text is regarded as the oldest evidence of the French language.

In **843** the brothers agreed at **Verdun**. **Louis the German** received the **East Frankish Kingdom** east of the Rhine. From it the Holy Roman Empire later developed. **Charles the Bald** received the **West Frankish Kingdom**, from which **France** later became. **Lothair I** received the **Middle Kingdom** and the title of emperor. His realm stretched from the North Sea through the Rhône valley to Italy.

After Lothair's death the Middle Kingdom was divided among his sons. The northern part was inherited by **Lothair II**. The region of **Lorraine**, the “realm of Lothair”, is named after him. When Lothair II died, his uncles divided his territory between the East and West Franks in **870** in the **Treaty of Meerssen**. In this way the Middle Kingdom gradually disappeared.

gewusst: France and Germany were still quarrelling over Lorraine more than a thousand years later.
Charles the Bald and Louis the German are nicknames that were only given to them later.
